fromJSONSchema ignores additionalProperties:false when patternProperties is present
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

`fromJSONSchema` accepts object properties that match neither `properties` nor `patternProperties` when the source JSON Schema sets `additionalProperties: false`, as long as `patternProperties` is present. This makes the generated Zod schema more permissive than the source JSON Schema.

## Code path

- `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/from-json-schema.ts`: the `patternProperties` branch builds loose records and returns from that branch.
- `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/from-json-schema.ts`: the later `additionalProperties === false` handling is only reached when the earlier `patternProperties` branch is not taken.

## Steps to reproduce

Checked against `912f0f51b0ced654d0069741e7160834dca742ee`.

```ts
import { fromJSONSchema } from "zod/v4";

const schema = fromJSONSchema({
  type: "object",
  patternProperties: {
    "^S_": { type: "string" },
  },
  additionalProperties: false,
});

console.log(schema.safeParse({ S_name: "ok" }).success);
console.log(schema.safeParse({ X_A: false }).success);
```

Actual output:

```txt
true
true
```

## Expected behavior

The second parse should fail. `X_A` does not match `^S_`, so it is an additional property. With `additionalProperties: false`, JSON Schema rejects properties that match neither `properties` nor `patternProperties`.

Expected output:

```txt
true
false
```

## Actual behavior

The generated Zod schema accepts `{ X_A: false }`.

## Existing coverage

I found related but not equivalent coverage:

- #5449 covered adding general `patternProperties` support.
- #5702 covers an `allOf` + `additionalProperties: false` interaction.

I did not find an issue or PR covering the `patternProperties` + `additionalProperties: false` interaction above.

## Suggested fix

Apply `additionalProperties` after accounting for keys matched by `properties` and `patternProperties`, instead of returning from the `patternProperties` branch before the `additionalProperties` logic runs.

## Suggested tests

- `fromJSONSchema({ type: "object", patternProperties: { "^S_": { type: "string" } }, additionalProperties: false })` accepts `{ S_name: "ok" }`.
- The same schema rejects `{ X_A: false }`.
- A matching pattern key with the wrong value type, such as `{ S_name: 1 }`, still fails.

---
Submitted with Codex.

problems.title: fromJSONSchema requires prefixItems tuple elements when minItems is omitted
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

`fromJSONSchema` converts JSON Schema tuple-style array schemas into Zod required tuples. As a result, arrays shorter than the number of positional schemas are rejected even when the JSON Schema does not set `minItems`.

In JSON Schema, `prefixItems` / draft-7 array-form `items` constrain the elements that are present. They do not make every positional schema required unless `minItems` says so.

## Code path

- `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/from-json-schema.ts`: `prefixItems` is mapped to `z.tuple(...)`.
- `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/from-json-schema.ts`: draft-7 array-form `items` is also mapped to `z.tuple(...)`.
- `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/tests/from-json-schema.test.ts`: the current `prefixItems` test expects a shorter array to throw, which appears stricter than JSON Schema semantics.

## Steps to reproduce

Checked against `912f0f51b0ced654d0069741e7160834dca742ee`.

### Draft 2020-12 `prefixItems`

```ts
import { fromJSONSchema } from "zod/v4";

const schema = fromJSONSchema({
  $schema: "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  type: "array",
  prefixItems: [{ type: "string" }],
});

console.log(schema.safeParse([]).success);
console.log(schema.safeParse(["ok"]).success);
```

Actual output:

```txt
false
true
```

Expected output:

```txt
true
true
```

### Draft-7 array-form `items`

```ts
import { fromJSONSchema } from "zod/v4";

const schema = fromJSONSchema({
  $schema: "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  type: "array",
  items: [{ type: "string" }],
  additionalItems: false,
});

console.log(schema.safeParse([]).success);
console.log(schema.safeParse(["ok"]).success);
console.log(schema.safeParse(["ok", "extra"]).success);
```

Actual output:

```txt
false
true
false
```

Expected output:

```txt
true
true
false
```

## Expected behavior

Without `minItems`, shorter arrays should be valid as long as every present positional item satisfies its schema.

For example:

- `prefixItems: [{ type: "string" }]` should accept `[]` and `["ok"]`.
- draft-7 `items: [{ type: "string" }], additionalItems: false` should accept `[]` and `["ok"]`, but reject `["ok", "extra"]`.

## Actual behavior

The generated Zod schema rejects `[]` because `z.tuple([z.string()])` requires the first tuple element to be present.

## Existing coverage

Related open PRs exist, but they appear to cover the trailing/rest side rather than the shorter-array side:

- #6020 fixes open-by-default tuple rest behavior for omitted `items` / `additionalItems`.
- #6023 fixes boolean `true` rest behavior for `items: true` / `additionalItems: true`.

Both directions are related, but adding `.rest(...)` to `z.tuple([z.string()])` still leaves the first tuple element required, so arrays shorter than the prefix length remain rejected unless the fix also changes required-prefix handling.

#6193 / #6194 are about `toJSONSchema()` emitting length constraints for closed Zod tuples, which is the opposite conversion direction.

problems.title: treeifyError throws TypeError when an issue path contains a key inherited from Object.prototype (e.g. toString)
problems.issue_body:
`treeifyError` throws a `TypeError` whenever a validation issue's `path` contains a segment whose name matches a property inherited from `Object.prototype` (for example `toString`, `valueOf`, `constructor`, or `hasOwnProperty`).

Minimal reproduction:

```
import zod, { treeifyError } from 'zod';

const schema = zod.object({ toString: zod.string() });
const result = schema.safeParse({}); // success: false

if (!result.success) {
    treeifyError(result.error); // throws TypeError
}
```

The parse correctly fails: `{}.toString` resolves to the inherited `Object.prototype.toString` function, so the `toString` field is reported as `invalid_type (expected string, received function)` with `path: ["toString"]`. That part is expected. The bug is that `treeifyError` then throws while building the tree:

```
node_modules/zod/v4/core/errors.js:113
                        curr.errors.push(mapper(issue));
                                    ^
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'push')
    at processError (node_modules/zod/v4/core/errors.js:113:37)
    at treeifyError (node_modules/zod/v4/core/errors.js:120:5)
```

Root cause:

`treeifyError` builds the tree using a plain object as a dictionary:

```
curr.properties ?? (curr.properties = {});
(_a = curr.properties)[el] ?? (_a[el] = { errors: [] });
curr = curr.properties[el];
```

When the path segment `el` is an `Object.prototype` key, `curr.properties[el]` returns the inherited member (e.g. the `toString` function) instead of `undefined`. The `??` short-circuits, so the node is never created, and `curr` is assigned the inherited function which has no `errors` array. The following `curr.errors.push(...)` then throws.
A null-prototype object (`Object.create(null)`) or a `Map` for `properties`, or an `Object.hasOwn` guard, would fix it.

Environment:
zod: 4.4.3
Node.js: v24.15.0

fromJSONSchema date-time rejects valid RFC 3339 offsets
problems.issue_body:
`fromJSONSchema({ type: "string", format: "date-time" })` currently maps to `z.iso.datetime()` and rejects valid RFC 3339 timestamps with numeric UTC offsets.

```ts
const schema = z.fromJSONSchema({ type: "string", format: "date-time" });

schema.parse("2026-07-29T14:30:00Z"); // accepted
schema.parse("2026-07-29T16:30:00+02:00"); // rejected
```

JSON Schema defines `date-time` using RFC 3339, where both `Z` and numeric offsets are valid. A local timestamp without an offset should remain invalid.

The mapping can preserve that behavior by using `z.iso.datetime({ offset: true })`. Authored JSON Schema constraints such as `pattern` should continue to compose with the format check.

fix(v4): skip __proto__ key in object catchall
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

In `handleCatchall()`, an unrecognized `__proto__` key in the input is currently assigned directly to a fresh `{}` result object via `(final.value)[key] = result.value`. Because that goes through the `__proto__` setter on a plain object, the assignment **replaces the prototype of the parsed result**, giving the validated object attacker-controlled inherited properties. `Object.prototype` itself is not affected.

PoC on `4.3.6`:

```ts
const schema = z.looseObject({ name: z.string() });
const input = JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"isAdmin":true},"name":"alice"}');
const parsed = schema.parse(input);
parsed.isAdmin // true  ← inherited from injected prototype
```

Same shape reproduces with `passthrough()` and `catchall(...)`, sync/async, and `{ jitless: true }` (the JIT fastpass falls through to the same `handleCatchall` for unknown keys).

## Fix

One-line guard in the catchall loop:

```ts
for (const key in input) {
  if (key === "__proto__") continue;
  ...
}
```

Mirrors the existing `__proto__` skip in `$ZodRecord` (`schemas.ts:2867`) and the v3 object-assembly guard at `parseUtil.ts:144`. Deliberately conservative — `for..in` iteration of input is preserved, so behavior for any input *other than* one with a `__proto__` own key is unchanged. Inherited prototype-chain enumeration (the separate concern in GHSA-9hmj-h52h-mxcf) is not addressed here; that's a narrower attack model and a noisier behavior change worth handling separately.

Reported in:

- GHSA-r34p-xfmx-58wv (critical)
- GHSA-84jv-fqfx-wxhr

## Test plan

- [x] 5 new tests in `object.test.ts` covering `looseObject` / `passthrough` / `catchall(unknown)` / `safeParseAsync` + `{ jitless: true }` / `strict()`, asserting `Object.getPrototypeOf(parsed) === Object.prototype` and that the injected key is not visible on the result.
- [x] `pnpm vitest run` — 3753 passed across 333 files, no regressions.

problems.title: fix(v4): formatError and treeifyError no longer throw on inherited-name path elements (__proto__, constructor, ...)
problems.issue_body:
Closes #6211

### Problem

`z.formatError()` and `z.treeifyError()` throw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'push')` when an issue path element is a name inherited from `Object.prototype` (`__proto__`, `constructor`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`). Reachable via a custom issue path from `.check()` / `.superRefine()`, or any flow that puts user-controlled keys into an issue path. Verified on published 4.4.3: all 5 names throw in both functions. For `__proto__`, plain bracket assignment additionally hits the prototype setter instead of creating an own key.

### Fix

In both tree builders, replace the truthy / nullish node-existence checks with an own-property guard, and create nodes with `Object.defineProperty` (enumerable, writable, configurable, so behavior is unchanged for normal keys):

- `formatError`: `curr[el] = curr[el] || { _errors: [] }` saw the inherited member as truthy, never created the node, then crashed on `._errors.push`.
- `treeifyError`: `curr.properties[el] ??= { errors: [] }` saw the inherited member as non-nullish, same failure.

`defineProperty` also makes `__proto__` a real own data property, so no prototype is mutated.

### Tests

Added a regression test in `error-utils.test.ts` covering `__proto__`, `constructor`, `toString`, and `hasOwnProperty` against both functions, plus a no-pollution assertion. `error-utils.test.ts` passes 36/36 and `error.test.ts` 54/54, with no type errors.

### Scope

2 files, ~50 lines: `packages/zod/src/v4/core/errors.ts` and `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/tests/error-utils.test.ts`.

### Relation to existing PRs

#6083, #6139, and #6181 address the `formatError` half of this. This PR covers `treeifyError` as well, which fails identically (see the issue for the executed repro matrix). Credit to those authors for prior art on the `formatError` side.

toJSONSchema(schemaRegistry, opts) is very slow with a large registry
problems.issue_body:
As I add more types to a schema registry, calling `toJSONSchema` on that registry gets very slow, growing much faster than the growth in the size of the registry.

In a private repo I have, a registry with only about 3000 types in it takes 30 seconds to process on a MacBook M3.

I've collected some perf dumps, and the problem might be coming from one or both of these places:

### Finalize iteration

`finalize` is called on every schema, but for each schema it goes through all of the refs and checks each one:

https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/blob/main/packages/zod/src/v4/core/to-json-schema.ts#L449

A lot of that ends up being noop, as everything only needs to be procesesd once.  But it's still building all of those new arrays for iteration and revisiting every member of `ctx.seen` many times over.

When I hack my copy of zod to only run this loop once per context, the schema generation time for my example goes down from about 30s to about 18s.

### Nested parent computation

When a schema has a parent, registry get walks the chain recursively to get ancestor data:

https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/blob/main/packages/zod/src/v4/core/registries.ts#L65

This data can be recomputed many times as registry get is called many times, even though no registry data is written during the process.

When I add a subclass of $ZodRegistry that can cache the results of these get calls, the schema generation time for my example goes down from about 30s to about 20s.

problems.title: fromJSONSchema: propertyNames with enum is treated as required keys
problems.issue_body:
### Summary

`z.fromJSONSchema()` converts an object schema that constrains its keys with
`propertyNames: { enum: [...] }` into a Zod schema where each enum value becomes a
**required** property. `propertyNames` restricts which key *names are allowed*; it
does not make any key *required*. As a result, a valid object that contains only a
subset of the allowed keys is incorrectly rejected.

### Zod version

`zod@4.4.3` (Node 20)

### Reproduction

```js
import { z } from "zod";

const schema = {
  type: "object",
  propertyNames: { enum: ["a", "b"] },
  additionalProperties: { type: "string" },
};

const zodSchema = z.fromJSONSchema(schema);

// `{ a: "x" }` is valid against the JSON Schema (an allowed key, string value),
// but Zod rejects it:
zodSchema.parse({ a: "x" });
// ✖ ZodError: [{ path: ["b"], code: "invalid_type",
//     message: "Invalid input: expected string, received undefined" }]
```

### What's happening

Round-tripping the converted schema back through `z.toJSONSchema()` shows the enum
property names were turned into `required`:

```jsonc
{
  "type": "object",
  "propertyNames": { "type": "string", "enum": ["a", "b"] },
  "additionalProperties": { "type": "string" },
  "required": ["a", "b"]   // ← injected; not present in the source schema
}
```

### Expected

- `{ a: "x" }` and `{ b: "y" }` should pass (as should `{}`, unless `minProperties`
  or an explicit `required` say otherwise).
- Only keys *not* in `["a", "b"]` should fail (via `propertyNames`).
- No property should be required unless it appears in the schema's own `required`.

### Notes

This looks like the object-keyword sibling of #6200 (`fromJSONSchema` requiring
`prefixItems` tuple elements when `minItems` is omitted) — both over-require
members that the source schema leaves optional.

problems.issue_body:
This is more of a feature request than a bug. Currently `string().max()` (and other length validators) count the UTF-16 length of a string rather than the number of unicode characters. The latter can be calculated using `[...value].length` where `value` is the desired string, so a custom transformer can work, but this would probably benefit most users of this library seeing as the length people usually care about in validation is the number of unicode characters (also called Unicode Scalars), not the UTF-16 length.

We could either option this out, e.g. `.max(5, {char: true})`, or use a separate method, e.g. `.charMax(5)`.

problems.title: z.url(), z.ipv6() and z.cidrv6() accept ASCII tab/newline because the URL parser deletes them
problems.issue_body:
`z.url()`, `z.httpUrl()`, `z.ipv6()` and `z.cidrv6()` all validate by calling `new URL()` and treating "didn't throw" as valid. Step 2 of the WHATWG basic URL parser **deletes** every ASCII tab, LF and CR from the input before parsing — it flags a validation error but recovers rather than failing — so `new URL()` succeeds on strings containing them and reports on a string that isn't the one it was given.

On 4.4.3:

```ts
z.ipv6().parse("::1\n");                    // "::1\n"     — net.isIPv6() says false
z.cidrv6().parse("::1\n/64");               // "::1\n/64"
z.url().parse("https://exa\nmple.com");     // "https://exa\nmple.com"
z.httpUrl().parse("https://exa\nmple.com"); // "https://exa\nmple.com"
```

The host case is the sharp one: `new URL("https://exa\nmple.com").host` is `example.com`, so the string Zod validated and the string Zod returned are URLs pointing at different hosts.

Tab, LF and CR are the only characters with this property. I enumerated all 32 C0 controls at host, path, query, fragment, leading and trailing positions: every other one is either percent-encoded (`https://example.com/pa%00th`) or rejected, and U+0009/U+000A/U+000D are the only three that can be injected into the **host** and still validate.

It also breaks a self-consistency invariant — `regexes.ipv6` is still emitted as the `pattern` by `toJSONSchema()`, and it rejects these:

```ts
new RegExp(z.toJSONSchema(z.ipv6()).pattern).test("::1\n"); // false
z.ipv6().safeParse("::1\n").success;                        // true
```

I scanned every code point 0x0000–0x10FFFF inserted into `::1` and `::1/64`: `z.ipv6()` disagrees with `net.isIPv6` on exactly those three characters and nothing else.

`isValidBase64` already handles the identical hazard one section down — "atob ignores whitespace, so reject it up front" — so the shape of the fix is settled by precedent: scan for `[\t\n\r]` ahead of each `new URL()` call. Happy to open a PR.

problems.title: [E2.3.3] Durable JetStream consumers + explicit ack + redelivery handling
problems.issue_body:
## Context
Task 2.3 created durable JetStream **streams** for the safety-critical subjects (`proposal.new` / `decision.*` / `code.proposal`) - landed in #55. The **consumer** side is only partially in place: there is not yet an explicit durable consumer with a defined ack policy and redelivery handling, so a consumer that crashes mid-processing may not get safe at-least-once redelivery, and there is no defined path for poison messages.

## Goal
Durable consumers for the safety-critical streams with **explicit ack** (ack-on-success, nak/term on failure), bounded redelivery with backoff, and a defined poison-message path - so a critical message is processed where it must be and is never silently dropped on a consumer crash.

## Scope (checklist)
- [ ] Define durable consumer(s) per critical stream (ack policy = explicit, ack-wait, max-deliver).
- [ ] Wire consumers into the SDK `EventBus` / `nats_client.py` so safety subscribers ack explicitly on success.
- [ ] Nak/term on handler failure with bounded redelivery + backoff; route exhausted deliveries to a poison/DLQ path (seed for P5 DLQ work).
- [ ] Ensure idempotent processing across redelivery (ties to E2.3.5 dedup keys).
- [ ] Tests: a consumer that crashes before ack receives redelivery; a handler that fails `max-deliver` times is terminated to the poison path; a successful handler acks exactly once.

## Out of scope
Stream creation (E2.3.2, landed #55); dedup/idempotency-key design (E2.3.5); retention/ops runbook (E2.3.6).

## Acceptance criteria
- A consumer killed mid-processing redelivers and the message is not lost.
- A repeatedly-failing message stops redelivering after `max-deliver` and lands on the poison path (not infinite redelivery, not silent drop).
- Successful processing acks exactly once; covered by integration tests in the Governance CI job.

## Affected files / areas
`sdk/.../nats_client.py`, kernel / safety-supervisor subscribers, `sdk/tests/` (next to `test_jetstream.py` / `test_jetstream_durability.py`).

## Dependencies
Blocked-by E2.3.2 (#55, landed). Pairs with E2.3.5 (dedup). Milestone M2.

## Skills & effort
NATS JetStream consumers / ack semantics, pytest. Effort **M**. Maintainer review required (safety).

## Definition of Done
Consumer/ack/redelivery tests green in CI; poison-message path documented; no invariant weakened; reviewed & merged to `dev`.

problems.title: [E1.9.2] Post-deploy health-check + auto-rollback on failure
problems.issue_body:
## Context
Atomic deploy + rollback and DEFER-expiry landed (#38), and the human-approval consumer is filed (E1.9.1, #69). But a deploy that passes the sandbox can still break the running system; there is no post-deploy health check that automatically restores the prior artifact on failure.

## Goal
After a deploy, the meta-programmer runs a health probe; on failure it auto-rolls-back to the prior artifact (using the existing atomic-deploy machinery) and records a fail-closed result.

## Scope (checklist)
- [ ] Define a post-deploy health probe (service comes up, key subjects respond, no crash within a window).
- [ ] On probe failure: restore the previously-deployed artifact atomically; publish a rollback/gap result.
- [ ] On probe success: confirm/commit the deploy.
- [ ] Distinguish "deploy bad -> rolled back" from "deploy ok" in logs/metrics.
- [ ] Tests: a deliberately-broken artifact is deployed, fails the probe, and is rolled back to the working prior version.

## Out of scope
The human-approval consumer (E1.9.1, #69); watchdog-driven SAFE_HALT (E1.9.3); dashboard countdown (E1.9.5).

## Acceptance criteria
- A deploy that fails its health probe is automatically rolled back; the prior working artifact is restored; a fail-closed result is published.
- A healthy deploy is committed.

## Affected files / areas
`meta-programmer/.../service.py`, deploy/rollback machinery, `meta-programmer/tests/`.

## Dependencies
Builds on #38 (atomic deploy + rollback). Relates to E1.9.1 (#69). Milestone M1.

## Skills & effort
Python async, health-probe design, fail-closed reasoning. Effort **M**. Maintainer review required (safety).

## Definition of Done
Auto-rollback test green in CI; documented in the meta-programmer README; no invariant weakened; reviewed & merged to `dev`.

problems.title: [E1.9.3] Kernel-loss watchdog -> system SAFE_HALT (heartbeat timeout)
problems.issue_body:
## Context
SAFE_HALT exists at the Kernel (#38) but is only triggered by an explicit `safety.halt`. If the **Kernel itself dies**, nothing detects its absence and the system can keep acting without the gate - the opposite of fail-closed. A watchdog must SAFE_HALT the system when the Kernel's heartbeat stops.

## Goal
A watchdog (in the launcher/supervisor) that monitors the Kernel heartbeat and, on a heartbeat timeout, drives the system into SAFE_HALT so no proposal can be acted on without the gate.

## Scope (checklist)
- [ ] Define/confirm a Kernel heartbeat (subject or liveness signal) and a timeout budget.
- [ ] Watchdog in `launcher/` (or supervisor) that detects heartbeat loss.
- [ ] On timeout: publish `safety.halt` (or invoke SAFE_HALT) so downstream defaults to DENY; record the cause.
- [ ] Recovery: when the Kernel returns healthy, require explicit operator resume (`safety.resume`), not auto-resume.
- [ ] Tests: kill the Kernel -> system SAFE_HALTs within the timeout; restart -> stays halted until resume.

## Out of scope
Safety-Supervisor-loss watchdog (E1.9.4); the SAFE_HALT UI button (E1.9.6, #70); halt/resume audit trail (E1.9.7).

## Acceptance criteria
- With the Kernel killed, the system enters SAFE_HALT within the timeout and proposals default to DENY.
- Resume is operator-gated, never automatic.

## Affected files / areas
`launcher/`, supervisor, kernel heartbeat emit site, `launcher/tests/`.

## Dependencies
Builds on #38 (SAFE_HALT). Pairs with E1.9.4. Relates to E1.9.6 (#70). Milestone M1.

## Skills & effort
Python async, supervision/watchdog, fail-closed reasoning. Effort **M**. Maintainer review required (safety).

## Definition of Done
Watchdog SAFE_HALT test green in CI; fail-closed-on-Kernel-loss documented; no invariant weakened; reviewed & merged to `dev`.

problems.title: [E1.1.4] Subject-permission allowlist for the safety services (Kernel = sole decision.*/policy.* publisher)
problems.issue_body:
## Context
The NATS account/permission model (E1.1.1, #64) and per-service credentials (E1.1.2, #94) establish identities; this issue applies the least-privilege subject allowlist to the **safety** services (kernel, safety-supervisor, beliefs, overrides). The load-bearing rule: **only the Kernel** may publish `decision.*`, `code.decision.*`, `policy.*`, and `cognitive.response.validated`. Today a shared token lets any process publish these (the #1 transport bypass).

## Goal
Per-service publish/subscribe allowlists for the four safety services in the enforced NATS authz config, deny-by-default, with the Kernel as the sole publisher of the privileged decision/policy subjects.

## Scope (checklist)
- [ ] From the E1.1.1 subject x service matrix, encode the publish/subscribe allowlist for kernel, safety-supervisor, beliefs, overrides in `deploy/nats-*.conf`.
- [ ] Kernel: sole publisher of `decision.*`, `code.decision.*`, `policy.*`, `cognitive.response.validated`; subscribe set per matrix.
- [ ] safety-supervisor / beliefs / overrides: least-privilege publish/subscribe only (advisory risk, belief queries, human-presence) - no decision/policy publish rights.
- [ ] Deny-by-default: any subject not listed is rejected.
- [ ] Dev-mode fallback preserved (single account) mirroring the `ENGRAM_DECISION_KEY` fail-safe-by-config pattern.
- [ ] Verify against a repo-wide subject grep - no safety service relies on a denied subject.

## Out of scope
The brain/sensory allowlist (E1.1.3); support-services allowlist (E1.1.5); dashboard/operator publisher (E1.1.6); the red-team regression that proves rejection (E1.1.9, #95).

## Acceptance criteria
- With enforced authz, safety-supervisor/beliefs/overrides identities are broker-rejected when publishing `decision.*`/`policy.*`; the Kernel identity succeeds.
- No safety service loses a subject it legitimately needs (validated against the matrix + grep).

## Affected files / areas
`deploy/nats-1m.conf`, `deploy/nats-*.conf`, kernel/safety-supervisor/beliefs/overrides `service.py` connect sites.

## Dependencies
Blocked-by E1.1.1 (#64), E1.1.2 (#94). Pairs with E1.1.3 / E1.1.5. Proven by E1.1.9 (#95). Milestone M1.

## Skills & effort
NATS account/permission config, security architecture. Effort **M**. Maintainer review required (safety).

## Definition of Done
Allowlist enforced; matrix/grep validation green; dev fallback intact; no invariant weakened; reviewed & merged to `dev`.

problems.title: [Bug]: Kernel emits no decision (fails open) when a code proposal hits an internal error — unlike the action path which
problems.issue_body:
### Component

kernel / safety-supervisor (safety layer)

### Description

`KernelService._handle_code_proposal()` swallows internal errors: on any
exception it logs and returns **without publishing a decision**. The Kernel is
documented as "the sole authority that may emit a decision" and must "fail safe
(DENY) on internal error" (CLAUDE.md §3). The sibling `_handle_action_proposal()`
implements exactly that — on exception it publishes a fail-safe DENY
(`risk_score=1.0`) "so the caller's Future doesn't hang." The code-proposal path
does **not**, so an internal error in the self-modifying-code gate produces
**no decision at all** instead of a fail-closed DENY.

#### Root cause (code)

`kernel/src/kernel/service.py`, `_handle_code_proposal`:

```python
        except Exception as e:
            self.logger.error(f"Error handling code proposal: {e}")
```

Compare `_handle_action_proposal` in the same file:

```python
        except Exception as e:
            self.logger.error(f"Error handling action proposal: {e}")
            # Always publish a decision so the caller's Future doesn't hang.
            # Fail-safe: DENY on internal errors.
            try:
                deny = KernelDecision(
                    trace_id=trace_id, type=DecisionType.DENY,
                    reason=f"Kernel internal error: {e}", risk_score=1.0,
                )
                await self._publish_and_log_decision(trace_id, proposal_type, source, deny)
                self._deny_count += 1
            except Exception:
                pass  # best-effort — caller will timeout
```

The action handler emits a fail-safe DENY; the code handler emits nothing.

#### Why it matters

The Meta-Programmer publishes `code.proposal` and waits for a decision on
`code_decision_subject(trace_id)`. If `_get_risk_analysis`,
`evaluate_code_proposal`, `_log_decision`, or the publish raises, the Kernel
emits no decision on that subject. The self-modifying-code path is the most
safety-sensitive one in the system (the Meta-Programmer may "only deploy code
the Kernel approved"), yet here the Kernel — by its own documented contract the
sole decision authority that must fail closed — stays silent on internal error.
The end state then depends entirely on the consumer's timeout behavior rather
than on the Kernel affirmatively denying, and it is asymmetric with the action
path that already does the right thing.

### Steps to Reproduce

Drive the handler with an evaluator that raises (mirrors an internal error), via
a fake event bus:

```python
import asyncio, logging
from activelearning import KernelDecisionType as DecisionType
from activelearning.subjects import code_decision_subject
from kernel.service import KernelService

class FakeBus:
    def __init__(self): self.published = []
    async def publish(self, subject, payload): self.published.append((subject, payload))

svc = KernelService.__new__(KernelService)        # bypass __init__ (no NATS/DB)
svc.logger = logging.getLogger("t"); sv…

problems.title: [Bug]: Meta-Programmer source scanner misses `from os import system` — dangerous-sink calls bypass the deploy gate (fail
problems.issue_body:
### Component

coordinator / meta-programmer / beliefs

### Description

`meta_programmer.safety.scan_source` is the defence-in-depth AST taint scan that
blocks LLM-generated code containing dangerous sinks (`os.system`, `subprocess`,
sockets, `ctypes`, …) before it is written to disk and hot-loaded. It only
detects a dangerous module call in **attribute form** (`os.system(...)`). A call
to a name pulled in via `from <module> import <sink>` — e.g.

```python
from os import system
system("rm -rf /")
```

reaches the `ast.Name` branch, which only checks `_DANGEROUS_BUILTINS` /
`_REFLECTION_BUILTINS`. `"system"` is in neither, and the `ImportFrom` only
produces a **medium** `dangerous_import` finding. Since `is_dangerous()` (and the
deploy gate in `service.py`) block **only high-severity** findings, the code is
classified **not dangerous** and proceeds to staging → Kernel (which sees only a
500-char preview) → sandbox → deploy/hot-load. This is a fail-open in the safety
layer: an arbitrary-command-execution sink the scanner exists to block sails
through.

#### Root cause (code)

`meta-programmer/src/meta_programmer/safety.py`, `scan_source`:

```python
        if isinstance(node, ast.Call):
            fn = node.func
            if isinstance(fn, ast.Name):
                if fn.id in _DANGEROUS_BUILTINS:
                    findings.append(Finding("high", "dangerous_builtin", f"{fn.id}()"))
                elif fn.id in _REFLECTION_BUILTINS:
                    ...
            elif isinstance(fn, ast.Attribute) and isinstance(fn.value, ast.Name):
                mod, attr = fn.value.id, fn.attr        # <-- only attribute form (os.system)
                allowed = _DANGEROUS_MODULES.get(mod, "MISS")
                if allowed != "MISS" and (allowed is None or attr in allowed):
                    findings.append(Finding("high", "dangerous_call", f"{mod}.{attr}()"))
        ...
        elif isinstance(node, ast.ImportFrom):
            ...
            if top in _DANGEROUS_MODULES:
                findings.append(Finding("medium", "dangerous_import", ...))   # medium only
```

```python
def is_dangerous(code: str) -> bool:
    return any(f.severity == "high" for f in scan_source(code))
```

A bare-`Name` call to a `from`-imported sink is never matched, and the import
itself is only medium — so nothing high fires.

### Steps to Reproduce

```python
# from meta-programmer/src:
from meta_programmer.safety import is_dangerous

print(is_dangerous("import os\nos.system('rm -rf /')"))        # control
print(is_dangerous("from os import system\nsystem('rm -rf /')"))
print(is_dangerous("from subprocess import run\nrun(['ls'])"))
print(is_dangerous("from os import popen as p\np('id')"))
print(is_dangerous("from os import *\nsystem('id')"))
```

### Expected Behavior

All of these contain a dangerous sink and must be flagged (blocked):

```
True     # import os / os.system(...)
True     # from os import system / system(...)
True     # from subprocess import run…

problems.title: [Bug]: Cache tag invalidation never removes entries, so stale LLM responses survive deploys and overrides
problems.issue_body:
### Component

neuromorphic (spiking neural network core)

### Description

**Component:** cache (and the shared SDK SQLite schema)

The cache invalidator subscribes to `code.deployed`, `override.applied.*`, and `task.saved`, and each handler calls into a routine that is meant to drop the related cached responses. That routine is empty, so the events log a line and remove nothing. Cached LLM responses keep being served long after the change that should have retired them, until the slow age based sweep would eventually catch them up to seven days later.

Two gaps cause the symptom:

1. Cached entries are never tagged, so there is nothing for an event to match against.
2. The lookup that should find entries by tag is a placeholder that returns without touching the cache.

A third problem sits underneath. The SQLite mirror writes to columns that the shared schema does not define (`model`, `cached_at`) and omits a `NOT NULL` column, so every mirror write raises and is swallowed. Because the hourly age based cleanup reads that same table (and queries a column that does not exist), it also never runs. In practice the cache has no working eviction at all.


### Steps to Reproduce

1. Start the core profile with the cache and autopilot enabled.
2. Cache an LLM response, then publish `code.deployed` (or `override.applied.*`, or `task.saved`).
3. Query the same prompt again.


### Expected Behavior

The response that was generated against the old code is evicted, and the next query is a miss that fetches a fresh answer.


### Actual Behavior

```shell
The cached response is still served. The event evicts nothing, and the age based fallback never fires either, so the entry can stay live and wrong for days.
```

### Environment

- Component: cache, sdk
- Run mode: `python run.py` (core profile) and Docker Compose
- Reproducible every time, on every platform


### Pre-submission checks

- [x] I searched existing issues and this is not a duplicate.
- [x] I am running the latest `main` (or I have stated my version/commit).

problems.title: M6: End-to-end test coverage for sandbox "fail-closed deploy" (E1.3.2)
problems.issue_body:
## Context
`docs/SANDBOX-THREAT-MODEL.md` references a "fail-closed deploy" guarantee (refuse to run if the image is missing or the runtime is unavailable) and notes *"the broader fail-closed guarantees land in E1.3.2."* This needs end-to-end test coverage, not just the narrow deploy-refusal case, before meta-programmer autonomy can safely expand.

## Proposal
Extend the sandbox containment test suite (building on the existing `feat/kernel-loss-watchdog-safe-halt` and sandbox-containment-integration work already merged) to cover fail-closed behavior across all failure modes described in the threat model doc, not just missing-image.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Threat-model doc's fail-closed claims enumerated as explicit test cases
- [ ] Integration tests added for each failure mode (runtime unavailable, resource exhaustion, network denial, etc.)
- [ ] `docs/SANDBOX-THREAT-MODEL.md` updated to mark E1.3.2 as covered

problems.title: M6: Track Kernel ALLOW/TRANSFORM/DENY rates as a meta-programmer quality signal
problems.issue_body:
## Context
The Kernel (`kernel/`) is the sole authority emitting ALLOW/TRANSFORM/DENY/DEFER decisions on meta-programmer code proposals. There's currently no longitudinal tracking of these decision rates, which would be an early-warning signal for drift in generated-code quality or risk as the meta-programmer is used more.

## Proposal
Add a lightweight metric/benchmark (paralleling the M3 "Learning Evidence" panel) that records Kernel decision outcomes over time for meta-programmer proposals specifically, and surface it on the dashboard.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Decision outcomes logged/aggregated (reuse existing Kernel decision persistence where possible)
- [ ] Trend visible via dashboard or a report script
- [ ] Documented as a signal maintainers should watch before expanding autonomy (ties into the M6 gating issue)

problems.title: M5: Extend MuJoCo motor feedback to a real-actuator adapter
problems.issue_body:
## Context
`neuromorphic/tests/test_mujoco_motor_feedback.py` and `test_motor_feedback.py` cover the virtual-body (MuJoCo) motor loop. README notes real-actuator support is "partial or planned." There is currently no path from a sim-trained motor policy to physical hardware.

## Proposal
Define a common `ActuatorPlugin` interface (mirroring the SDK's `SensorPlugin`) and implement a real-actuator adapter (e.g. servo/motor controller over serial or a common robotics bus) behind it, so the existing motor-feedback loop can drive physical actuators without changing the neuromorphic core.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `ActuatorPlugin` interface defined (likely in `sdk/`)
- [ ] MuJoCo path refactored to implement this interface (no behavior change)
- [ ] At least one real-actuator adapter implementing the same interface
- [ ] Test coverage with a mocked actuator

problems.title: M5: Add a depth-camera sensor driver for cross-modal binding
problems.issue_body:
## Context
Same Known Limitations gap as the IMU driver issue. A depth stream (e.g. stereo/RealSense-style) alongside the existing camera pipeline would give the cross-modal binding work in M3 a richer, more realistic input to bind (Invariant 4).

## Proposal
Add a depth-camera driver under `sensory-gateway/sensors/`, feeding depth data through `encoding.py` alongside the existing RGB camera pipeline so binding can correlate depth with visual/audio input.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] New driver under `sensory-gateway/sensors/` following the existing plugin interface
- [ ] Depth data encoded to spikes and time-aligned with the existing camera pipeline for binding
- [ ] Unit test with a mocked depth source
- [ ] Documented in `docs/SENSORY-GATEWAY.md`

problems.title: M5: Add an IMU sensor driver under sensory-gateway/sensors/
problems.issue_body:
## Context
README's Known Limitations: *"IMU / depth / real-actuator support is partial or planned."* `sensory-gateway/sensors/` already has the plugin pattern for camera/microphone/serial devices.

## Proposal
Add an IMU driver following the existing sensor-plugin pattern, encoding orientation/acceleration readings to spikes via `neuromorphic/src/neuromorphic/encoding.py`, and register it with the sensor-discovery mechanism.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] New driver under `sensory-gateway/sensors/` implementing the existing `SensorPlugin` interface (see `sdk/`)
- [ ] Orientation/acceleration encoded to spike trains via `encoding.py`
- [ ] Discoverable through the existing sensor-discovery flow (graceful no-op if hardware absent)
- [ ] Unit test with a mocked IMU device

problems.title: M6: Gate meta-programmer autonomy on M1 (Safety Real) completion
problems.issue_body:
## Context
`CLAUDE.md` §3 is explicit: *"the decision bus is not yet authenticated/signed, and the sandbox is being made fail-closed. Until that lands, do not build new autonomy on top of the gate."* This issue exists to make that gate a **hard, automated dependency** rather than a documentation-only rule, so M6 work can't accidentally ship ahead of M1.

## Proposal
Add an explicit runtime/CI check in `meta-programmer/` that refuses to expand deploy scope or autonomy level for code proposals unless decision-bus signing (M1 Task 1.2) and sandbox fail-closed (M1, tracked via `docs/SANDBOX-THREAT-MODEL.md` E1.3.2) are both confirmed complete (e.g. via a capability flag or M1 milestone-closed check).

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] A single source of truth (e.g. a capability/version flag) records M1's signing + fail-closed status
- [ ] `meta-programmer/` refuses higher-autonomy proposals when that flag is unset
- [ ] Fails closed (deny) if the check itself errors, consistent with the Kernel's existing fail-safe behavior
- [ ] Requires maintainer review per `CLAUDE.md` §3 rule 3 (safety-critical area)

problems.title: M3: Turn test_concept_probe.py into a scored concept-separability benchmark
problems.issue_body:
## Context
`neuromorphic/tests/test_concept_probe.py` currently checks concept-probe behavior as pass/fail unit tests. README's "Known Limitations" says: *"large-scale, quantitative evidence that the system learns useful abstractions is still a work in progress."*

## Proposal
Extend the concept-probe machinery into a scored benchmark (not just assertions): define a quantitative separability/clustering metric for learned representations, run it across multiple training runs/seeds, and record results under `neuromorphic/benchmarks/` alongside the existing `benchmark_*.json` outputs.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] A metric (e.g. silhouette score or linear-probe accuracy) is computed from concept-probe activations
- [ ] `scripts/benchmark_report.py` (or a new script) can report the metric trend across runs
- [ ] Documented in `docs/` with the metric's definition and how to interpret it
- [ ] Existing `test_concept_probe.py` assertions still pass

problems.title: M4: Investigate a GPU backend (CuPy/JAX) for CSR sparse synapse operations
problems.issue_body:
## Context
`CLAUDE.md` §6 mandates CSR sparse matrices, `float32` throughout, and vectorized hot paths. README lists GPU/compiled kernels or neuromorphic hardware as the path to real-time performance at scale.

## Proposal
Spike a GPU-backed variant of the CSR synapse operations in `neuromorphic/src/neuromorphic/synapses.py` (CuPy or JAX), with automatic fallback to the current NumPy/SciPy path when no GPU is present, so this doesn't raise the baseline hardware requirement for `python run.py` local dev.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Spike branch demonstrates correctness parity with CPU path on existing tests
- [ ] Measured speedup at a representative neuron count
- [ ] Fallback path verified to work with no GPU (default dev experience unaffected)
- [ ] Write-up of feasibility/tradeoffs (new dependency weight, portability) for maintainer review

problems.title: M4: Prototype a compiled kernel for the STDP + eligibility-trace update path
problems.issue_body:
## Context
Invariant 1 (`CLAUDE.md` §2) requires STDP and eligibility traces to remain mathematically equivalent to per-step updates even when batched via "compensated decay," and any change here **must be covered by an equivalence test**. This is one of the likely top bottlenecks per the profiling issue in this milestone.

## Proposal
Prototype a compiled implementation (Numba, Cython, or JAX — pick based on the profiling ADR's recommendation) of the STDP + eligibility-trace update in `neuromorphic/src/neuromorphic/synapses.py`, behind a feature flag, with a fallback to the existing NumPy path.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Compiled path produces bit-for-bit or tolerance-bounded equivalent output to the existing path
- [ ] New equivalence test added per Invariant 1's enforcement note
- [ ] Measured speedup reported
- [ ] Falls back cleanly when the compiled dependency is unavailable

problems.title: M3: Cross-modal binding accuracy benchmark
problems.issue_body:
## Context
Invariant 4 requires cross-modal binding via temporal correlation (`neuromorphic/src/neuromorphic/instincts.py`, `encoding.py`, `network.py`), covered functionally by `test_cross_modal_probe.py`. There's currently no quantitative measure of *how accurate* the binding is.

## Proposal
Define a binding-accuracy metric (precision/recall of correctly bound modality pairs against known ground-truth correlated stimuli) and add it as a benchmark, following the pattern of `neuromorphic/src/neuromorphic/benchmarks.py`.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Ground-truth correlated-stimulus test fixtures (e.g. synchronized audio/visual pulses)
- [ ] Precision/recall (or equivalent) metric computed and logged to `neuromorphic/benchmarks/`
- [ ] Regression threshold enforced in CI (fails if binding accuracy drops significantly)

problems.title: feat(coordinator): implement IMU sensor detection via serial port probing
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

`sensor_manager.py` defines `SensorType.IMU` and calls `_detect_imu()` at startup, but the method is a stub that always returns `False`. M5 already ships a JSON-over-serial IMU driver in `sensory-gateway/sensors/imu.py`; the coordinator should discover compatible USB IMUs so learning tasks can include proprioceptive observations.

## Proposed behavior

- Probe available serial ports (pyserial, optional dependency — same pattern as camera/microphone detection)

- Skip gracefully when pyserial is absent or no IMU hardware is connected

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `_detect_imu()` registers at least one `SensorInfo` when a compatible serial IMU is present (mocked in tests)
- [ ] Detection is a no-op (no crash) when pyserial is missing or ports are empty
- [ ] Unit tests cover successful detection, absent hardware, and malformed port data

## Context

Closes the coordinator side of partial hardware integration noted in project docs. Complements merged sensory-gateway IMU support (#136).

problems.title: feat(external-api): semantic similarity for knowledge conflict detection
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

`ExternalAPIManager._detect_conflict()` uses crude word-overlap heuristics and flags a conflict when fewer than 30% of words match. This produces false positives for paraphrased answers that agree semantically but share little vocabulary.

## Proposed behavior

- Add cosine-similarity conflict detection using the shared embedding service when available
- Fall back to the existing word-overlap heuristic when embeddings are unavailable or return zero vectors
- Expose pure helpers in a small `conflict_detection` module for unit testing without network access

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Paraphrased local/external descriptions with high embedding similarity are **not** flagged as conflicts
- [ ] Contradictory descriptions with low embedding similarity **are** flagged as conflicts
- [ ] Word-overlap fallback preserved when no embedding service is configured
- [ ] Unit tests cover semantic path (mocked embeddings) and fallback path

## Context

Replaces the TODO in `external-api/src/external_api/manager.py` to use semantic similarity instead of word overlap only.

problems.title: feat(sdk): batch embedding API with Ollama /api/embed fallback
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

`EmbeddingService.embed_batch()` currently loops sequentially over `embed_text()`, issuing one HTTP request per uncached string. Ollama's `/api/embed` endpoint accepts multiple inputs in a single call, which reduces latency for memory recall, task lookup, and cache warming.

## Proposed behavior

- Resolve cache hits first and preserve input order in the returned vectors
- Batch-fetch uncached texts via `/api/embed` when possible
- Fall back to sequential `embed_text()` when the batch endpoint fails or returns invalid payloads
- Do not cache zero-vector failure sentinels

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `embed_batch([])` returns `[]`
- [ ] Cached texts avoid extra HTTP calls
- [ ] Uncached texts are requested in one `/api/embed` call when the backend succeeds
- [ ] Sequential fallback preserves order and existing validation rules
- [ ] Unit tests mock HTTP and cover cache hits, batch success, and batch fallback

## Context

Replaces the TODO in `sdk/src/activelearning/embeddings.py` for real batching instead of sequential-only processing.

problems.title: [M1.9] SAFE_HALT resume accepts any unverified operator_id — no identity check
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Verified: `kernel/src/kernel/service.py`'s `_handle_safety_resume` reads `operator_id` as an unchecked free-form string (`data.get("operator_id", "unknown")`) and immediately calls `self._evaluator.resume()`. There is no authentication or authorization check on who is allowed to resume from SAFE_HALT.

**Why:** SAFE_HALT is the system's emergency-stop mechanism (#70). Anyone able to publish to `Subjects.SAFETY_RESUME` can resume the system just by including any string as `operator_id` — this defeats the purpose of a human-in-the-loop safety control.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Add real operator-identity verification to the resume path (e.g. signed/authenticated operator tokens, not a free-text field)
- [ ] Add a regression test proving an unauthenticated resume attempt is rejected

problems.title: [M1.5] Extend sandbox containment tests to cover disk-quota exhaustion
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** `meta-programmer/tests/test_sandbox_containment_integration.py` covers exactly 5 containment properties: network isolation, read-only-FS, pids limit, memory limit, privilege-escalation prevention. **Verified: there is no disk-quota test, and no disk-quota enforcement anywhere in `sandbox_manager.py`.**

**Why:** A sandboxed process could fill disk (e.g. writing an unbounded log or temp file) without being contained by any existing guard.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Add disk-quota enforcement to the sandbox container config (`sandbox_manager.py`)
- [ ] Add a containment integration test proving a disk-filling payload is capped, following the existing "baseline vs. guarded" pattern

problems.title: [M1.8] Add belief-graph confidence-floor mutation audit logging
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Every attempt to lower a constitutional VALUE's confidence floor should be logged as an auditable event, not just silently rejected (current behavior per #67's non-lowerable floor).

**Why:** A rejected attempt to weaken a constitutional safety value is itself security-relevant signal — right now that signal isn't captured anywhere queryable.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Add an audit-log write whenever a confidence-floor-lowering attempt is rejected in `beliefs/src/beliefs/graph.py`
- [ ] Make the audit trail queryable (dashboard or direct DB query)

problems.title: [M1.7] Kernel decisions are not checked for expiry at accept time — replay-attack gap
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Verified: `sdk/src/activelearning/nats_client.py`'s decision-waiter calls `verify_decision(data)` (HMAC signature check only) and accepts the decision immediately on success. `expires_at` is a signed field (`sdk/src/activelearning/signing.py`), and `core.py`'s `Decision` dataclass has an `is_expired` property — but nothing invokes it at the accept path. A captured, still-validly-signed old ALLOW could in principle be replayed.

**Why:** This is a live gap in the "unforgeable gate," not a documentation task — the signed expiry field exists but isn't enforced.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Add an expiry check (`current_timestamp() > expires_at` → reject) at the decision-accept path in `nats_client.py`
- [ ] Add a regression test proving an expired-but-validly-signed decision is rejected
- [ ] Document the replay-resistance model once fixed

problems.title: [M1.12] Beliefs graph fails open (not closed) on SQLite corruption at boot
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Verified: `beliefs/src/beliefs/service.py`'s `_load_from_db` wraps the entire node/edge load in a bare `except Exception: log warning, continue`, then falls straight through to `seed_constitutional_beliefs()` on the next line — corruption gets silently treated as "first boot" and constitutional VALUEs get reseeded from hardcoded defaults rather than halting.

**Why:** This directly contradicts CLAUDE.md §3's fail-closed rule ("if a check cannot run, deny/halt — never degrade open"). This is the highest-priority item in the whole M1 Phase 2 list.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Distinguish "empty DB, legitimate first boot" from "DB present but corrupted/unreadable" in `_load_from_db`
- [ ] On corruption, halt/deny rather than silently reseeding
- [ ] Add a regression test that corrupts the belief store and asserts fail-closed behavior

problems.title: [M1.20] Add a governance-suite smoke test against a real (not mocked) NATS broker
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Verified: the `governance` job's two largest test steps ("Kernel + Meta-Programmer + Coordinator + Dashboard + Safety-Supervisor tests" and "...+ Beliefs safety tests" in `.github/workflows/test.yml`) run without a real broker — their own inline comments confirm modules are loaded directly and dependencies are mocked/injected. Only the separate red-team suite (#95) uses a real `nats-server`.

**Why:** Unit-level mocking can hide integration-shape bugs (e.g. the `EventBus.subscribe()` 4-positional-arg bug found in PR #194's review — a real broker wouldn't have hidden that the second handler never registers, but a mocked one might).

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Add one end-to-end governance smoke test that runs the Kernel + at least one dependent service against a real `nats-server`
- [ ] Confirm it would have caught the `POLICY_RESTRICT_REQUEST` subscribe bug as a concrete validation of the test's value

problems.title: [M1.11] Pentest the meta-programmer's sandbox escape surface with a red-team payload corpus
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Build a library of known Python sandbox-escape techniques (e.g. `__subclasses__`/`__globals__` chains, ctypes/pickle tricks, resource-exhaustion probes) and run them against the hardened sandbox container.

**Why:** `test_sandbox_containment_integration.py` proves specific guards (network, FS, pids, memory, privilege) hold — a payload corpus tests the container's overall resilience against known escape *techniques*, not just individual guard properties in isolation.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Assemble a corpus of known Python sandbox-escape techniques
- [ ] Run each against the current hardened container; document pass/fail
- [ ] File follow-up issues for any technique that succeeds

problems.title: [M1.13] No tested key-rotation runbook for decision-bus signing
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Task 1.2 added HMAC decision-bus signing (`ENGRAM_DECISION_KEY`, `sdk/src/activelearning/signing.py`). No rotation runbook exists anywhere; the key is referenced only in ADR/architecture docs, not operationally.

**Why:** A signing key with no rotation procedure is a long-lived secret by default — if it's ever compromised, there's no documented, tested path to rotate it without an outage or a window of forged-decision risk.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Document a key-rotation procedure (e.g. dual-key overlap window)
- [ ] Add an end-to-end test exercising rotation without dropping in-flight decisions

problems.title: [M1.14] Add rate-limiting to the Kernel's code-proposal intake path
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** No current cap on how fast `code.proposal` messages are accepted for evaluation.

**Why:** A misbehaving (or compromised) meta-programmer could flood the Kernel with proposals, degrading its ability to service legitimate traffic — this is a resource-exhaustion angle on the safety gate itself.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Add a rate limit on `code.proposal` intake per source
- [ ] Define the fail mode when the limit is hit (deny vs. defer vs. drop) — should be fail-closed, not silently dropped

problems.title: [M1.15] Audit remaining bare except Exception: pass in kernel/ for silent fail-open
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Grep-driven audit. PR #122 already found and fixed several fail-open bugs of this shape this session. Verified two remain: `kernel/src/kernel/service.py:637` and `:706`, both `except Exception: pass  # best-effort — caller will timeout`, in the DENY-publish path.

**Why:** These two look defensible on inspection — the DENY decision is already made before the try block, and the comment claims the caller times out and treats a missing response as closed — but that reasoning isn't verified or tested anywhere, and "looks defensible on inspection" is exactly how the PR #122 bugs looked before they were checked. `safety-supervisor/` had no matches for this grep pattern.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Confirm (with a test, not just reading) that a caller genuinely fails closed if these two publishes silently fail
- [ ] Either add an explanatory comment citing that test, or fix if the fail-closed assumption doesn't hold
- [ ] Re-run the grep audit periodically as new code lands (this class of bug has recurred multiple times this session)

problems.title: feat(cache): wire autopilot live LLM fallback via SDK LLMClient
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

`AutopilotController.query_llm()` falls back to a hardcoded placeholder (`"Live LLM response (not implemented)"`) on cache miss. The cache service should call Ollama through the shared SDK `LLMClient`, matching meta-programmer and external-api patterns.

## Proposed behavior

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Cache miss returns the LLM-generated text, not a placeholder
- [ ] Cache hits never invoke the live LLM client
- [ ] `LLMClient` is injectable for unit tests (mocked, no network)
- [ ] Unit tests cover live-call path, cache-hit skip, and disabled autopilot behavior

## Context

Closes the TODO in `cache/src/cache/autopilot.py` and completes the load-bearing autopilot stub referenced in issue #45.

problems.title: feat(coordinator): add GPS serial detection to SensorManager
problems.issue_body:
## Problem

`SensorManager.detect_sensors()` stops after camera, microphone, and IMU. `SensorType.GPS` is defined with a priority weight, but no runtime detection exists — knowledge-gap payloads and learning flows cannot discover GPS hardware.

## Proposed solution

Coordinator lane only — mirrors the IMU detection added in #171.

problems.title: [M2.33] Add structured logging for EventBus connection-lifecycle events

problems.title: [M2.20] Add EventBus metrics (publish/subscribe counts, latency) to the dashboard
