problems.title: fix(sdk): reject expired decisions at accept time — replay-attack gap…
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

`EventBus.wait_for_decision()`'s JetStream handler (`sdk/src/activelearning/nats_client.py`) called `verify_decision(data)` (HMAC signature check only) and accepted the decision immediately on success.

`expires_at` is one of the signed fields (`sdk/src/activelearning/signing.py`), and `core.py`'s `KernelDecision` has an `is_expired()` method — but nothing invoked it at the accept path.
A captured, still-validly-signed old `ALLOW` could in principle be replayed past its intended TTL.
Closes #190.

- Added an expiry check right after signature verification in `wait_for_decision`'s `_js_handler`: a decision whose `expires_at` has passed is rejected the same way a bad signature is — logged, acked (removed from the stream, since it will never become valid), and ignored, so the caller keeps waiting and ultimately times out (fails closed) instead of silently accepting stale authorization.
  A decision with no `expires_at` never expires, matching `is_expired()`'s own semantics.
- Documented the replay-resistance model in `signing.py`'s module docstring (the acceptance criteria's "document once fixed" ask): a valid signature proves a decision was issued by the Kernel at *some* point, not that it's still current.
  Expiry enforcement at accept time is what closes that gap.
- Fixed a pre-existing test that this change made newly (and correctly) fail: `test_base_service_migration.py::test_decision_wait_accepts_signed_decision` used a fixed dummy `expires_at=9999999` (1970-01-01 in Unix ms) — harmless before this fix since nothing checked it, but now correctly rejected as expired.
  Swapped for a real `current_timestamp()`-relative future value.
- Added `test_wait_for_decision_rejects_expired_signed_decision` (the required regression test) plus a companion `test_wait_for_decision_accepts_signed_decision_before_expiry` to `sdk/tests/test_nats_client.py`, matching the file's existing signed/unsigned decision test pattern (real embedded `nats-server`, not mocked).

## Type of change

- [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue)
- [ ] New feature (non-breaking change that adds functionality)
- [ ] Breaking change (fix or feature that changes existing behavior)
- [ ] Documentation only
- [ ] Refactor / tooling / CI

## Component(s) affected

sdk

## How was this tested?

```
cd sdk && uv run --extra dev python -m pytest tests/test_nats_client.py -v
# → 11 passed, including the two new expiry tests

cd sdk && uv run --extra dev python -m pytest tests/ -v
# → 225 passed (full SDK suite — confirms the one pre-existing test this
#   change legitimately broke is fixed, and nothing else regressed)

cd sdk && uv run --extra dev python -m pytest tests/red_team/ -v
# → 12 passed (Kernel-exclusivity guarantee unaffected — orthogonal to
#   expiry, this only touches the decision-accept path)

uvx ruff check --select E9,F63,F7,F82 sdk/src/activelearning/nats_client.py sdk/tests/test_nats_client.py sdk/tests/tes…

problems.title: [M2.4] Formalize a message-schema versioning policy for NATS subjects
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Verified: `WireModel` (`sdk/src/activelearning/messages.py`) has no `version` field at all — nothing to build a compatibility policy on top of yet.

**Why:** As payloads evolve, there's no way to distinguish an old-shape message from a new one at the wire level.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Add a `version` field to `WireModel`
- [ ] Document a compatibility policy for evolving payloads

problems.title: [M2.10] Formalize the EventBus request-reply timeout policy across all services
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Verified at least 3 different hardcoded timeout values in `nats_client.py` alone (`5.0`, `10.0`, plus a caller-supplied param with no shared default) — ad hoc per call site.

**Why:** Inconsistent timeouts make failure behavior unpredictable across services.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Centralize default request-reply timeouts
- [ ] Document the policy and override mechanism

problems.title: [M2.27] Make launcher/supervisor.py's restart-backoff constants configurable
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Verified: `_BACKOFF_INITIAL`, `_BACKOFF_MAX`, `_BACKOFF_RESET` are hardcoded module constants in `launcher/supervisor.py`.

**Why:** An operator tuning restart behavior for a specific deployment (e.g. a flakier cloud host) can't do so without a code change.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Expose backoff constants via env vars with current values as defaults

problems.title: [M2.40] Add a chaos test for KernelWatchdog losing its own NATS connection
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** `launcher/watchdog.py`'s `KernelWatchdog` (E1.9.3) exists to catch Kernel loss via heartbeat — untested is what happens if the watchdog itself loses its NATS connection.

**Why:** A watchdog that silently goes blind on its own disconnect defeats its purpose — this has direct safety-domain consequences since SAFE_HALT depends on this watchdog working.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Add a chaos test disconnecting the watchdog's own NATS connection
- [ ] Verify it fails toward SAFE_HALT (safe), not silent inaction (unsafe)

problems.title: [M2.37] Verify BaseService.stop()'s shutdown ordering can't strand a half-processed message
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Shutdown ordering is unsubscribe -> bus-close -> custom `_cleanup()`; unverified whether a kill mid-shutdown can leave a message acked-but-not-fully-handled (or handled-but-not-acked).

**Why:** A message stranded mid-processing during shutdown could be silently lost or double-processed on restart.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Add a test killing the process mid-shutdown during message handling
- [ ] Confirm no message loss or duplicate processing

problems.title: [M3.8] Add statistical significance testing (multiple seeds) to the benchmark suite
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Current benchmarks run once per invocation; add a --seeds N mode with confidence intervals. `BenchmarkSuite.run_all(seed=42)` and `CrossModalBindingAccuracyBenchmark.run(seed=seed)` both hardcode or default to a single seed per invocation, and there is no multi-run averaging anywhere in `benchmarks.py`. Beyond the CLI flag itself, this likely requires deciding how confidence intervals get reported — per-metric percentile bands in the JSON output, or a simpler mean±stddev — and how `benchmark_ci_gate.py` should consume that, since a regression against a mean is different from a regression against a single run. This is foundational enough that items #20, #37, and #44 all either depend on or overlap with it.

**Why:** A single-seed score can't distinguish "the network learned this" from "this particular initialization got lucky" — this is the single biggest gap between the current suite and a defensible quantitative claim.

**Source:** Proposed in `NewRoadMap.md`, milestone M3 (Validated Intelligence), item #8. This is a vetted-for-relevance backlog item (GitHub issue/PR counts re-fetched live; not independently re-derived line-by-line against the code the way the M1 items were) — treat as a starting point to investigate, not a pre-confirmed finding.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Add a `--seeds N` flag to the `python -m neuromorphic.benchmarks` CLI that reruns the suite N times with distinct seeds
- [ ] Report mean ± confidence interval per metric in `summary()`'s output

problems.title: [M2.39] Add a schema-migration path for unified.db
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Verified: `grep -c "ALTER TABLE" schema.sql` returns 0. Every table uses `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`, so an already-deployed database with an outdated column set never picks up a schema change added later.

**Why:** Same class of risk as this session's SQLite-scaling discussion, but about schema drift rather than row growth — a deployed instance can silently diverge from the current schema forever.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Add a migration mechanism (e.g. versioned ALTER TABLE scripts run on startup)
- [ ] Add a regression test proving an old-schema DB gets migrated correctly

problems.title: [M2.29] Audit _is_safety_critical()'s hardcoded subject-prefix allowlist for completeness
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** `_is_safety_critical()` is a fixed check against `PROPOSAL_NEW`/`CODE_PROPOSAL` plus two prefixes.

**Why:** A newly-added safety-relevant subject could be added elsewhere in the codebase without also being added here, making it silently non-persistent.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Audit all current safety-relevant subjects against this allowlist
- [ ] Add a process/check to keep it in sync as new subjects are added

problems.title: [M1.17] Formalize and test the DEFER to human-review TTL expiry path under NATS partition
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** What happens if the dashboard can't reach NATS to approve/deny a DEFER'd decision before its TTL expires?

**Why:** DEFER is one of the Kernel's four decision types (ALLOW/TRANSFORM/DENY/DEFER); its expiry behavior under a network partition is safety-relevant and currently untested.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Document the intended behavior on TTL expiry (should default to DENY, per fail-closed)
- [ ] Add a test simulating a NATS partition between dashboard and Kernel during a DEFER window

problems.title: [M2.23] DLQ messages are published but nothing consumes or alerts on them
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Verified: `_route_to_poison()` republishes to `dlq.<subject>`, but no subscriber, monitor, or dashboard panel exists for the `dlq.>` namespace anywhere in the codebase.

**Why:** Dead letters accumulate silently and invisibly forever — a real production failure could be actively poisoning messages with zero operator visibility.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Add a DLQ consumer/monitor
- [ ] Surface dead-letter counts/content in the dashboard or alerting

problems.title: [M2.29] Audit _is_safety_critical()'s hardcoded subject-prefix allowlist for completeness
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** `_is_safety_critical()` is a fixed check against `PROPOSAL_NEW`/`CODE_PROPOSAL` plus two prefixes.

**Why:** A newly-added safety-relevant subject could be added elsewhere in the codebase without also being added here, making it silently non-persistent.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Audit all current safety-relevant subjects against this allowlist
- [ ] Add a process/check to keep it in sync as new subjects are added

problems.title: feat(coordinator): wire TaskCoordinator sensor list to SensorManager
problems.issue_body:
## Problem

`TaskCoordinator._get_available_sensors()` returns a hardcoded stub (`[\"camera_0\", \"microphone_0\"]`) instead of querying the live `SensorManager`. Knowledge-gap payloads published to Meta-Programmer therefore report phantom sensors and miss real ones (IMU, GPS, etc.).

## Proposed solution

- Accept an optional injectable `sensor_manager` on `TaskCoordinator`
- Have `_get_available_sensors()` call `sensor_manager.get_sensor_ids()` when present
- Fall back to `[]` when no manager is injected (tests / partial setup)
- Wire `CoordinatorService` to pass its `SensorManager` into `TaskCoordinator`
- Add unit tests covering injected manager and no-manager fallback

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Knowledge-gap `available_sensors` reflects detected sensor IDs
- [ ] No hardcoded camera/microphone defaults remain
- [ ] Existing task-coordinator tests still pass
- [ ] Coordinator governance tests pass

## Scope

Coordinator lane only — closes the TODO left after SensorManager IMU/GPS detection (#171, #269).

problems.title: [M1.18] Add mutation testing to kernel/evaluator.py's risk-clamping logic
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Systematically catch the class of bug found in PR #122 (NaN risk-score handling silently clamped to 0.0) via mutation testing, not just the specific regression tests written for that one bug.

**Why:** The original NaN bug passed existing tests until specifically probed — mutation testing would surface similar latent gaps in the risk-clamping logic's test coverage.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Add a mutation-testing tool (e.g. `mutmut`/`cosmic-ray`) scoped to `kernel/evaluator.py`
- [ ] Achieve a defined mutation-kill-rate threshold on the risk-clamping functions

problems.title: [M3.47] Add a benchmark-suite runtime budget check
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** BenchmarkSuite.run_all() runs all 6 benchmarks serially; as more per-region benchmarks are proposed (items #30-#36), verify total suite runtime stays compatible with the CI-integration goal in item #1 rather than becoming too slow to run per-PR. Establishing the baseline measurement should happen now, before items #30-#36 land, specifically so there's a clean "before" number to compare against as the suite grows — measuring after the fact would lose that comparison point. The actual budget threshold is a judgment call that should account for how frequently item #1 proposes running the suite, since every merge to `dev` would need a tighter budget than a nightly run.

**Why:** Each new per-region benchmark proposed in this milestone adds to run_all()'s serial runtime; without a budget check, the suite could grow slow enough that item #1's CI-integration goal becomes impractical before anyone notices the trend.

**Source:** Proposed in `NewRoadMap.md`, milestone M3 (Validated Intelligence), item #47. This is a vetted-for-relevance backlog item (GitHub issue/PR counts re-fetched live; not independently re-derived line-by-line against the code the way the M1 items were) — treat as a starting point to investigate, not a pre-confirmed finding.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Measure current `run_all()` wall-clock time as a baseline
- [ ] Add a CI assertion that total runtime stays under an agreed budget as items #30–36 add more benchmarks

problems.title: [M3.46] Cross-reference EnergyEfficiencyBenchmark's per-region firing-rate breakdown with the new per-region benchmarks
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Once region-specific benchmarks exist, compare against this benchmark's existing per-region approx_energy_units to see whether quiet regions are undertrained or intentionally sparse. This item's value is entirely contingent on items #30-#36 landing first — before then, there's no per-region learning-quality signal to compare `EnergyEfficiencyBenchmark`'s existing per-region firing rates against, so this should be sequenced as one of the last items in this milestone to tackle. Once available, the comparison itself is a straightforward join across two already-computed per-region datasets.

**Why:** "Quiet" firing rates are consistent with two very different explanations — healthy sparsity vs. an undertrained region; per-region benchmarks landing (items #30–#36) give the missing second signal needed to tell them apart.

**Source:** Proposed in `NewRoadMap.md`, milestone M3 (Validated Intelligence), item #46. This is a vetted-for-relevance backlog item (GitHub issue/PR counts re-fetched live; not independently re-derived line-by-line against the code the way the M1 items were) — treat as a starting point to investigate, not a pre-confirmed finding.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Once items #30–36 land, join their per-region scores with `EnergyEfficiencyBenchmark`'s existing per-region `approx_energy_units`
- [ ] Flag regions that are both quiet and low-scoring (likely undertrained) vs. quiet and high-scoring (likely intentional sparsity)

problems.title: [M3.45] Verify ConceptSeparabilityBenchmark's pure-NumPy silhouette/linear-probe implementation matches the textbook def
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** The benchmark deliberately avoids an sklearn dependency; verify the hand-rolled silhouette score doesn't quietly diverge from the standard definition it's named after. This comparison should stay strictly a dev-time/CI-time verification step and not become a runtime dependency, consistent with the original design decision to avoid adding `sklearn` to the shipped benchmark code. If a divergence is found, the fix path — correct the hand-rolled implementation, or document the deviation as intentional — should be decided based on how large the divergence is and whether it changes any conclusion the benchmark suite has been used to support.

**Why:** A hand-rolled reimplementation of a named statistical method is exactly the kind of code that can quietly drift from its textbook definition without any test catching it, since the tests would need to assume the same (possibly wrong) definition.

**Source:** Proposed in `NewRoadMap.md`, milestone M3 (Validated Intelligence), item #45. This is a vetted-for-relevance backlog item (GitHub issue/PR counts re-fetched live; not independently re-derived line-by-line against the code the way the M1 items were) — treat as a starting point to investigate, not a pre-confirmed finding.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Compare the hand-rolled silhouette score against `sklearn.metrics.silhouette_score` on a small fixture in a scratch/dev-only script (not adding the dependency to the shipped code)
- [ ] Document any deliberate deviation, or fix it if the comparison reveals an unintentional divergence

problems.title: [M3.42] Investigate whether generate_test_patterns()'s synthetic pattern diversity is sufficient for the benchmark suite
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** All 6 BenchmarkSuite benchmarks share this one pattern-generation helper; limited diversity there would mean every downstream metric inherits the same blind spot (related to item #16's held-out-classes ask, but about the generator itself). Because this generator is a single shared dependency for all 6 `BenchmarkSuite` benchmarks, even a modest diversity improvement here has an unusually wide blast radius compared to most other items in this milestone — it's worth treating carefully and testing against the full suite, not just the benchmark it happens to have been investigated from. A parameter audit, counting distinct pattern "classes" actually produced, is a cheap first step before deciding whether more diversity is even needed.

**Why:** Every one of the 6 BenchmarkSuite benchmarks depends on this single generator; if its diversity is a bottleneck, fixing it is a single high-leverage change rather than something each downstream benchmark would need to work around independently.

**Source:** Proposed in `NewRoadMap.md`, milestone M3 (Validated Intelligence), item #42. This is a vetted-for-relevance backlog item (GitHub issue/PR counts re-fetched live; not independently re-derived line-by-line against the code the way the M1 items were) — treat as a starting point to investigate, not a pre-confirmed finding.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Audit `generate_test_patterns()` for parameter diversity (how many genuinely distinct pattern classes it produces)
- [ ] Add more diverse patterns if the audit finds a narrow set

problems.title: [M2.3] Add automatic reconnect-storm backoff to nats_client.py
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Verified: `connect()` sets `max_reconnect_attempts=-1` (infinite retries) with no `reconnect_time_wait`/jitter override — every service reconnects on the nats.py client's fixed default interval.

**Why:** A broker restart could see every service retry in lockstep, thundering-herding the broker right as it comes back up.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Add jittered backoff to reconnect configuration
- [ ] Test that simultaneous multi-service reconnects don't spike in lockstep

problems.title: [M2.26] Harden force_reconnect()'s per-subject resubscribe loop
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Verified: each resubscribe attempt in `force_reconnect()` is wrapped in its own `try/except: log and continue`.

**Why:** A single subject that fails to resubscribe leaves that service silently deaf on that subject until the next full restart, with only a log line as evidence.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Surface resubscribe failures more prominently (metric/alert, not just a log line)
- [ ] Add a retry path for failed resubscribes rather than a single attempt

problems.title: [M2.31] Add locking to get_event_bus()/get_database() to prevent a startup race
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Both `get_event_bus()` and `get_database()` check-then-set a global singleton with no lock.

**Why:** Two coroutines calling either getter concurrently during startup could race and create two connections/instances.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Add an `asyncio.Lock` (or equivalent) around singleton creation in both getters
- [ ] Add a regression test for concurrent first-call race

problems.title: [M3.39] Add a scheduled (not just manually-invoked) benchmark run after long training sessions
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** python -m neuromorphic.benchmarks --checkpoint is a manual CLI entrypoint; nothing automatically triggers a benchmark pass after a completed long training run, unlike the CI-triggered path proposed in item #1. The most natural hook point is wherever `run.py` or the training supervisor currently detects a completed long-running session, since that code already exists and just needs an additional callback rather than new session-detection logic. This item and item #1 (CI-triggered benchmarking) together would mean benchmark results exist both after every merge and after every long training run, covering the two moments learning quality is most likely to change.

**Why:** Today, benchmark results only exist if someone remembers to run the CLI after a long training session — the most learning-relevant moments (right after a long run) are exactly when this is most likely to be forgotten.

**Source:** Proposed in `NewRoadMap.md`, milestone M3 (Validated Intelligence), item #39. This is a vetted-for-relevance backlog item (GitHub issue/PR counts re-fetched live; not independently re-derived line-by-line against the code the way the M1 items were) — treat as a starting point to investigate, not a pre-confirmed finding.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Add a hook (e.g. in `run.py` or a training-completion callback) that invokes the benchmark CLI automatically
- [ ] Store results using the same `neuromorphic/benchmarks/*.json` convention `resolve_benchmark_dirs()` already scans

problems.title: [M3.38] Investigate matched_to_decoy_ratio in CrossModalBindingAccuracyBenchmark for decoy realism
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** The metric compares matched pairs to decoys from binding_fixtures.py; verify decoys are hard enough to be a meaningful negative control, not trivially distinguishable. A useful first pass doesn't require new statistical machinery — just manually reviewing a sample of the decoys `binding_fixtures.py` currently generates and judging by inspection whether they're meaningfully different from the matched pairs, or suspiciously easy to tell apart (e.g. obviously mismatched timing rather than plausibly mismatched). If they're too easy, the fix is a change to the fixture-generation logic itself.

**Why:** A benchmark's precision/recall numbers are only as meaningful as its negative examples are hard; trivially-distinguishable decoys would inflate matched_to_decoy_ratio without the network having learned anything discriminative.

**Source:** Proposed in `NewRoadMap.md`, milestone M3 (Validated Intelligence), item #38. This is a vetted-for-relevance backlog item (GitHub issue/PR counts re-fetched live; not independently re-derived line-by-line against the code the way the M1 items were) — treat as a starting point to investigate, not a pre-confirmed finding.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Inspect the decoy-generation logic in `binding_fixtures.py` for obvious distinguishing artifacts
- [ ] Add a "hard decoy" fixture variant and confirm the ratio doesn't trivially saturate against it

problems.title: [M3.37] Formalize a CLI flag to override BenchmarkSuite's hardcoded seed=42
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Every benchmark call (run_all(seed=42), CrossModalBindingAccuracyBenchmark.run(seed=seed)) defaults to the same fixed seed; combined with item #8/#20's multi-seed ask, there's no CLI-level way to even manually re-run with a different seed without editing source. This is a small, mechanical change — a new argparse flag threaded through two call sites (`run_all()` and `generate_correlated_stimulus_fixtures()`) — being called out as its own item specifically because items #8 and #20 both depend on it existing first, even though neither strictly requires it to be built as a standalone deliverable. Landing it early unblocks two higher-value items.

**Why:** This is the smallest possible fix that unblocks items #8's and #20's multi-seed asks — right now even a maintainer who wants to manually spot-check reproducibility by hand has to edit source to do it.

**Source:** Proposed in `NewRoadMap.md`, milestone M3 (Validated Intelligence), item #37. This is a vetted-for-relevance backlog item (GitHub issue/PR counts re-fetched live; not independently re-derived line-by-line against the code the way the M1 items were) — treat as a starting point to investigate, not a pre-confirmed finding.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Add a `--seed` flag to the `python -m neuromorphic.benchmarks` CLI entrypoint
- [ ] Thread it through to `run_all()` and `binding_fixtures.py`'s `generate_correlated_stimulus_fixtures()`

problems.title: [M3.33] Add a GlobalWorkspace region benchmark for cross-region information broadcast
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** GlobalWorkspace is one of 13 regions; no benchmark currently measures whether it's actually integrating/broadcasting information across the other 12, vs. just being wired but inert. The information-injection protocol this needs — injecting a signal into one region and checking if it's decodable from another — is methodologically similar to how `CrossModalProbe` already validates cross-modal binding in `CrossModalRecallBenchmark`, so that existing probe infrastructure may be reusable rather than needing to be built from scratch. A negative result here, the workspace isn't actually broadcasting, would be a significant architectural finding, not just a benchmark gap.

**Why:** A "global workspace" architecture is only meaningfully different from 13 independent regions if information actually gets broadcast and integrated across them — right now that's an assumption baked into the region's name, not a measured property.

**Source:** Proposed in `NewRoadMap.md`, milestone M3 (Validated Intelligence), item #33. This is a vetted-for-relevance backlog item (GitHub issue/PR counts re-fetched live; not independently re-derived line-by-line against the code the way the M1 items were) — treat as a starting point to investigate, not a pre-confirmed finding.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Measure whether information injected into one region's activity becomes decodable from `GlobalWorkspace`'s output
- [ ] Compare against a control region not architecturally expected to broadcast, to confirm the effect is specific

problems.title: [M3.34] Add a MetaControllerRegion benchmark for executive/gating decisions
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Parallel gap to GlobalWorkspace — the region exists in regions.py but nothing benchmarks its actual gating behavior against ground truth. Unlike GlobalWorkspace's more diffuse "is information broadcast" question, this region's function (executive/gating decisions) is more concretely testable against an unambiguous ground truth, since a task-switching protocol has a clearly correct gate at each point in time. That makes this item, despite the parallel framing to #33, potentially easier to get a clean pass/fail signal from.

**Why:** An executive/gating region that's never benchmarked against ground truth could be doing nothing useful without anyone noticing — the same blind spot flagged for GlobalWorkspace in item #33.

**Source:** Proposed in `NewRoadMap.md`, milestone M3 (Validated Intelligence), item #34. This is a vetted-for-relevance backlog item (GitHub issue/PR counts re-fetched live; not independently re-derived line-by-line against the code the way the M1 items were) — treat as a starting point to investigate, not a pre-confirmed finding.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Design a benchmark task requiring executive gating (e.g. a task-switching protocol with a known correct gate)
- [ ] Measure `MetaControllerRegion`'s activity/output against the known-correct gating decision

problems.title: [M2.24] The safety-critical JetStream stream has no retention/size configuration
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Verified: `_ensure_safety_stream()`'s `StreamConfig` sets no `max_age`/`max_msgs`/`storage` — the stream carrying `decision.>`, `code.decision.>`, `proposal.new`, `code.proposal` runs entirely on undocumented, untested NATS server defaults.

**Why:** This is the JetStream stream backing the Kernel's own safety-critical decision persistence — its retention behavior should be a deliberate choice, not a default.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Explicitly configure retention/size limits on `SAFETY_STREAM_NAME`
- [ ] Document and test the chosen policy

problems.title: [M2.19] Add a startup-order dependency graph validator to launcher/registry.py
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Verified: `deps=(...)` is declared on every `Service` entry, but no cycle-detection or missing-dependency validation function exists in `registry.py`.

**Why:** A typo'd or cyclic `deps` declaration would only surface as a confusing runtime startup failure.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Add cycle detection over the `deps` graph
- [ ] Validate every declared dependency actually exists in the registry

problems.title: [M2.14] Unify the two different zero-vector recall guard mechanisms
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** `memory/service.py` uses an explicit `is_zero_vector()` check (#72). `cache/llm_cache.py` has separate protection via its `EmbeddingService` raising instead of returning a zero vector. Both guard against the same failure mode with two different, unformalized approaches.

**Why:** Divergent guard mechanisms for the same risk make it easy for a future Qdrant-backed service to miss the pattern entirely.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Compare the two mechanisms for equivalent protection
- [ ] Unify into one documented pattern for all Qdrant-backed services

problems.title: [M3.1] Add a longitudinal learning-evidence regression test to CI
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** The Learning Evidence panel (PR #166) reads benchmark JSON; nothing yet fails CI if the trend regresses. `dashboard/src/dashboard/learning_evidence.py`'s `extract_learning_metrics()`/`build_learning_evidence_series()` read this data via `resolve_benchmark_dirs()`, which scans `neuromorphic/benchmarks/*.json`, `$ENGRAM_BENCHMARK_DIR`, and `/data/benchmarks` — but nothing re-runs that path in CI and fails the build if the trend regresses. A regression test would need to snapshot each of the 6 benchmark metrics after every merge to `dev` and compare against a rolling window of prior runs, similar in spirit to how `benchmark_ci_gate.py` already snapshots perf metrics against a committed baseline. Today that comparison only happens implicitly when a maintainer looks at the dashboard, which given this session's finding that CI was broken repo-wide for days (M7 item #9) is not a reliable substitute for an automated check.

**Why:** Without an automated regression gate, a change that silently degrades learning quality could ship and only be noticed if someone manually eyeballs the dashboard — the same blind spot item #24 flags for benchmark_ci_gate.py, but for the trend rather than a single run.

**Source:** Proposed in `NewRoadMap.md`, milestone M3 (Validated Intelligence), item #1. This is a vetted-for-relevance backlog item (GitHub issue/PR counts re-fetched live; not independently re-derived line-by-line against the code the way the M1 items were) — treat as a starting point to investigate, not a pre-confirmed finding.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Add a CI job that runs `BenchmarkSuite` and compares against a committed baseline the way `benchmark_ci_gate.py` already does for perf
- [ ] Wire it to the same `neuromorphic/benchmarks/*.json` convention `resolve_benchmark_dirs()` already scans, so it exercises the real dashboard-reading code path

problems.title: [M2.8] Document and test SQLite WAL-mode behavior under concurrent service writes
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Verified: no WAL-specific or concurrent-write test exists anywhere in the repo, despite multiple services writing to a shared SQLite file.

**Why:** Lock contention under concurrent writers could silently degrade or block services sharing `unified.db`.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Add a concurrent-write stress test against the WAL-mode database
- [ ] Document observed behavior/limits

problems.title: [M2.22] Database.insert() doesn't return the actual inserted row ID
problems.issue_body:
**Summary:** Verified: `sdk/src/activelearning/database.py`'s `insert()` is documented as returning "the ID of the inserted row" but its implementation is `return cast(str, data.get("id", ""))` — the caller's own input, not the cursor's actual assigned ID.

**Why:** If a caller relies on autoincrement and doesn't pass an `id`, this silently returns `""`, corrupting any code that expects a real ID back.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Return the cursor's actual `lastrowid`/assigned ID when the caller didn't supply one
- [ ] Add a regression test for the autoincrement case

problems.title: [Bug]: Status requests over NATS never receive a reply and time out
problems.issue_body:
### Description

The `EventBus` supports request and reply. A handler registered with `is_request_handler=True` receives the message object and answers through `msg.respond()`, while the caller uses `EventBus.request()`. Cache, external-api, and overrides already use this correctly.

Five services instead answer a status request by publishing to a separate subject, or do not answer at all:

- kernel subscribes to `kernel.status` as a plain subscription, then publishes to `kernel.status.response`.
- meta-programmer subscribes to `metaprogrammer.status`, then publishes to `metaprogrammer.status.response`.
- safety-supervisor subscribes to `safety.status`, then publishes to `safety.status.response`.
- coordinator subscribes to `coordinator.status`, then publishes to `coordinator.status.result`.
- planner subscribes to `planner.status`, then only logs the status and never replies.

Nothing subscribes to those response subjects. A caller that does `event_bus.request("<service>.status", ...)` waits on the reply inbox and times out, because the handler answered on a different subject or did not answer at all. Status reporting is read only and advisory, so this is a correctness and consistency gap rather than a safety regression, but every status query to these five services fails today.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Start an affected service, for example `python run.py --only kernel`.
2. From any NATS client, send a request to its status subject, for example `nats req kernel.status '{}'`, or in code `await event_bus.request("kernel.status", {}, timeout=2.0)`.
3. Watch the request inbox: no reply ever arrives.
4. The request times out.

### Expected Behavior

The status handler replies on the request inbox via `msg.respond()`, the same way cache, external-api, and overrides do, so `event_bus.request(...)` returns the status payload.

### Actual Behavior

```shell
$ nats req kernel.status '{}'
12:00:00 Sending request on "kernel.status"
nats: error: nats: timeout

# In code the request raises after the timeout, because the handler published the
# status to kernel.status.response (which has no subscribers) instead of replying:
#   asyncio.TimeoutError
```

### Environment

- OS: Ubuntu 24.04 (Linux)
- Python: 3.11 and 3.12
- Run mode: `python run.py` (pure Python); also reproduces under Docker Compose
- Hardware: not relevant
- Note: this is a logic defect in the request handling, independent of platform
  and hardware.

### Pre-submission checks

- [x] I searched existing issues and this is not a duplicate.
- [x] I am running the latest `main` (or I have stated my version/commit).

problems.title: [E1.1.1] Design the NATS account & permission model
problems.issue_body:
> Tracked as **E1.1.1** in [ISSUES.md](ISSUES.md). Part of the master plan; see ROADMAP.md for phase context.

## Context
deploy/nats-1m.conf uses a single shared token for every client; there are no per-service users or subject permissions, so the broker enforces nothing about *who* may publish *what*. problems.title: [Bug]: eligibility-trace interval batching is not "mathematically equivalent to every-step" — three-factor weight update
problems.issue_body:
<!--
Filed using the repository's Bug Report template (.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug_report.yml).
Section headings below map 1:1 to the template fields.
-->

### Component

neuromorphic (spiking neural network core)

### Description

`Synapses.apply_neuromodulation_and_decay()` is the **single live integration
path** for three-factor (neuromodulator × eligibility) learning. For
performance, `network.py` batches it: instead of applying it every step it
accumulates the modulator and applies once every `elig_apply_interval` steps
(default **3**) with "compensated decay" (`decay**interval`).

The method's own docstring asserts this is exact:

> ```python
> # Compensated decay: decay^interval is mathematically equivalent to
> # applying decay once per step for `interval` steps.
> ```
> — `neuromorphic/src/neuromorphic/synapses.py:702-703`

**It is not equivalent.** The interval path compensates the *trace decay*
correctly but applies the *weight increment only once* instead of summing it
over the `interval` steps. The result is that every reward/neuromodulator-gated
weight update is systematically too small by the geometric-sum factor

```
geo = 1 + decay + decay² + … + decay^(N-1) = (1 - decay^N) / (1 - decay)
```

With the shipped defaults (`trace_decay = 0.999`, `elig_apply_interval = 3`)
this factor is **2.997**, i.e. the brain applies only **~33%** of the weight
change it would apply running every step. The error grows linearly with the
interval (N=10 → ~10× too weak).

This directly violates **Architecture Invariant 1** (CLAUDE.md §2), whose
enforcement note states interval updates must use compensated decay "so the
result is **mathematically equivalent to running every step**." It silently
weakens STDP / R-STDP / reward learning across the whole network — not by
disabling a mechanism, but by mis-scaling its core integration.

#### Root cause (code)

`neuromorphic/src/neuromorphic/synapses.py` — active-set path:

```python
# 754-762
dw = np.float32(modulator_signal) * elig_slice      # applied ONCE
if plasticity_mask is not None and len(plasticity_mask) == len(self.eligibility):
    dw *= plasticity_mask[idx]
data[idx] = np.clip(data[idx] + dw, p.w_min, p.w_max)

# Decay eligibility traces (compensated for interval)
elig_slice *= decay                                  # e *= decay^N  (correct)
self.eligibility[idx] = elig_slice
```

The identical defect is in the full-array branch (`708-712`).

The math of the every-step process this is meant to reproduce: over `N` steps
with modulator `M` and a trace that decays each step, the trace at step `k` is
`e_k = e₀·decay^k`, so the true accumulated weight change is

```
Δw_truth = Σ_{k=0}^{N-1} M · e₀ · decay^k = M · e₀ · (1 - decay^N)/(1 - decay)
```

and the final trace is `e_N = e₀·decay^N`. The interval path reproduces the
final trace (`decay**interval` ✔) but applies `Δw_interval = M · e₀` — missing
the `(1 - decay^N)/(1 - decay)` factor entirely.

(Note: `network.py:1156` *averages* the modulator ov…

problems.title: [Bug]: Kernel body-profile motor clamp masks a DENY-level risk — high-risk actions degrade open to TRANSFORM (fail-open
problems.issue_body:
<!--
Filed using the repository's Bug Report template (.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug_report.yml).
Section headings below map 1:1 to the template fields.
-->

### Component

kernel / safety-supervisor (safety layer)

### Description

`KernelEvaluator.evaluate_action_proposal()` runs its safety checks in an order
that lets a **body-profile motor clamp short-circuit the risk-threshold DENY**.
When a body profile is loaded (the normal deployment case), any action whose
intensity exceeds the profile's motor cap is returned as a **TRANSFORM** —
*before* the `risk_score >= deny_threshold` check ever runs. So an action the
Safety Supervisor (or the Beliefs norm graph) flagged as DENY-worthy is silently
**downgraded to "allowed, with intensity clamped"** and even has its reported
risk rewritten to `0.3`.

This violates the safety architecture's core rule (CLAUDE.md §3): the Kernel
must DENY high-risk actions and must **never degrade open**. Here a high
supervisor/Beliefs risk is masked purely because the action *also* happened to
exceed a motor cap — and motor-cap-exceeding (high-intensity) actions are
exactly the ones most likely to be high-risk.

#### Root cause (code)

`kernel/src/kernel/evaluator.py`, `evaluate_action_proposal()`. The risk score
(including Beliefs norm-violation boosts) is computed up front:

```python
# ~line 159
risk_score = max(0.0, min(risk_analysis.risk_score, 1.0)) if risk_analysis else 0.0
...
if norm_violations:
    for violation in norm_violations:
        risk_score += violation.get("risk_boost", 0.1)
    risk_score = min(risk_score, 1.0)
```

…but the **body-profile check runs first and returns immediately**:

```python
# ~line 181 — runs BEFORE the risk thresholds
profile_result = self._check_body_profile(action, flags)
if profile_result is not None:
    return KernelDecision(
        trace_id=trace_id,
        type=profile_result["type"],          # TRANSFORM
        reason=profile_result["reason"],
        risk_score=profile_result.get("risk_score", 0.9),   # 0.3 for a clamp
        transformations=profile_result.get("transformations"),
        ...
    )

# ~line 206 — NEVER REACHED when the profile clamps
if risk_score >= self.deny_threshold:
    return KernelDecision(..., type=DecisionType.DENY, ...)
if risk_score >= self.defer_threshold:
    return KernelDecision(..., type=DecisionType.DEFER, ...)
```

The motor-clamp branch of `_check_body_profile` (~line 482) returns the
masking TRANSFORM:

```python
# 2. Motor-limit clamping — TRANSFORM if intensity exceeds profile max
if channel and isinstance(intensity, (int, float)):
    limit = profile.get_motor_limit(channel)
    if intensity > limit.max_intensity:
        clamped = limit.max_intensity
        transformed = action.copy()
        transformed["intensity"] = clamped
        return {
            "type": DecisionType.TRANSFORM,
            "reason": f"Body profile '{profile.name}' caps ...",
            "risk_score": 0.3,                # <-- overwrites the real risk
…

problems.title: [E1.8.3] safety-supervisor: code-path/AST analysis tests + evasion regressions
problems.issue_body:
## Context
The safety-supervisor performs code-path / AST analysis on code proposals as advisory risk input to the Kernel, but it has **zero tests** (Task 1.8). The Kernel's full-source AST taint scan (Task 1.5) landed with regressions in #36; the supervisor's analyzer needs equivalent coverage so its risk signal cannot be silently evaded.

## Goal
A unit + regression suite for the safety-supervisor's code-path / AST analysis that proves it flags the dangerous constructs it claims to (self-referential / self-modifying code, dangerous imports, exec/eval, file/network/subprocess sinks) and resists known evasion techniques.

## Scope (checklist)
- [ ] Tests that each high-risk construct (exec/eval, `__import__`, subprocess, socket/network, filesystem writes, self-referential edits) is detected at the expected risk level.
- [ ] Evasion regressions: obfuscated imports, aliased / dynamic attribute access, string-built calls, comment/whitespace tricks - analyzer must not be fooled into a lower risk.
- [ ] Benign-code cases assert no false-positive over-escalation.
- [ ] Wire `safety-supervisor/tests/` into the Governance CI job (PYTHONPATH + addopts override pattern, mirroring E1.8.1 #67).

## Out of scope
Risk-heuristic envelope/threshold tests (E1.8.2, #68); homoglyph/Unicode-spoof defense (E1.8.4); cross-service governance integration (E1.8.6).

## Acceptance criteria
- Each dangerous construct and each enumerated evasion is covered by a test that fails without the guard.
- `safety-supervisor/tests/` runs in CI and is green; benign code does not over-escalate.

## Affected files / areas
new/expanded `safety-supervisor/tests/`, `safety-supervisor/.../*.py` (the analyzer), `.github/workflows/test.yml`.

## Dependencies
Mirrors Task 1.5 (#36). Reuses the E1.8.1 (#67) CI wiring pattern. Milestone M1.

## Skills & effort
Python AST, pytest, adversarial test design. Effort **M**. Maintainer review required (safety).

## Definition of Done
Analysis + evasion suite green in CI and gating; no invariant weakened; reviewed & merged to `dev`.

problems.title: Add preset style selection and preview
problems.issue_body:
Build the next creator-facing step after episode setup: let the user choose from a small set of distinct podcast visual presets, adjust basic layout and pacing options, and see an immediate preview of how their imported speakers would appear before applying the style. This should keep simple users out of a blank canvas while making the product feel like a visual podcast workspace rather than only an upload form.

## Acceptance (definition of done)
Running `node scripts/run-tests.mjs` passes. In the app, after the completed episode setup flow, a creator can view at least three clearly different visual style presets, change layout and pacing choices, see the preview update using the assigned Host/Guest speaker buckets, select one preset, and continue with that style visibly applied or summarized for the episode.

---

_Why this step now: The first setup flow already exists, so the highest-value next move is the preset-driven visual experience promised by the vision. It establishes the default path to a polished result before investing in advanced canvas editing, audio cleanup, or export workflows._

problems.title: Add the reusable podcast canvas editor
problems.issue_body:
Build the first usable canvas editor for customizing a selected podcast style into a reusable show layout. The editor should let creators open the chosen preset as a starting point, adjust visible layout elements such as speaker frames, captions, title text, background, and overlay areas, and save the result as a named show template. This is the next foundation because the product already has episode setup and preset choice, but it still lacks the Canva-like direct manipulation workspace that makes styles personal and reusable.

A reviewer can create or load an episode setup, choose a preset style, open a canvas editor from that style, visibly customize the layout elements without manually editing code, save the design as a named reusable show template, and see that saved template available for future episode use. The existing verification command `node scripts/run-tests.mjs` passes and includes coverage for opening the canvas editor, changing at least one layout element, saving a template, and reselecting it.

---

problems.title: `RuntimeError("No response returned")` in `BaseHTTPMiddleware`
problems.issue_body:
Previously, a "No response returned"-error has been discussed in this discussion: https://github.com/encode/starlette/discussions/1527, and was supposedly fixed in this PR: https://github.com/encode/starlette/pull/1715

However, the bug is still present. It's a race condition, so quite tough to reproduce, but the following reproducer works.

Reproducer
--

Use anyio 4.2.0 It does happen also with anyio 3.0.0, but it happens much more regularly on 4.2.

First, apply the following patch to the Starlette codebase, so that we have a breakpoint in case it happens:
```diff
--- a/starlette/middleware/base.py
+++ b/starlette/middleware/base.py
@@ -134,7 +134,8 @@ class BaseHTTPMiddleware:
             async def send_no_error(message: Message) -> None:
                 try:
@@ -163,6 +164,7 @@ class BaseHTTPMiddleware:
             except anyio.EndOfStream:
                 if app_exc is not None:
                     raise app_exc
+                breakpoint()
                 raise RuntimeError("No response returned.")

             assert message["type"] == "http.response.start"
```

Then run this code:

```python
import asyncio
from hypercorn.asyncio import serve
from hypercorn.config import Config

from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.responses import JSONResponse
from starlette.routing import Route
from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware
from starlette.requests import Request
from starlette.responses import Response
from starlette.middleware.base import RequestResponseEndpoint
from starlette.middleware import Middleware


class DummyMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):
    async def dispatch(
        self, request: Request, call_next: RequestResponseEndpoint
    ) -> Response:
        return await call_next(request)


async def homepage(request):
    return JSONResponse({})


app = Starlette(
    routes=[
        Route("/", homepage),
    ],
    middleware=[Middleware(DummyMiddleware) for i in range(100)],  # Yes, 100x the same middleware.
)

config = Config.from_mapping({})
config.bind = ["127.0.0.1:8000"]
asyncio.run(serve(app, config))
```

Open either Firefox or Chrome, navigate to http://localhost:8000 and hold down command-r (refresh) to repeatedly have the browser refresh the page. After a couple of seconds, we'll enter the breakpoint.

(Feel free to turn this issue into a discussion if that's more appropriate. I'm also looking for a fix but have a hard time understanding `BaseHTTPMiddleware`.)

This PR contains a possible fix: https://github.com/encode/starlette/pull/2519

problems.title: Mismatch Between ASGI Specification and httpx's `raw_path` Definition in TestClient
problems.issue_body:
According to the ASGI specification [1](https://asgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/specs/www.html#http-connection-scope), the `raw_path` field is defined as:

> raw_path (byte string) – The original HTTP path component, excluding any query string, unmodified from the bytes that were received by the web server.

In Starlette's `TestClient`, the `raw_path` is directly taken from the `httpx` request without modification:

https://github.com/encode/starlette/blob/2d0dde8defe9e3d4df0baacdb20faf273152f1cb/starlette/testclient.py#L307
https://github.com/encode/starlette/blob/2d0dde8defe9e3d4df0baacdb20faf273152f1cb/starlette/testclient.py#L254

However, `httpx`'s definition of `raw_path` includes the query string, which differs from the ASGI specification. This discrepancy was previously noted in a related issue on `httpx` [2](https://github.com/encode/httpx/issues/2810).

### Proposed Solution:

To align with the ASGI specification, the `raw_path` in Starlette's `TestClient` should be adjusted to exclude the query string before being passed to the ASGI application.

### References:
- [1] ASGI Specification: [https://asgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/specs/www.html#http-connection-scope](https://asgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/specs/www.html#http-connection-scope)
- [2] Related httpx Issue: [https://github.com/encode/httpx/issues/2810](https://github.com/encode/httpx/issues/2810)

problems.title: Enable autoescape by default in Jinja2Templates
problems.issue_body:
# Summary

Noticed that `Jinja2Templates` currently defaults to having `autoescape` disabled. It puts the burden on the developer to remember to enable it, which I've seen lead to XSS vulnerabilities in applications that render user-provided content.

While investigating, I also discovered that `Jinja2Templates` was missing support for `**env_options` in its constructor, making it difficult to customize the environment even though the documentation suggested it was supported.

Updated the implementation to:
- Use `jinja2.select_autoescape()` by default for HTML/XML files to ensure a secure baseline.
- Add support for `**env_options` in the `Jinja2Templates` constructor, allowing full customization of the Jinja2 environment.

### Changes
- Modified `Jinja2Templates.__init__` to accept and use `**env_options`.
- Enabled `autoescape` by default using `select_autoescape()` if not explicitly provided.
- Added test cases in `tests/test_templates.py` to verify both the secure default and the ability to override it.

# Checklist

- [x] Understood that this PR may be closed in case there was no previous discussion. (This doesn't apply to typos!)
- [x] Added a test for each change that was introduced, while I tried as much as possible to make a single atomic change.
- [x] Updated the documentation accordingly.

problems.title: SessionMiddleware sends a new set-cookie for every request, with unintended results
problems.issue_body:
### Discussed in https://github.com/encode/starlette/discussions/2018

<div type='discussions-op-text'>

<sup>Originally posted by **sm-Fifteen** January 27, 2023</sup>
The way SessionMiddleware currently works is that it encodes session data in a signed base64 object with timestamp, in a format not entirely dissimilar to (but incompatible with) JWT. Because of the way it works, being run right before the headers for an HTTP response are sent, and because it doesn't perform many checks besides whether or not there is session data to encode, it will try to update the session cookie whenever a route is called. This is somewhat wasteful, as session data is not usually updated on every request, but it leads to interesting issues as well.

I have a FastAPI application where login is handeled via a session cookie with a separate login process. Several routes are unlocked based on whether or not the cookie is present and based on the user authorizations recorded in said session cookie. When the frontend fetches API data, if the user is logged in, every response contains a new `Set-Cookie` header, which *Firefox ignores, but Chrome acknowledges*. None of the API routes alter session data, so the cookie value is always the same, save for the timestamp and signature at the end. This actually runs into [an interesting Chrome issue](https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=696204#c107) where responses to fetch requests that arrive after the page has been navigated away from still alter the session cookie, even if if the new page changed the session data on load. This means I have this strange, Chrome-exclusive, race-condition-y bug that matches lepture/authlib#334, where the session state data setup by the Oauth flow before redirecting to the third party login form may get clobbered if some `/api/slow_route` query was pending when the user clicked the login button.

It's unclear if it's actually a chrome bug or unintended behavior from everything working as intended. If Starlette wasn't updating cookies for every request, and the ``Set-Cookie`` was actually important here, it's difficult to argue whether or not Chrome should have ignored it.

See here the Starlette test case from the Chromium bug report, which doesn't use SessionMiddleware, but shows the Chrome behavior in action.

```py
from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.responses import HTMLResponse, RedirectResponse, JSONResponse, PlainTextResponse
from starlette.routing import Route
import uvicorn
import datetime
from asyncio import sleep

html_content = """
    <!DOCTYPE html>
    <html>
        <head>
            <meta http-equiv="refresh" content="2;url=/set_cookie_and_redirect" />
            <script>fetch("/set_cookie_on_fetch")</script>
        </head>
        <body>
            Calling slow route via fetch() before changing page.
        </body>
    </html>
"""


async def homepage(request):
    return HTMLResponse(html_cont…

problems.title: FileResponse accepts inverted single-byte Range like bytes=5-4
problems.issue_body:
### Bug

`FileResponse._parse_range_header` rejects a Range only when `start > end`, but `bytes=5-4` parses to the empty half-open range `(5, 5)` and slips past that guard. The result is a malformed `206 Partial Content` (`Content-Length: 0`, a backwards `Content-Range: bytes 5-4/...`) instead of a `400`.

`bytes=10-5` is caught (it parses to `(10, 6)`, so `10 > 6`), but the off-by-one boundary case where `end + 1 == start` is not.

### Reproduce

```python
from starlette.responses import FileResponse
FileResponse._parse_range_header("bytes=5-4", 100)   # -> [(5, 5)]  (accepted; should be 400)
FileResponse._parse_range_header("bytes=5-5", 100)   # -> [(5, 6)]  (valid one-byte range)
FileResponse._parse_range_header("bytes=10-5", 100)  # -> MalformedRangeHeader (already correct)
```

### Fix

The guard should be `start >= end` (an empty range is not satisfiable). A genuine one-byte request `bytes=5-5` parses to `(5, 6)` and is unaffected.

I have a fix + tests ready and opened it as a draft PR for reference. Happy to adjust or drop it if you'd prefer to handle it differently.

problems.title: Limit max request size
problems.issue_body:
### Discussed in https://github.com/encode/starlette/discussions/1516
Originally posted by **aviramha** April 5, 2020 As discussed in the Gitter, my opinion is that starlette should provide a default limit for request size. The main reason is that without it, any Starlette application is vulnerable to very easy DoS. For example, newbie me can write a program as follows: ``` from starlette.requests import Request from starlette.responses import Response async def app(scope, receive, send): assert scope['type'] == 'http' request = Request(scope, receive) body = b'' json = await request.json() response = Response(body, media_type='text/plain') await response(scope, receive, send) ``` As a malicious user, I could send a 30GB sized JSON and cause the memory to go OOM. Other frameworks support this also - Django, Quart. My proposal is to add a default limit which can be overrided in the app configuration.

problems.title: `apply_busy_delta` / `apply_event` not idempotent on restart replay
problems.issue_body:
If the validator crashes mid-block, the same block is reprocessed on restart ([allways/validator/event_watcher.py:381-413](allways/validator/event_watcher.py#L381-L413)).

`insert_swap_outcome` uses `INSERT OR REPLACE` (fine), but the busy-delta increments double — each replayed event bumps the counter again.

**Direction:** dedupe by `(block, extrinsic_index, event_index)`, or store an absolute busy count instead of applying deltas.

problems.title: TAO receive address not SS58-checksum-validated — user typo sends funds irrecoverably
problems.issue_body:
**Severity:** S0 (money-at-risk, user-error amplification)

**Location:** [allways/chain_providers/subtensor.py:276-283](allways/chain_providers/subtensor.py#L276-L283), gated by [allways/cli/swap_commands/swap.py:751](allways/cli/swap_commands/swap.py#L751)

### Bug
`SubtensorProvider.is_valid_address` only checks 48-char length and Base58 charset via regex — no SS58 checksum. The string `'xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx'` passes. The swap flow gates on `to_provider.is_valid_address(receive_address)`, so a user who mistypes their TAO destination gets past the only validation gate. The miner later sends TAO to that literal address and the funds are unrecoverable.

### Comparison
- Bitcoin has proper validation via [bitcoin.py:319-330](allways/chain_providers/bitcoin.py#L319-L330) (bech32 / base58check decode).
- The correct SS58 pattern already exists at [helpers.py:117-130](allways/cli/swap_commands/helpers.py#L117-L130) wrapping `scalecodec.ss58_decode` — but it's only used in admin commands.

### Fix
Replace the regex body of `SubtensorProvider.is_valid_address` with `scalecodec.ss58_decode(address)` wrapped in try/except. Zero behavior change for legitimate addresses; catches all typos.

The same gap exists for `user_from_address` at [swap.py:757-766](allways/cli/swap_commands/swap.py#L757-L766) but the validator's sender-mismatch check catches that one on-chain.

problems.title: SwapConfirm allows reservation hijacking by a different user
problems.issue_body:
### Problem
handle_swap_confirm() does not verify that the confirming from_address matches the from_addr stored in the active reservation.

The validator reads get_reservation_data(miner), but does not enforce that the reservation owner and the confirmer are the same address. Instead, it trusts the from_address supplied in the incoming SwapConfirm request and uses it for transaction verification and vote_initiate().

### Root Cause
The reservation already stores the user source address as from_addr, but handle_swap_confirm() never compares it against synapse.from_address.

Because that check is missing, confirmation is authorized by:
- active reservation exists for the miner
- submitted tx matches expected deposit address and amount
- submitted tx sender matches the caller-supplied from_address

It is not authorized by the address that actually created the reservation.

### Impact
A malicious user can take over another user’s active reservation.
A concrete attack flow is:
- User A reserves a miner.
- The reservation becomes active.
- User B sends the required source amount from User B’s own address.
- User B submits SwapConfirm with User B’s from_address, proof, tx hash, and payout address.
- Validators accept the confirm because the code never checks that the confirmer matches the reserved from_addr.
- Validators call vote_initiate() using User B’s addresses, even though User A created the reservation.

This breaks reservation ownership. An active reservation can be consumed by a different user than the one who reserved it, which is an authorization flaw and should be fixed urgently.

problems.title: [Bug] Repository registration rejects common GitHub repository URLs
problems.issue_body:
## Description

The repository registration form only accepts an exact root repository URL such as `https://github.com/owner/repo`. Common GitHub URLs copied from a browser can include query strings, hash fragments, or repository subpaths, such as `?tab=readme-ov-file`, `#readme`, or `/tree/main`.

The parser/validator should normalize these URLs to `owner/repo` before validation and mirror tracking checks.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open `/repository-registration`.
2. Enter a repository URL copied from GitHub with a suffix, for example `https://github.com/owner/repo?tab=readme-ov-file`.
3. Fill the rest of the form and confirm the GitHub App installation.
4. Submit the form.

## Expected Behavior

The form should normalize valid GitHub repository URLs to `owner/repo` before validation and mirror tracking checks. These should resolve to the same repository:

- `https://github.com/owner/repo`
- `https://github.com/owner/repo?tab=readme-ov-file`
- `https://github.com/owner/repo#readme`
- `https://github.com/owner/repo/tree/main`

## Actual Behavior

The form either rejects the URL or checks a malformed repo name such as `owner/repo?tab=readme-ov-file` against the mirror health response. That can incorrectly show the repository as not installed/tracked.

## Environment

- Browser: Any
- OS: Any

## Additional Context

This is a follow-up edge case in the repository registration flow. A narrow fix can parse with `URL`, extract only the first two path segments, and reject URLs that do not contain a valid owner/repo pair.

problems.title: Repositories page: align OSS vs issue-track metrics on Repository list
problems.issue_body:
## Summary
The **Repositories** page leaderboard currently emphasizes **OSS contribution** metrics in the repo list/cards (e.g. **Total score**, **PRs**, **Contributors**). It does **not** adequately surface **issue discovery** program data for the same rows. The main work is to **add issue discovery details** to the repository list (and keep card/list consistent with the same information).
This issue tracks implementing that feature; secondary fixes (wording, `-` when another column has activity, sort/tooltips) are in service of a **clear OSS vs. issue discovery** presentation, not a substitute for it.
## Problem
- **What users see today:** The repo grid/list highlights OSS-style numbers (weight, total score, PR count, contributor count) but **issue discovery** (pro-rated / discovery-scoped issue score, solved/completed issues, issue-specific contributors) is missing or not visible in the same way for each repository.
- **Why that’s wrong:** Gittensor has **two** reward programs (OSS contributions and issue discovery). The Repositories view should make **both** programs’ signals inspectable per repo, not only OSS.

## Goals
1. **Show issue discovery details on the repository leaderboard** (cards **and** list) for each repo where data exists—at minimum: **issue (discovery) score**, **issues** (completed/solved-oriented counts per product rules, not raw open totals if that conflicts with the rest of the app), and **issue discovery contributors** (or equivalent), so they are **not confused with OSS contributors**.
2. **Visual structure:** Use a **clear two-track layout** (e.g. two bands/rows: “OSS” vs “Issue discovery / discovery track”) with distinct labels, matching the mental model used elsewhere in the app.
3. **Parity:** **Card and list** show the **same** underlying facts for the same repo; no column or card section should only exist in one mode without a good reason.
4. **Data:** Reuse existing aggregation helpers and miner-backed rollups (e.g. `buildRepoDiscoveryRollupFromMiners`, `useAllMiners`, merged-PR + discovery rules as documented in code) so numbers match the **Issue discovery** program semantics, not a duplicate of PR-only stats.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Each repository card in the grid shows **issue discovery** metrics in addition to OSS metrics, with unambiguous labels (e.g. not “score” for both without qualification).
- [ ] The **list** view exposes the same discovery fields with column headers that read clearly (e.g. **Issue score**, **Issues**, **Issue contrib.** or agreed naming).
- [ ] OSS **Contributors** and issue-**track** contributor counts are **not** the same when miners have no discovery attribution for that repo.
- [ ] Rows with PR activity do not show misleading `-` in one column when another column on the same row already shows activity (consistency of “empty” vs. “zero”).
- [ ] Sorting and chart tooltips, where they reference these fields, stay aligned with the table/card labels.
- [ ] `npm run build` passes;…

problems.title: feat(watchlist): show why each PR is in the Pull Requests tab
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

After #784, the Watchlist *Pull Requests* tab auto-shows PRs from any starred PR, watched miner, or watched repository — but the resulting list is flat. There is no visual indication of *why* each PR is shown.

Add a small **Source** indicator (a column in the list view, an inline chip group on the card view) that displays up to three badges per row, one for each source the PR matches:

- **Starred** — the user explicitly starred this PR.
- **Miner** — the PR's author is in the user's watched-miners list.
- **Repo** — the PR's repository is in the user's watched-repositories list.

A PR can match multiple sources and should show all matching badges side-by-side.

## Motivation

The most common confusion after #784 is *"why is this PR here? I don't remember starring it."* Users have to mentally cross-reference their three watchlists to figure it out, which undermines the value of auto-show.

A Source indicator directly visualizes the original ask of #784 (*"auto displaying all PRs for any miner or repo added to the watch list"*) by making the relationship explicit on every row. It also gives onboarding users and reviewers a single-screenshot understanding of how the tab works.

## Notes

This enhancement was discussed with and approved by the maintainer in chat ahead of filing.

problems.title: Make the watchlist column sortable across tables
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

The ★ column shows up on a few tables — the Repositories list view (OSS and Issue Discovery), the Top Miners list, and the Watchlist Pull Requests tab. It holds the row-level watchlist star (add / remove from your watchlist). Right now the column header isn't clickable — clicking it does nothing — so there's no way to pull your starred rows to the top of the list.

I'd like clicking the ★ header to sort the table by watchlist status, the same way every other column header does. First click puts watched rows at the top; a second click flips the order. Stars added or removed should re-sort the list right away.

## Motivation

When I scan one of these long tables, the rows I care about most are the ones I've already starred. To find them today I have to scroll, search by name, or jump over to the Watchlist page. The ★ column already tells me which rows are watched, so it feels natural that clicking its header would sort by it — that's how the other columns work.

This helps in a few everyday situations:

- On the Repositories page (OSS or Issue Discovery), seeing where my tracked repos rank against the rest without leaving the leaderboard.
- On Top Miners, surfacing the miners I follow alongside the full ranking.
- On the Watchlist Pull Requests tab, grouping still-starred PRs above any I've since unstarred.

The watchlist data is already in local storage, the ★ column already exists on these tables, and the sort plumbing is already wired up for the other columns. This is mostly about plugging the ★ header into the same sort state so the click does what it visually promises.

problems.title: Add time-decay chart to PR details view
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

Add a PR time-decay chart to the PR details view that visualizes how the time-decay multiplier changes after merge and shows the current scored state in a compact, easy-to-read format.

## Motivation

PR scoring already includes time decay, but the current UI does not explain how that multiplier evolves over time. Users can see the current score, but not why it is lower than the original merged value or where the PR sits on the decay curve.

A dedicated time-decay chart helps users understand:

- how quickly score falls after merge
- the current multiplier and score state at a glance

This improves transparency around scoring behavior and makes PR detail pages more informative for contributors tracking earned score over time.

problems.title: Redesigning Miner Details Page
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

The miner details page was originally designed as a reviewer-facing tool that enabled maintainers to evaluate a contributor's track record before merging their work. That context no longer applies. The link to miner profiles is no longer embedded in PR descriptions, so reviewers rarely land here anymore.

The page's actual audience is now miners themselves — people checking their scores, tracking tier progression, monitoring open PR risk, and understanding how their contributions translate into earnings.

UX still feels oriented toward an external evaluator rather than the person whose data it is.

All the underlying data is solid. coring breakdowns, tier unlock progress, credibility metrics, earnings estimates, per-repository performance, contribution activity, and individual PR details are all available and surfaced. The question is whether the page presents that data in the most useful, intuitive, and visually compelling way for a miner managing their own performance.

---

## Motivation

Miners care about different things at different stages — a new contributor wants to understand what they need to unlock the next tier, while an established miner wants to monitor earnings and score trends. The current page treats everyone identically.

The page also serves as the primary hub where miners contextualize their scoring. Each PR has a composite score built from multiple multipliers (repository weight, credibility, issue bonuses, time decay, uniqueness), token-level code analysis (structural vs. leaf scoring), tier-specific breakdowns, and collateral mechanics for open PRs. This scoring data exists and is partially surfaced, but could be presented in ways that help miners actually understand why they earned what they earned and what levers they can pull to improve.

The current tables (PRs, repositories) also lack meaningful filtering, sorting, and search — making it difficult for active miners to find specific data. Some of the tabular data is redundant across sections (e.g., PR table vs. repositories table surface overlapping information). Consider whether every table earns its place, and whether the data could be consolidated or made more navigable.

---

## Scope

- The miner details page and all its sub-components- Data access — filtering, sorting, and search across tables and data views
- Data presentation — all currently available API data should remain accessible; don't discard useful metrics
- Responsive behavior across desktop, tablet, and mobile viewports

API documentation is available at https://api.gittensor.io/swagger for understanding the available data and endpoints.

---

## Task

Redesign the miner details page to serve as a miner's personal performance dashboard. The page should feel like it belongs to the miner — a place they want to come back to regularly to understand their standing, track progress, and identify opportunities.

problems.title: Add `JsonNode.optional(String name)` and `JsonNode.optional(int index)` to be able to get an Optional `JsonNode`
Add `Optional<JsonNode> JsonNode.asOptional()` convenience method
problems.issue_body:
(note: part of https://github.com/FasterXML/jackson-future-ideas/wiki/JSTEP-3 changes)

Currently there is concept of "missing" node (impl `MissingNode`, detectable via `JsonNode.isMissingNode()`), returned in cases where `Java 8` `Optional.empty()` would commonly be used. Partly this is due to "missing node" concept predating Jackson using Java 8 as base line, and partly due to wanting to avoid extra layering for common case of "not-missing" nodes.
Be that as it may, use of `Optional` is convenient with Java 8 Stream methods, so it makes sense to add some support.

To this end, let's add method

    Optional<JsonNode> asOptional();

which will return

* `Optional.empty()` for `MissingNode`
* `Optional.of(this)` for all other `JsonNode` types
* that is, `Optional.ofNullable(this.isMissingNode() ? null : this)` if implemented at `JsonNode` level

### Describe your Issue

Due to eager binding of number type when reading `JsonNode` -- basically, decision must be made between reading:

1. Slightly faster,  but potentially lossy `Double` vs
2. Bit slower but unlimited range/precision `BigDecimal`

(to get either `DoubleNode` or `BigDecimalNode`)

there are cases where common buffering use cases expose unexpected precision loss -- particular since by default `Double` is used. See, for example:

https://github.com/FasterXML/jackson-modules-java8/issues/326

This behavior can be changed via `DeserializationFeature.USE_BIG_DECIMAL_FOR_FLOATS`, but that is global setting. Instead, it would perhaps make sense to add a `JsonNodeFeature` which would only affect `JsonNode` reading, but would have precedence over `DeserializationFeature`.

I haven't thought this fully through wrt implementation but this seems like potentially useful thing to have.

problems.title: Custom `Throwable` not serializable if using `JsonAutoDetect` settings that only detect Fields
`NullPointerException` in `ObjectMapper.valueToTree(UUID)`
problems.issue_body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched in the [issues](https://github.com/FasterXML/jackson-databind/issues) and found nothing similar.

### Describe the bug

When calling mapper.valueToTree(UUID.randomUUID()), a NullPointerException is thrown inside the private _writeAsBinary(...) method.
The root cause is that _writeCapabilities is null when ctxt.isEnabled(...) is checked.

### Version Information

3.0.0-rc5

### Reproduction

```java
ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper();
JsonNode node = mapper.valueToTree(UUID.randomUUID());
```

### Expected behavior

No NullPointerException is thrown

### Additional context

The root cause is that _assignGenerator isn’t called when valueToTree is invoked; since valueToTree isn’t actually performing serialization, it’s appropriate to handle it by not calling _assignGenerator.

here seem to be two possible approaches:

1. Null-check in isEnabled
Add a null check for _writeCapabilities inside isEnabled, and return false if it’s null. This is safe because valueToTree doesn’t actually serialize—instead, the JsonNode simply holds the UUID as a string.

```java
public final boolean isEnabled(StreamWriteCapability cap) {
    return _wirteCapabilities != null && _writeCapabilities.isEnabled(cap);
}
```


2. Default initialization in the SerializationContext
Initialize _writeCapabilities with a default value when the SerializationContext is created. This ensures it’s never null, but may be wasteful since a fresh capabilities object will be created anyway once actual serialization occurs.

```java
JacksonFeatureSet<StreamWriteCapability> _writeCapabilities
        = JacksonFeatureSet.fromDefaults(StreamWriteCapability.values());

problems.issue_body:
(note: result of #5417)

Jackson 3.0 changed coercion behavior for existing 2.x methods such as `asString(String defValue)` for `NullNode`s (mapped from explicit JSON `null` values) so that instead of returning `defValue`, they coerce into "empty" value of type -- in case of `asString()`, empty String "". In 2.x, matching method (named `asText()`) returned `defValue`.
Similarly new `Optional<String> asStringOpt()` returns `new Optional<String>("")` instead `Optional.empty()`.
This applies consistently across all various `asXxx()` and `asXxxOpt()` methods, for `NullNode`s.

Note: problem does not affect `MissingNode`. Also, plain `asString()` coerces `NullNode` into "", and this is expected due to lack of defaulting.

Based on Strong developer feedback, we should change the behavior of `NullNode` so that following is true:

* `asXxx()` will coerce into default/empty value of type `Xxx`: "" for `String`s, `0` for `Int`s, `false` for `Boolean` and so on. THIS IS EXISTING BEHAVIOR of 3.0 (no change)
* `asXxx(Xxx defValue)` will simply return `defValue`. THIS IS CHANGING
* `asXxxOpt()` will simply return "missing" optional: `Optional.empty()`, `OptionalInt.empty()` and so on. THIS IS CHANGING

Note: no changes suggested for behavior of non-coercing accessors (`xxxValue()`, `xxxValue(defValue)`, `xxxValueOpt()` -- `stringValue()`, `stringValue(String defValue)`, `Optional<String> stringValueOpt()`
