problems.title: Cop idea: recommend `exception: false` over `rescue nil` when using `Integer()` and `Float()`
problems.issue_body:
A common pattern found in Ruby codebases is:

```ruby
Integer(foo) rescue nil

# or sometimes

begin
  Integer(foo)
rescue ArgumentError
  nil
end
```


This new cop would recommend (for Ruby 2.6+):

```ruby
Integer(foo, exception: false)
```

Benefits: if `foo` is a method call that raises an exception, the `rescue nil` swallows the underlying exception, whereas the `exception: false` form strictly swallows conversion errors.

It's also [supposedly 2x faster](https://www.bigbinary.com/blog/ruby-2-6-adds-option-to-not-raise-exception-for-integer-float-methods) (haven't tested myself)

problems.title: `Style/TrailingCommaIn{Array,Hash}Literal` should not put a trailing comma immediately preceding a `}`/`]`
problems.issue_body:
## Context As far as I am aware, the rationale for trailing commas has always been: - they make for cleaner diffs when adding/removing elements ```diff { foo: 123, + bar: 456, } ``` vs ```diff { - foo: 123 + foo: 123, + bar: 456 } ``` - they avoid the risk of accidentally forgetting to add a comma following the proceeding element when appending a new one ```diff { foo: 123 # ❌ + bar: 456 } ``` Therefore, a trailing comma proceeding a `}` on the same line serves no purpose, as the line would still need to be edited to change values, trailing comma or not: ```diff { foo: 12, bar: 34, - biz: 56, baz: 78, } + biz: 56, baz: 78, + more: 90, } ``` ```diff { foo: 12, bar: 34, - biz: 56, baz: 78 } + biz: 56, baz: 78, + more: 90 } ``` ## Expected behavior `Style/TrailingCommaInHashLiteral`, when using `consistent_comma`, should consider the following code correct: ```ruby { foo: 12, bar: 34, biz: 56, baz: 78 } ``` ## Actual behavior `Style/TrailingCommaInHashLiteral`, when using `consistent_comma`, requires the following change ```diff { foo: 12, bar: 34, - biz: 56, baz: 78 } + biz: 56, baz: 78, } ```
rubocop --debug output ``` $ bundle exec rubocop --only Style/TrailingCommaInHashLiteral --debug For ~/src/local/rubocop-bug: configuration from ~/src/local/rubocop-bug/.rubocop.yml Default configuration from ~/.gem/ruby/2.7.1/gems/rubocop-1.18.3/config/default.yml [...] Inspecting 2 files Scanning ~src/local/rubocop-bug/Gemfile Loading cache from ~/.cache/rubocop_cache/8909d50e923b0c43f2209673b32e44a0bb04a8f9/1acc38264efb39768ff7b6c492dd2cbf87baf7ae/28c790a0a9c5b27103db82cc6c4bc236a59e3112 .Scanning ~/src/local/rubocop-bug/script.rb Loading cache from ~/.cache/rubocop_cache/8909d50e923b0c43f2209673b32e44a0bb04a8f9/1acc38264efb39768ff7b6c492dd2cbf87baf7ae/005dc2221bf5756dc9e26d1f4166040e37b98ff1 C Offenses: script.rb:2:12: C: [Correctable] Style/TrailingCommaInHashLiteral: Put a comma after the last item of a multiline hash. uiz: 56, baz: 78 } ^^^^^^^ 2 files inspected, 1 offense detected, 1 offense auto-correctable Finished in 0.4630139999790117 seconds ```
**This same issue is present in `Style/TrailingCommaInArrayLiteral`.** ## Steps to reproduce the problem - ```yml # .rubocop.yml Style/TrailingCommaInHashLiteral: EnforcedStyleForMultiline: consistent_comma ``` - ```ruby # example.rb { foo: 12, bar: 34, biz: 56, baz: 78 } ``` ## RuboCop version ```sh $ bundle exec rubocop -V 1.18.3 (using Parser 3.0.2.0, rubocop-ast 1.8.0, running on ruby 2.7.1 x86_64-darwin19) ```

problems.title: `Lint/Void` and unary operators
problems.issue_body:
We're having a bit of a discussion over at https://github.com/minimagick/minimagick/issues/584 as to `Lint/Void` and an effectful `+` or `+@` definition.

The issue at hand is that it's considered a "safe" cop which is corrected by `--safe`. In this case, `+` and `+@` are giving commands directly to an invocation of `ImageMagick`; see [an example in the README](https://github.com/minimagick/minimagick?tab=readme-ov-file#plus-options):

> ### "Plus" options
> 
> ```rb
> MiniMagick.convert do |convert|
>   convert << "input.jpg"
>   convert.repage.+
>   convert.distort.+("Perspective", "more args")
> end
> ```
> ```
> magick input.jpg +repage +distort Perspective 'more args'
> ```

Running Rubocop with `--safe` will change these invocations to `convert.repage` and `convert.distort`, which in turn modifies the resulting command.

There isn't a very clear way to avoid this, as detailed by a maintainer over in that issue, and while it may be unusual, I think it's valid to question the assumption that all prefix/infix operators are effect-free and safe to change automatically.

Thoughts appreciated!

problems.title: Option for `Naming/VariableName` to disallow certain identifiers
problems.issue_body:
## Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

There are certain methods or predefined variables that shouldn't be overwritten/redefined.

#### Don't do this
```ruby
require = "I'm required"
# In a rails controller
request = UserRequest.find(id)
params = { lookup: 'string' }
```

#### Do this instead
```ruby
require_str = "I'm required"
# In a rails controller
user_request = UserRequest.find(id)
my_params = { lookup: 'string' }
```

## Describe the solution you'd like

Add an option or two similar but opposite to `AllowedIdentifiers` and `AllowedPatterns`, perhaps `DisallowedIdentifiers` and `DisallowedPatterns`

## Describe alternatives you've considered

There may be a way to achieve this with a regex in `AllowedPatterns` but that requires more regex knowledge than I currently have. It would be much easier to throw a list of identifiers that shouldn't be used into a `DisallowedIdentifiers` option

problems.title: `Style/HashSlice` cop wrongly recommends slicing on a `.select` block argument
problems.issue_body:
## Expected behavior

I don't expect RuboCop to recommend `.slice` with an expression like this:

```ruby
results = referenced_types_by_source_type
  .select { |source_type, referenced_types| referenced_types.include?(source_type) }
```

The `.include?` inside the `.select` is using a block argument from the `.select` block itself. I don't believe there's any way to replace this with `.slice`, and I don't expect RuboCop to recommend it.

## Actual behavior

RuboCop recommends something that doesn't work (and can never work):

```
Inspecting 1 file
Scanning /Users/myron/Development/rubocop_bug.rb
For /Users/myron/Development: Default configuration from /Users/myron/.rvm/gems/ruby-3.3.4/gems/rubocop-1.72.2/config/default.yml
C

Offenses:

rubocop_bug.rb:16:4: C: [Correctable] Style/HashSlice: Use slice(*referenced_types) instead.
  .select { |source_type, referenced_types| referenced_types.include?(source_type) }
   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

1 file inspected, 1 offense detected, 1 offense autocorrectable
```

...but `slice(*referenced_types)` can't work since `referenced_types` no longer exists when the `.select` block is removed.

## Steps to reproduce the problem

Put this into a Ruby script and run it.

```ruby
require "bundler/inline"

gemfile do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  gem "rubocop", "1.72.2"
end

referenced_types_by_source_type = {
  "Foo" => ["Foo", "Bar"],
  "Bar" => [],
  "Bazz" => ["Bar"]
}

results = referenced_types_by_source_type
  .select { |source_type, referenced_types| referenced_types.include?(source_type) }

if ENV["PRINT"]
  puts results
end

require "rubocop"
RuboCop::CLI.new.run(["--format", "progress", "--only", "Style/HashSlice", "--debug", __FILE__])
```

## RuboCop version

1.72.2.

problems.title: `Lint/LiteralAsCondition` makes invalid autocorrections
problems.issue_body:
After upgrading to 1.73.0, Lint/LiteralAsCondition is causing the following autocorrections:

```ruby
- h.label_tag(name, class: errors[name.to_sym] && "error")
+ h.label_tag(name, class: errors[name.to_sym])
```

```ruby
 def message
   "Remote provider %s returned %s%s" % [
-    provider, result, desc && " (#{desc})",
+    provider, result, desc,
   ]
 end
```

In both cases, the value of the expression is used for more than just a boolean check. This would be safe for boolean expressions in conditionals (`if bool`, `elsif bool`, `unless bool`, `while bool`, `until bool`, `bool ? expr1 : expr2`).  But for anything else we may care about the distinction between `nil` vs `false` or `true` vs other truthy values.

Could this be related to #13117?

--------

## Expected behavior

These should not be reported as offenses, nor should they be autocorrected.

## Actual behavior

They are reported as offenses and incompatibly autocorrected.

## Steps to reproduce the problem

See examples above.

## RuboCop version

1.73.0

problems.title: `Style/RedundantCondition` is doing unsafe corrections
problems.issue_body:
After https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/pull/13729 the `Style/RedundantCondition`  is doing corrections that I don't believe are safe.

One example from the Rails codebase:

```ruby
     def save(**) # :nodoc:
-      Suppressor.registry[self.class.name] ? true : super
+      Suppressor.registry[self.class.name] || super
     end
```

This change the code from returning `true` to return anything that is "thruthy", which in some case could be a problem.

problems.title: Split "ClassAndModuleChildren" rule in 2 rules
problems.issue_body:
## Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

In my company we use this rules:

- Use always plural for namespaces. This namespaces need to be `Module`s.
- Use always singular for object. This object need to be `Class`es.

The result is:

```ruby
module Companies::Products
  class TagService
  end
end
```

Then then rubocop is always complaying. The rubocop rule that complains is `ClassAndModuleChildren`

## Describe the solution you'd like

I would like to split the rubocop rule `Style/ClassAndModuleChildren` in 2.

Having `Style/ClassChildren` and `Style/ModuleChildren`, it would allow me to define it this way:

```yml
Style/ModuleChildren:
  EnforcedStyle: "compact"
Style/ClassChildren:
  EnforcedStyle: "nested"
```

problems.title: EmptyConditionalBody autocorrect can result in breaking logic changes
problems.issue_body:
Looking at EmptyConditionalBody spec, some autocorrect scenarios (in `expect_correction` blocks) actually result in logic-breaking changes. For example:

https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/blob/3f24b822a37f08e54a3e076e3a091f808adc6fa9/spec/rubocop/cop/lint/empty_conditional_body_spec.rb#L115-L133

To make it clearer here's the same case but with more real-world-y variable names:

```rb
# before
if show_version
  puts VERSION
elsif dry_run
elsif delete_files
  `rm -rf *`
end

# after
if show_version
  puts VERSION
elsif delete_files
  `rm -rf *`
end
```

After an autocorrect run, `dry_run` flag is no longer used which is a breaking change.

problems.issue_body:
I found an interesting bug, `Lint/LiteralAsCondition` auto-correct was causing a syntax error. But I realized after checking more deeply, that the code was never doing what it was supposed to do, so not sure if this is still something that should be addressed or not.

--------

## Expected behavior

Not sure :)

## Actual behavior

```
❯ ruby test.rb 
test.rb: --> test.rb
unexpected void value expression
  1  def my_method(param)
> 2    puts return if param.nil?
> 3    puts param
  4  end

test.rb:2: void value expression (SyntaxError)
  puts return if param.nil?
```

## Steps to reproduce the problem
We have code like this, where param is checked and if it's not there we wanted to log (replaced by puts for the example) and return
```
def my_method(param)
  puts "param was nil" && return if param.nil?
  puts param
end
```
This get's corrected to
```
def my_method(param)
  puts return if param.nil?
  puts param
end
```
causing the SyntaxError, but even without it, the code was never logging, but just returned nil.

After fixing it to be `puts("param is nil") && return if param.nil?` `Lint/LiteralAsCondition` didn't complain anymore about it.

problems.title: Cop idea: Predicate Methods Suffix
problems.issue_body:
## Description

The names of predicate methods (methods that return a boolean value) should end in a question mark (i.e. `Array#empty?`). Methods that don't return a boolean, shouldn't end in a question mark.

https://rubystyle.guide/#bool-methods-qmark

## Describe the solution you'd like

```ruby
# bad
def my_method
  x == y
end

# good
def my_method?
  x == y
end
```

```ruby
# bad
def my_method
  return false if x == y

  true
end

# good
def my_method?
  return false if x == y

  true
end
```

```ruby
# good
def my_method
  return false if x == y

  nil
end
```

problems.title: ReturnInVoidContext false positive in dynamic module class initializer with `define_method`
problems.issue_body:
## False positive

When using `define_method` in a dynamic module class initializer I get a `Lint/ReturnInVoidContext: Do not return a value in initialize.`:

```ruby
class MyModule < Module
  def initialize
    define_method :my_method do
      return true if [true, false].sample # <-- Lint/ReturnInVoidContext

      false
    end
  end
end

class MyClass
  include MyModule.new
end

MyClass.new.my_method
```

The code above is simplified for brevity, in my real code the method names are dynamic based on arguments passed to the initializer.

I think `return` is doing what it is supposed to do there and only applied to the block/dynamically defined method, or am I mistaken?

I think the flagging got introduced in this PR: https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/pull/13960

problems.issue_body:
Given the following setup:

```
bundle exec rubocop -V

  - rubocop-rails 2.29.0
  - rubocop-rake 0.6.0

AllCops:
  TargetRubyVersion: 3.4
```

The following code suggests to use splat:

```ruby
def fetch(*, **, &)
  Foo.meth1(*, **) do
    Bar.meth2(*, **, &) # INCORRECT: Style/ArgumentsForwarding --> suggests ... splat
  end
end
```

The exact error is:

```
Style/ArgumentsForwarding Style/ArgumentsForwarding: Use shorthand syntax `...` for arguments forwarding.
```

Here I intentionally do **not** want to pass the `&` block into `Foo.meth1`, but I **do** want to pass it into `Bar.meth2`.

If I recall correctly prior to Ruby 3.4 (or 3.3.?) this usage of anonymous block `&` was not allowed, hence maybe the cop isn't updated for it.

problems.title: `--server` mode does not honor `--config` cli options
problems.issue_body:
When running `rubocop --server --config path/to/config.yml`, RuboCop server only restarts when picking up changes in the standard `.rubocop.yml` file and not to `path/to/config.yml`.

--------

## Expected behavior

RuboCop automatically restarts the server when changes occur in the file listed in the `--config` CLI argument

## Actual behavior

RuboCop detects exclusively detects changes to the standard `.rubocop.yml`, no matter the `--config` CLI option:

```
% rubocop  --config .rubocop-ci.yml --server app/models/user.rb
Inspecting 1 file
.

1 file inspected, no offenses detected
% echo 'Style: { Enabled: false }' >> .rubocop-ci.yml
% rubocop  --config .rubocop-ci.yml --server app/models/user.rb
Inspecting 1 file
.

1 file inspected, no offenses detected
% echo 'Style: { Enabled: false }' >> .rubocop.yml
% rubocop  --config .rubocop-ci.yml --server app/models/user.rb
RuboCop version incompatibility found, RuboCop server restarting...
RuboCop server starting on 127.0.0.1:59337.
Inspecting 1 file
.

1 file inspected, no offenses detected
```

## Steps to reproduce the problem

1. Start rubocop in server mode with a custom config `rubocop --server --config config.yml file.rb`
2. edit config.yml
3. Re-run `rubocop --server --config config.yml file.rb` and observe how the server does not restart
4. edit `.rubocop.yml`
5. Re-run `rubocop --server --config config.yml file.rb` and observe the server restart unnecessarily.

problems.title: `Style/RedundantSelf` is not safe for autocorrection
problems.issue_body:
Calling an `self.method` in a sentence modifier (`... if self.method`) should not be considered redundant if the left part is executing a variable assignment in non-plain form.

Example:

```rb
def foo
	# should be good
	if self.bar == '1'
		bar = 'one'
	else
		bar = self.bar
	end if self.bar.present?

	bar
end
```


--------

## Expected behavior

**🚨 This cop should not be safe for autocorrection.**

Personally i would prefer to correct the code, so reporting an offense is not bad, but the autocorrect removes the `self.` and breaks the code.

This is an example on how to manually correct this offense:

```rb
def foo
	# moving the assignment to the very beginning 
	# of the sentence modifier fixes the offense
	bar = if self.bar == '1'
		'one'
	else
		'other'
	end if self.bar.present?

	bar
end
```

## Actual behavior

This is what the autocorrect does:

```rb

	# this breaks as the local `bar` variable is always nil
	# when evaluating the right side of the sentence modifier
	if self.bar == '1'
		bar = 'one'
	else
		bar = self.bar
	end if bar.present?

	bar
end
```

* enable the cop (and AutoCorrect) in .rubocop.yml `Style/RedundantSelf`
* run the autocorrect `bin/rubocop --only Style/RedundantSelf -a`

problems.title: Refine `Style/FetchEnvVar` to preserve readability and intention
problems.issue_body:
## Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

I'm frustrated with how the `Style/FetchEnvVar` cop works. It currently encourages replacing `ENV["FOO"]` with `ENV.fetch("FOO", nil)`, but this replacement doesn’t offer any real advantage. Using `fetch` with `nil` as the fallback essentially mimics the behavior of `ENV["FOO"]`, while losing readability and not leveraging the main benefit of `fetch`, which is to explicitly handle missing keys.

## Describe the solution you'd like

I’d like to propose that the cop be smarter about when it suggests using `ENV.fetch`. Specifically, it should avoid autocorrecting or flagging `ENV["FOO"]` usages unless a meaningful default value is being provided (i.e., something other than `nil`). If the intention is to allow for a fallback value, `fetch` makes sense; otherwise, it does not add value and may even reduce code clarity.

## Describe alternatives you've considered

One alternative is to disable the cop entirely, but that removes any enforcement for meaningful uses of `ENV.fetch`. Another idea is to allow configuration of acceptable default values or provide an option to ignore `nil` as a second argument.

## Additional context

The current autocorrect suggestion creates code like `ENV.fetch("FOO", nil)` which is functionally identical to `ENV["FOO"]`, but more verbose and arguably harder to read. This reduces developer confidence in the value provided by the cop.

problems.title: Fix Style/RedundantParentheses pattern matching OR condition
problems.issue_body:
## Expected behavior

I would expect the following to be valid (and require the use of parentheses due to the OR condition):

``` ruby
def only_double_splats?(parameters) = (parameters in [[:keyrest]] | [[:keyrest, *]])
```

## Actual behavior

I'll get the following:

``` ruby
lib/marameters/probe.rb:60:31: C: [Correctable] Style/RedundantParentheses: Don't use parentheses around a one-line pattern matching.
    def only_double_splats? = (parameters in [[:keyrest]] | [[:keyrest, *]])
                              ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
```

If I use auto-correct, the above will go way but then my specs will fail because the OR condition (i.e. `[[:keyrest, *]]`) will not be respected.

## Steps to reproduce the problem

Use the following code:

``` ruby
def only_double_splats?(parameters) = parameters in [[:keyrest]] | [[:keyrest, *]]

parameters = Module.new { def test(**one) = super }
                   .instance_method(:test)
                   .parameters

only_double_splats?(parameters) == true # false
```

The problem with the above is that this is returned instead:

``` ruby
[
  [
    :keyrest,
    :one
  ]
]
```

...which is definitely _not_ `true`.

## RuboCop version

```
1.76.1 (using Parser 3.3.8.0, Prism 1.4.0, rubocop-ast 1.45.1, analyzing as Ruby 3.4, running on ruby 3.4.4) [arm64-darwin24.5.0]
  - rubocop-capybara 2.22.1
  - rubocop-disable_syntax 0.2.0
  - rubocop-packaging 0.6.0
  - rubocop-performance 1.25.0
  - rubocop-thread_safety 0.7.2
  - rubocop-rake 0.7.1
  - rubocop-rspec 3.6.0
```

## Notes 

This is a follow up to Issue #14239 where I mentioned this was a syntax error but I was incorrect. This is a logic error, instead, which will cause your specs to fail if you drop the parentheses.

problems.issue_body:
## Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

A new `Naming/PredicateMethod` cop seems quite useful 😻 

I noticed one case that it potentially could catch, but didn't, at the time: the return value is calculated by a predicate. For example:

```ruby
class File
  def ruby_file

  end
end

* the method should probably be named `ruby_file?`

problems.title: Unsafe `Style/RedundantSelf` cop auto-correct with conditional assignment operator
problems.issue_body:
(thanks for working on Rubocop! 🙏 apologies if this has already been addressed.)

When a local variable is set using conditional assignment with the result from another module method, and safe-autocorrect with `Style/RedundantSelf` is run, then `self` is removed but the behaviour of the code changes completely.

I think it makes sense for the cop warning to be raised, but the safe auto-correct shouldn't break the code or change its behaviour. An unsafe autocorrect would be fine, of course.

I understand that conditional assignment would be pointless in the example below, but sometimes you have a lot of these issues to comb through. Having the safe-autocorrect changing the behaviour of the code wasn't expected. 

Happy to try and put in a fix for this in case it's really a bug.

--------

## Expected behavior

Running `bundle exec rubocop --only Style/RedundantSelf rubocop_redundant_self.rb -a` should not change the behaviour of the code below.

```ruby
module RubocopRedundantSelf
  def self.example
    foo ||= self.foo
  end

  def self.foo
    "hello"
  end
end
```


## Actual behavior

The behaviour of the code changes - now `foo` is always nil:
```ruby
module RubocopRedundantSelf
  def self.example
    foo ||= foo # <-- self is removed here
  end

  # (...)
end
```

## Steps to reproduce the problem

Full sample code:
```ruby
module RubocopRedundantSelf
  def self.example
    foo ||= self.foo

    if foo.nil?
      raise "foo must not be nil"
    end

    foo
  end

  def self.foo
    "hello"
  end
end

puts RubocopRedundantSelf.example
```

1. if you run the code, it works fine:
```bash
$ ruby rubocop_redundant_self.rb
#=> hello
```

2. Run safe autocorrect:
```bash
$ rubocop --only Style/RedundantSelf -a

C: [Corrected] Style/RedundantSelf: Redundant self detected.
    foo ||= self.foo
            ^^^^

1 file inspected, 2 offenses detected, 1 offense corrected
```

3. Resulting code:
```ruby
module RubocopRedundantSelf

    foo ||= foo # <---- self is removed here

    if foo.nil?
      raise "foo must not be nil"
    end

    foo
  end

  def self.foo
    "hello"
  end
end

puts RubocopRedundantSelf.example
```

```bash

problems.title: Issue with `Layout/SpaceBeforeBrackets` in the `. [](key)` form
problems.issue_body:
## Expected behavior

Hashes and Arrays can be accessed using the `.[](key_or_index)` syntax.

```
irb(main):001> array = [1]
=> [1]
irb(main):002> array.[](0)
=> 1
irb(main):003> array. [](0)
=> 1
```

Even when this syntax is used, I expect `Layout/SpaceBeforeBrackets` to properly detect the presence of the space and offer an appropriate autocorrection.

```
collection. [](index_or_key)
           ^ Remove the space before the opening brackets.
```

## Actual behavior

However, when there is a space like this, it incorrectly reports the offense position.

```
collection. [](index_or_key)
          ^^ Remove the space before the opening brackets.
```

To make matters worse, when autocorrect is run, it transforms the code into one that results in a syntax error.

```
collection[](index_or_key)
```

## Steps to reproduce the problem

I verified it using an RSpec example:

```diff
diff --git a/spec/rubocop/cop/layout/space_before_brackets_spec.rb b/spec/rubocop/cop/layout/space_before_brackets_spec.rb

If it is known that a variable can't be `nil`, suggest removing useless safe navigation calls.

```ruby
# bad
x = var.foo # <--- here, if var is nil, an error will be raised in any case
var&.bar    # <--- unnecessary safe navigation

x = var.foo
var.bar

# bad
if var
  var&.foo
end

# good
if var
  var.foo
end
```

problems.title: Style/SafeNavigation reports on complex nil checks that should pass
problems.issue_body:
## Expected behavior

The following code is flagged as a Style/SafeNavigation violation.

```ruby
end_time = end_date.nil? ? nil : end_date.in_time_zone(timezone) + 1.day
```

The shape of the code actually matches one of the exceptions listed in the [documentation](https://docs.rubocop.org/rubocop/cops_style.html#stylesafenavigation):

```
foo ? foo * 42 : nil      # Ignored `foo&.*(42)` due to unclear readability benefit.
```

I think the correct fix is to ignore any safe navigation where there is arithmetic or other ignored methods (like `[]`) anywhere in the non-nil side of the conditional.

## Actual behavior

Arithmetic calls are excepted in the docs due to readability, but because there is a method call before the arithmetic but inside the conditional, rubocop incorrectly fixes to non-functional code.

```ruby
end_time = end_date&.in_time_zone(timezone) + 1.day
```

This seems to have started around 1.79, since we're only getting these violations now, whereas they weren't triggering before, though I'm not certain this is the exact version where it changed.

## Steps to reproduce the problem

Save the following code:

```ruby
end_time = end_date.nil? ? nil : end_date.in_time_zone(timezone) + 1.day
```

See that it violates Style/SafeNavigation. It should not.

Try auto-correct, see that it produces code that will error when `nil` receives `+`.

I don't mind if this code has offenses, but this auto-correction is WRONG; must not happen.

problems.title: Incorrect suggestion in Style/BitwisePredicate
problems.issue_body:
The following line:
```ruby
(1 & num) == 1
```
does raise the following error with Rubocop:
```
Style/BitwisePredicate: Replace with 1.allbits?(num) for comparison with bit flags.
  (1 & num) == 1
  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
```

But these are not the same statements. It's easiest to see with `num = 3`:
```
irb(main):001> (1 & 3) == 1
=> true
irb(main):002> 1.allbits?(3)
=> false
```
It looks like the actual fix in this case is the other way around:
```
irb(main):003> 3.allbits?(1)
=> true
```

If the original source is `(num & 1) == 1`, the suggested fix is `num.allbits?(1)`, which is actually correct.

The matcher is defined as follows:
```ruby
# @!method allbits?(node)
def_node_matcher :allbits?, <<~PATTERN
  {
    (send (begin (send _ :& _flags)) :== _flags)
    (send (begin (send _flags :& _)) :== _flags)
  }
PATTERN
```
And the suggestion as:
```ruby
bit_operation = node.receiver.children.first
lhs, _operator, rhs = *bit_operation
preferred = "#{lhs.source}.#{preferred_method}(#{rhs.source})"
```
So this probably needs to flip the `lhs` and `rhs` in the output in case the `_flags` matches the `lhs`.

--------

```
1.79.2 (using Parser 3.3.9.0, rubocop-ast 1.46.0, analyzing as Ruby 2.7, running on ruby 3.3.7) [x86_64-linux-gnu]
```

problems.title: VSCode LSP formatter crashes
problems.issue_body:
Hi there, I'm one of the maintainers of [Homebrew](https://brew.sh/), and we're running into a RuboCop/Ruby LSP issue in our [Homebrew/brew](https://github.com/Homebrew/brew) repository. When formatting a document with correctable RuboCop violations, the formatting fails with a message like this (full log is below):

```
An internal error occurred for the Layout/IndentationWidth cop. (RubyLsp::Requests::Support::InternalRuboCopError)
Updating to a newer version of RuboCop may solve this.
For more details, run RuboCop on the command line.
```

I reported this initially to the Ruby LSP in https://github.com/Shopify/ruby-lsp/issues/3723, but since it's only a problem when using the `rubocop` formatter and not `rubocop_internal`, it sounds like it's actually a Ruby LSP addon issue.

Unfortunately, I can't seem to reproduce the issue when running `rubocop` manually on the command line, or outside of VSCode.

When reporting to Ruby LSP, I was told the issue is related to "reusing the existing Prism parse result to avoid double parsing", and there are a handful of other issues that are related (https://github.com/Shopify/ruby-lsp/issues/3665, https://github.com/Shopify/ruby-lsp/issues/3657).

--------

## Expected behavior

Formatting the document should behave as expected

## Actual behavior

Here are the logs from VSCode. I'm happy to provide any additional information I can.

```
2025-08-23 00:35:16.872 [info] (homebrew) Determined that document should be indexed: file:///opt/homebrew/Library/Homebrew/formula.rb
2025-08-23 00:35:22.052 [info] (homebrew) [Error - 12:35:22 AM] Formatting failed with
: /opt/homebrew/Library/Homebrew/vendor/bundle/ruby/3.4.0/gems/rubocop-1.80.0/lib/rubocop/lsp/stdin_runner.rb:67:in 'RuboCop::Lsp::StdinRunner#run': An internal error occurred for the Layout/IndentationWidth cop. (RubyLsp::Requests::Support::InternalRuboCopError)

problems.title: Commas before closing brackets do not look consistent
problems.issue_body:
Rubocop has several style cops related to trailing commas. The meaning of trailing commas is often to allow adding new method arguments or structure elements without changing previous ones.

However, having syntax like [this](https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/blob/8a80173b48bbd16224903f462093dd985374f62b/spec/rubocop/cop/style/trailing_comma_in_arguments_spec.rb#L443) I won't be able to add new argument at the end without changing lines with existing arguments.

Should we disable comma before closing brackets?

--------

## Expected behavior

Commas right before closing brackets should not be allowed

## Actual behavior
```
some_method(a: "b",
  c: "d",)
```
is a valid syntax

## Steps to reproduce the problem

1. Use this cop
```
Style/TrailingCommaInArguments:
  EnforcedStyleForMultiline: consistent_comma

2. Add code described above
3. Run rubocop

problems.title: Arguments incorrectly identified as being shadowed by a local variable
problems.issue_body:
In certain situations, RuboCop incorrectly identifies arguments as being "shadowed by a local variable before it was used."

Take this example method that downloads a file if certain conditions are met, and then returns whether the file was downloaded or not

```ruby
# target_exists: whether the target file exists or not. If it doesn't exist, we must download
# other_conditions_met: if these conditions are met and the file exists, skip the download
# skip_download: don't download, even if `other_conditions_met` is true. However, always download if `target_exists` is false
def download_to_target?(endpoint, target_exists:, other_conditions_met:, skip_download: false)
  skip_download = false unless target_exists
  skip_download ||= target_exists && other_conditions_met

  begin
    puts "Downloading file #{endpoint}" unless skip_download
  rescue StandardError
    skip_download = false
  end

  !skip_download
end
```

Normally, the download process is skipped if `target_exists` and `other_conditions_met`. The `skip_download` argument is used to override `other_conditions_met`, and skip the download even if those conditions are false. However, we never want to allow skipping the download if `target_exists` is false.

The effect of `skip_download` is demonstrated here:

```console
$ bin/console
irb(main):001> download_to_target? "foo.txt", target_exists: true, other_conditions_met: false, skip_download: false
Downloading file foo.txt
=> true
irb(main):002> download_to_target? "foo.txt", target_exists: true, other_conditions_met: false, skip_download: true
=> false
```

As you can see, modifying `skip_download` has an effect on the output. However, `rubocop` gives the following message:

```console
$ bundle exec rubocop
Inspecting 8 files
...W....

Offenses:

lib/rubocop/test.rb:13:78: W: Lint/ShadowedArgument: Argument skip_download was shadowed by a local variable before it was used.
    def download_to_target?(endpoint, target_exists:, other_conditions_met:, skip_download: false)
                                                                             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

8 files inspected, 1 offense detected
```

I believe this is incorrect, because as shown in the console output above, passing different values to `skip_download` returns a different result, indicating that `skip_download` is not actually shadowed.

--------

## Expected behavior

No RuboCop violations

## Actual behavior

```console
$ bundle exec rubocop --debug
For /Users/rylanpolster/Desktop/rubocop-test: configuration from /Users/rylanpolster/Desktop/rubocop-test/.rubocop.yml
Use parallel by default.

problems.title: Private method has Style/EndlessMethod false-positive that would cause Layout/LineLength offense
problems.issue_body:
It seems like the `private` keyword is not counted when considering if a `Style/EndlessMethod` correction would exceed the line length. With a line-length of 100:

```ruby
class Example
  def without_private_this_will_not_exceed_line_length
    Other.my_mid_length_method_name
  end

  def without_private_this_will_exceed_line_length_aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa
    Other.my_mid_length_method_name
  end

  private def with_private_this_will_exceed_line_length_but_not_without
    Other.my_mid_length_method_name
  end
end
```

The first and third methods have `Style/EndlessMethod` offenses, but correcting the third leads to a line that is too long.

--------

## Steps to reproduce the problem

Ruby file as above. Rubocop config:
```
AllCops:
  TargetRubyVersion: 3.4
  EnabledByDefault: true
  NewCops: enable
Layout/LineLength:
  Max: 100
Style/EndlessMethod:
  Enabled: true
  EnforcedStyle: require_single_line
```

## Expected behavior

Offense for `without_private_this_will_not_exceed_line_length`, but no offense for `with_private_this_will_exceed_line_length_but_not_without` (because it exceeds the max line length due to `private`). N.b. there is no offense for `without_private_this_will_exceed_line_length_aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa`.

## Actual behavior

Offense for `without_private_this_will_not_exceed_line_length` and `with_private_this_will_exceed_line_length_but_not_without`, correcting causes a `Layout/LineLength` offense for `with_private_this_will_exceed_line_length_but_not_without`.

```

problems.title: `Style/ConstantVisibility` does not recognize multiple constants in visibility declarations
problems.issue_body:
## Description

`Style/ConstantVisibility` doesn't recognize visibility declarations when multiple constants are specified together, causing false positives.

## Current Behavior

These valid Ruby patterns incorrectly trigger offenses:

```ruby
class Foo
  BAR = 42
  BAZ = 43
  private_constant :BAR, :BAZ  # Not recognized
end
```

```ruby
class Foo
  BAR = 42
  BAZ = 43
  public_constant [:BAR, :BAZ]  # Not recognized
end
```

Both produce false positives:
```
Explicitly make `BAR` public or private using either `#public_constant` or `#private_constant`.
Explicitly make `BAZ` public or private using either `#public_constant` or `#private_constant`.
```

## Expected Behavior

The cop should recognize these valid forms for both `public_constant` and `private_constant`:
- Single: `private_constant :FOO` ✅ (currently works)
- Multiple arguments: `private_constant :FOO, :BAR` ❌ (doesn't work)
- Array: `private_constant [:FOO, :BAR]` ❌ (doesn't work)

## Proposed Solution

I'd like to submit a PR that:
- Enhances [visibility_declaration_for?](https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/blob/ad792dd84dfa8f11a3c4399885a1460380065d50/lib/rubocop/cop/style/constant_visibility.rb#L82) to handle multiple constant declarations
- Adds test cases for all scenarios
- Ensures all existing tests pass

Would this enhancement be welcome?

problems.title: Another potential false positive for Style/TrailingCommaInArguments
problems.issue_body:
In the example below, Rubocop expects commas between the `}` or `]` and the `)`, but I disagree.

I may be picking nits here since Ruby is a ninja and lets you omit curly braces when passing in `*args` to a method and it's generally the preferred way to handle an unknown number of method arguments. It becomes more relevant when the argument is a multi-line array, though.

Potentially related to #9935

--------

## Context

```yml
# .rubocop.yml
Style/TrailingCommaInArguments:
  EnforcedStyleForMultiline: consistent_comma
```

```ruby

problems.title: Style/ClassAndModuleChildren not safe within module or class
problems.issue_body:
The Style/ClassAndModuleChildren cop is not safe to correct when the code occurs within another scope. This led to a bug in JRuby's build when using automated corrections.

Nested module access will not walk up to the toplevel to look for modules or classes to open, while path-based access does do this.

--------

## Expected behavior

Code below should behave this way before or after correction, or else it should be considered an unsafe correction.

Original code:

```ruby
module X
  module Y
    puts object_id
  end
end
module Z
  module X::Y
    puts object_id
  end
end
# prints same object id for Y, because path-based access uses the toplevel X
# and reopens the existing modules
```

## Actual behavior

When corrected to nested modules, the reopen of X creates a new module tree rather than accessing the toplevel X.

Corrected code:

```ruby
...
module Z
  module X
    module Y
      puts object_id
    end
  end
end
# Reopen of X is a new module and Y is also new with a different object_id
```

Full script example of the behavior:

```ruby
module X
  module Y
    puts object_id
  end
end
module Z
  module X::Y
    puts object_id
  end
end
module Q
  module X
    module Y
      puts object_id
    end
  end
end
```

Output from example, showing that the correction is not safe:

```
$ cx 3.4 ruby -v blah.rb
ruby 3.4.5 (2025-07-16 revision 20cda200d3) +PRISM [arm64-darwin24]
16
16
24
```

$ rubocop -V

problems.title: Add setting to `Style/CaseEquality` to allow `x.===(y)` (explicit parentheses)
problems.issue_body:
## Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

```ruby
/some_pattern/ === x
```

This code is rejected by the `Style/CaseEquality` cop. The recommended style here requires doing

```ruby
case x when /some_pattern/ then true else false end
```

which is more verbose.

One of the main motivations for banning `===` is to ensure that people who frequently work with JavaScript doesn't use `===` out of habit, mistakenly assuming that it is the "normal" equality operator of `==`.

However, there are valid use cases for `===`. For example, if you tried to rewrite `/some_pattern/ === x` without, you either end up with the verbose solution above, or the more brittle solution of

```ruby
x =~ /some_pattern/
```

which will raise an exception if `x` doesn't have the `=~` method, or

```ruby
/some_pattern/ =~ x
```

which will raise an exception if `x` cannot be implicitly converted into a `String`.

In this case, `/some_pattern/ === x` is the least brittle and most concise solution to the problem. 

## Describe the solution you'd like

It would be nice to have an option for the `Style/CaseEquality` cop that permits the call if it uses the explicit `x.===(y)` syntax, i.e., an explicit `.` and parentheses.

- It's unlikely that people switching between a JavaScript and Ruby codebase would habitually write this form—it would be far more likely that they intend to call Ruby's case equality operator, not generic equality.
- It's still more terse than the alternative of fully expanding a `case/when` expression.

This would be guarded with an option (like the two existing options for the `Style/CaseEquality` cop: `AllowOnConstant` and `AllowOnSelfClass`).

As a suggestion: `AllowOnExplicitCall`, but I'm open to alternative names.

## Describe alternatives you've considered

There are some alternatives considered above, like

- just use `case/when`
- just disable the cop when this is needed
- codebases could define a separate helper method, like `Utils.case_equality(x, y)` to make things more explicit

## Additional context

The concrete problem we're encountering is when upgrading legacy Ruby codebases that relied on the existence of `Object#=~`, which was made deprecated and eventually removed. As we find instances where the code was relying on this, we would like to be able to use `===` to replace the call to `=~` but we run against this cop.


- - - - -

If adding such an option is a welcome change, I'd be happy to contribute this change.

## Steps to reproduce the problem

```bash

```
```rb
# lint.rb

def generate_pin
  tried_codes = Set.new
  i = 0
  try = 0

  # possible_code_combinations represents the theoretical maximum number of
  #   pins of the desired length
  # max_tries represents a sane number after which to stop trying to
  #   generate a pin
  #
  # Both are required as `i` (which counts up to possible_code_combinations)
  # increments only when a pin is tried for the first time. While `try` is
  # incremented in every iteration
  while i < possible_code_combinations && try < max_tries
    try += 1
    pin.code = generate_code_candidate

    # Populate validaton errors on the model
    pin.valid?

    # Skip codes that we've already tried
    # http://ruby-doc.org/stdlib-2.6.3/libdoc/set/rdoc/Set.html#method-i-add-3F
    next if tried_codes.add?(pin.code).nil? || weak?

    pin.save if persist

    if persist && pin.invalid? && available?
      # The pin isn't taken or weak but it's invalid - something went wrong
      raise(ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid, pin)
    elsif available?
      return pin
    end

    i += 1
    try = 0
  end

  # the loop exited without returning a pin - there are no more valid codes
  raise(CombinationPoolExhaustedError)
end

problems.title: --force-default-config does not prevent loading of project `.rubocop.yml` in v1.82.0+
problems.issue_body:
## Steps to reproduce the problem

1. Create a minimal project with a `.rubocop.yml` that references a non-existent file:

```bash
mkdir /tmp/rubocop-test && cd /tmp/rubocop-test

cat > Gemfile << 'EOF'
source "https://rubygems.org"
gem "rubocop", "1.82.0"
EOF

cat > .rubocop.yml << 'EOF'
inherit_from: config/defaults.yml

AllCops:
  TargetRubyVersion: 3.2
EOF

echo 'puts "hello"' > test.rb

bundle install
```

2. Run RuboCop with `--force-default-config`:

```bash
bundle exec rubocop --force-default-config --show-cops
```

## Expected behavior

According to the `--help` output:

> `--force-default-config` Use default configuration even if configuration files are present in the directory tree.

RuboCop should ignore the project's `.rubocop.yml` entirely and use only the default configuration. The command should succeed even if `.rubocop.yml` references non-existent files.

## Actual behavior

RuboCop still attempts to resolve the `inherit_from` chain in `.rubocop.yml` and fails:

```
Configuration file not found: /tmp/rubocop-test/config/defaults.yml
```

This is a regression introduced in v1.82.0. The same command works correctly in v1.81.7.

### Bisection results

| Version | Result |
|---------|--------|
| 1.81.7  | OK     |
| 1.82.0  | FAIL   |
| 1.82.1  | FAIL   |

### Root cause analysis

The issue appears to be caused by the following line added in v1.82.0 (`lib/rubocop/cli.rb:186`):

```ruby
ConfigLoader.cache_root = ResultCache.cache_root(@config_store, @options[:cache_root])
```

`ResultCache.cache_root` calls `config_store.for_pwd` which loads `.rubocop.yml` and resolves its inheritance chain before `--force-default-config` can take effect.

### Related issue

This may share the same root cause as #14745 (`--config` flag causes `Exclude` to be ignored), which is also a regression in v1.82.0 related to configuration loading order.

## RuboCop version

```
$ bundle exec rubocop -V
1.82.1 (using Parser 3.3.10.0, rubocop-ast 1.48.0, analyzing as Ruby 2.7, running on ruby 4.0.0) [arm64-darwin25]
```

  prop :bar, String # RuboCop[Layout/ClassStructure] offense raised
  SOME_CONSTANT = "constant" # NO OFFENSE RAISED (ISSUE)

problems.title: Incorrect autocorrect for Style/HashSyntax with shorthand notation
problems.issue_body:
When requiring shorthand notation either with `consistent` or `always`, the autocorrect for Style/HashSyntax creates semantically and sometimes syntactically incorrect Ruby in certain cases.

## Steps to reproduce the problem

1. Create a file `foo.rb` with:

   ```ruby
   # frozen_string_literal: true
 
   unless foo bar: bar
     baz qux: quuz
     baz zyxxy
   end
   ```
2. Create a file `.rubocop.yml` with:
   ```yaml
   AllCops:
     NewCops: enable
     TargetRubyVersion: 3.3
   
   Style/HashSyntax:
     Enabled: true
     EnforcedShorthandSyntax: always
   ```
3. run `rubocop -a`

## Expected behavior

The file `foo.rb` is corrected, and the `foo` method call has parentheses added, like so:
```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

unless foo(bar:)
  baz qux: quuz
  baz zyxxy
end
```

## Actual behavior

The file `foo.rb` is corrected, and the `foo` method call has shorthand syntax but no parentheses, leading to a syntax error:

```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

unless foo bar:
  baz qux: quuz
  baz zyxxy
end
```

## RuboCop version

```
$ rubocop -V
1.82.1 (using Parser 3.3.10.1, Prism 1.8.0, rubocop-ast 1.49.0, analyzing as Ruby 3.3, running on ruby 4.0.0) [x86_64-linux]

module Refinements

problems.title: Cover more cases in Layout/MultilineMethodCallIndentation
problems.issue_body:
I was surprised to learn that `Layout/MultilineMethodCallIndentation` does _not_ complain about the following code (despite very clearly inconsistent indentation).

```rb
# frozen_string_literal: true

def foo
  bar(
    key: VeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeryLongClassName
 .veeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeery_long_method_name
  )
end
```

However, it seems to have been the case ever since the cop was introduced in 5cf70902becb2b5db2c60482f84b4e3fc4d19195.

Digging a bit further, it seems that the behavior was introduced (475d652f4e35a6f085d6bd2999b623036155749d) as a change to `Style/MultilineOperationIndentation` in response to a bug report (#1362) filed by myself 😅

The decision to ignore this node happens when `#inside_arg_list_parentheses?` returns true here: https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/blob/6e5fc10964a6bc7e06c1e8cf62f16ab489d0a89b/lib/rubocop/cop/mixin/multiline_expression_indentation.rb#L197-L201

## Describe the solution you'd like

```rb
# EnforcedStyle: aligned
def foo
  bar(
    key: VeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeryLongClassName
    .veeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeery_long_method_name
  )
end

# EnforcedStyle: indented_relative_to_receiver
def foo
  bar(
    key: VeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeryLongClassName
           .veeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeery_long_method_name
  )
end

# EnforcedStyle: indented
def foo
  bar(
    key: VeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeryLongClassName
      .veeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeery_long_method_name
  )
end
```

problems.issue_body:
I suspect this is caused by some change with #12754. I admit the following report was mostly generated by AI.

## Steps to reproduce the problem

Create a file `example.rb` with this content:

```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

class Example
  def initialize
    @info = {
      last_failure: if some_condition
                      some_value
                    end,
      last_result: if another_condition

                some_object
              end,

              final_value
            end
    }
  end
end
```

Run:
```bash
rubocop --only Style/IfUnlessModifier example.rb
```

Process the code

problems.title: False positive for Style/FormatStringToken in Rails validates format
problems.issue_body:
In one of our Rails apps we've a validation that uses the "format" helper to constrain a value to a matching regex, it seems the Style/FormatStringToken cop has incorrectly matched this a use of the format method, which it is not.

--------

## Expected behavior

Given an `example.rb` file with the following content:

``` ruby
class SomeModel < ApplicationRecord
  validates :colour, format: { with: /\A#[0-9a-fA-F]{6}\Z/, message: '%{colour} is not a valid hex colour' }
end
```

and running the command

```
rubocop example.rb --only Style/FormatStringToken

  validates :colour, format: { with: /\A#[0-9a-fA-F]{6}\Z/, message: '%{colour} is not a valid hex colour' }
                                                                      ^^^^^^^^^

1 file inspected, 1 offense detected

problems.title: The `Style/EmptyClassDefinition` cop warning message wording.
problems.issue_body:
The cop works fine, but the warning message it uses confused me a bit the first time I encountered it.

In particular, the `two-line class definition` wording. I believe the intention behind this cop isn't that it checks whether an empty class is a single-line or a two-line definition. For me, what the cop tries to achieve is to inform about the preference of the **'standard'** syntax over the **'dynamic'** by default. The use of the standard word includes a single or two-line preference without encouraging either. In this case, I would suggest the following wording:

> Prefer standard class definition over `Class.new` for classes with no body.

> Prefer `Class.new` over standard class definition for classes with no body.

Provided this is a desirable change, I can submit a PR.

problems.title: The `Style/EmptyClassDefinition` cop default enforced style option naming.
problems.issue_body:
This is related to https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/issues/14827, but will require more than a documentation change.

The `class_definition` configuration option, as one of the enforced styles, is misleading. Whether we use the `class` keyword or `Class.new`, they are both class definitions. The `class_new` option suggests to the reader what type of class definition we want to apply, but the `class_definition` doesn't. Therefore, I would like to propose a complementary term for the standard class definition - the `class_keyword`. 

Then the message that would include the prior considerations, use familiar language(beginner-friendly), and be more concise would look as follows:

> Use the `class` keyword instead of `Class.new` to define an empty class.

The opposite would then be:

> Use `Class.new` instead of the `class` keyword to define an empty class.

This is a breaking change, but since the cop is pending, it may still be viable to do.

problems.title: Calling map/collect with block inside method that accepts block produces unexpected result
problems.issue_body:
## Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

I spent 45 minutes trying to work out why this didn't work:

```ruby
render json: queries.map do |q|
  { _id: q.id }
end
```

Turns out, Ruby is parsing it like this (giving block to the first method called, not the nearest):

```ruby
render(json: queries.map) do |q|
  { _id: q.id }
end
```

And apparently `queries.map` without a block is valid syntax, and returns an array of the raw objects.

Rails then serializes the array of raw objects into a hash containing all the records attributes.

I had to change to this:

```ruby
results = queries.map do |q|
  { _id: q.id }
end

render json: results
```

## Describe the solution you'd like

A Rubocop rule that catches when using a block method (like map, collector, filter, etc) inside another method that also takes a block.

## Describe alternatives you've considered

Is there any? Ruby accepts this syntax, and only becomes evident at runtime.

problems.title: Template files are not correctly autocorrected
problems.issue_body:
There is an issue where the template support feature does not work correctly with RuboCop's autocorrect feature, and I’m not sure how to modify `lib/rubocop/runner.rb` to fix it, so could you help me?

The problem is as follows:

For example, suppose `example.erb` contains three `<% ... %>` blocks, and each of them has one offense.

```erb
<% ... %>
<% ... %>
<% ... %>
```

When running `rubocop --autocorrect example.erb`, RuboCop detects all three offenses and shows them as `[Corrected]` in the output, but in reality only the last reported offense is actually autocorrected in the file. Because of this problem, for example, with this template file, you would need to run `rubocop --autocorrect example.erb` a total of three times before all corrections are actually applied.

Inside `RuboCop::Runner`, what happens is that autocorrect is applied three times for `example.erb`. However, each of these is treated as if it were a different file. As a result, the `File.write` from the second autocorrect overwrites the changes from the first, and the `File.write` from the third overwrites the second, so only the last correction remains.

The reason this happens is that, to support templates, the existing implementation represents each embedded Ruby snippet in the same template file as a combination of file path + offset. `RuboCop::Runner` then treats these as different files.

I believe this issue can be resolved if we can modify the code so that these snippets are recognized as the same file and autocorrections for the same file are properly grouped and applied.

Also, although this is unrelated to the autocorrect issue, it seems that the caching mechanism doesn’t work properly for files analyzed using the template API. I haven’t investigated this issue in detail yet, so I can’t say anything definitive at this point.

---

problems.issue_body:
## Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

[Style/EmptyClassDefinition](https://docs.rubocop.org/rubocop/latest/cops_style.html#styleemptyclassdefinition) currently requires one to select between:

  ```ruby
  # class_keyword style
  class MyModel < ApplicationRecord  # <--- Should be good
  end
  ```
and:
  ```ruby
  class MyService
    # class_new style
    Error = Class.new(StandardError)  # <--- Should also be good
  end
  ```

Must these be mutually exclusive options? They have different contexts.

## Describe the solution you'd like

Maybe we need a distinction between top-level classes and sublclasses? Could be a separate cop even. But in my above example, I want both to be good. I think what I want to be able to have an empty top-level class, but not an empty subclass.

So, could have Style/EmptyClassDefinition only consider top-level classes. Then could have Style/EmptySubClassDefinition consider only subclasses? (Might prefer renaming Style/EmptyClassDefinition -> Style/EmptyTopLevelClassDefinition as well, for symmetry?)

## Describe alternatives you've considered

I've currently disabled Style/EmptyClassDefinition. Essentially all I really care about here is the ability to define "Error" classes using the `class_new` style, tbh.

## Additional context

I'm currently on Rubocop 1.85.0. Was testing the new changes to Style/EmptyClassDefinition.

---

By the way, I think the [documentation for Style/EmptyClassDefinition](https://docs.rubocop.org/rubocop/latest/cops_style.html#styleemptyclassdefinition) fell out of date in v1.85.0. It still says:

> The supported styles are:
> class_definition (default) - prefer standard class definition over Class.new
> class_new - prefer Class.new over class definition

But I think the top option is meant to be `class_keyword` now.

Also, Configurable Attributes table at the bottom lists 3 options (not 2) under Configurable values. Remove `class_definition` here?

problems.title: Spurious warning: "[Cop] does not support SafeAutoCorrect parameter" when SafeAutoCorrect is a valid parameter for all c
problems.issue_body:
## Steps to reproduce the problem

Create a `.rubocop.yml` with `SafeAutoCorrect: false` for any cop that does not already have `SafeAutoCorrect` listed in its default configuration:

```yaml
# .rubocop.yml
Lint/UselessAssignment:
  SafeAutoCorrect: false
```

Run RuboCop against any Ruby file:

```
$ bundle exec rubocop test.rb
```

The same warning is produced with `Safe: false` for cops that do not have `Safe` in their default config.

## Expected behavior

No warning should be emitted. `SafeAutoCorrect` (and `Safe`) are documented, recognized configuration parameters that are valid for all cops. They appear in `CONFIG_CHECK_KEYS` and are actively read at runtime via `cop_config.fetch('SafeAutoCorrect', true)` in `autocorrect_logic.rb`.

## Actual behavior

```
Warning: Lint/UselessAssignment does not support SafeAutoCorrect parameter.

Supported parameters are:

  - Enabled
  - AutoCorrect
```

The warning fires for any cop that does not have `SafeAutoCorrect` explicitly listed in its entry in `config/default.yml`. Only the ~53 cops that already have `SafeAutoCorrect:` in `default.yml` are unaffected.

The root cause is in `config_validator.rb`. `COMMON_PARAMS` does not include `Safe` or `SafeAutoCorrect`, so `each_invalid_parameter` treats them as unknown when they are absent from a cop's default config entry:

```ruby
COMMON_PARAMS = %w[Exclude Include Severity inherit_mode AutoCorrect StyleGuide Details
                   Enabled Reference References].freeze

def each_invalid_parameter(cop_name)
  default_config = ConfigLoader.default_configuration[cop_name]
  @config[cop_name].each_key do |param|
    next if COMMON_PARAMS.include?(param) || default_config.key?(param)
    # SafeAutoCorrect is neither in COMMON_PARAMS nor in most cops' default_config,
    # so it falls through and triggers the warning.
    yield param, supported_params
  end
end
```

The fix is to add `Safe` and `SafeAutoCorrect` to `COMMON_PARAMS`.

problems.title: Layout/EmptyLineAfterGuardClause disallows consecutive guard clauses if they span multiple lines
problems.issue_body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and this hasn't been reported yet.
- [x] I am running the latest stable version of RuboCop.

### Issue type

False positive

### Cop name

Layout/EmptyLineAfterGuardClause

### Steps to reproduce the problem

Using lengthy conditions and error message for guard clauses makes Rubocop want to separate them with empty lines.
I am using a method that has the only purpose of validating something and raising in case a condition is not met, so it is basically a long chain of guard clauses.

```ruby
def validate_something
  raise SomeError, "this check has failed" unless short_condition # rubocop complains
  if some_lengthy_condition_does_not_meet_requirements
    raise LengthyError.new("this is some lengthy error message that must be split into multiple lines",
                           because: "i need to add some metadata while satisfying Layout/LineLength cop")
  end
  raise AnotherError, "another check has failed" unless another_check_succeeds # rubocop does not complain
  if another_lengthy_condition_does_not_meet_requirements
    raise ShortError.new("this is a short error that fits into one line and everyone is happy", because: "it is treated as one line")
  end

  return true
end
```

### Expected behavior

The `Layout/EmptyLineAfterGuardClause` cop should not complain because the code in question are two consecutive guard clauses with no additional statements in between them.
So to me, it should still count as a "one-liner", just like the last check, which is *technically* 3 lines, because of `if ...` and `end`, but Rubocop already recognizes this and does not require an empty line.

### Actual behavior

Rubocop complains.
I think it should not complain, because the code in question are two consecutive guard clauses without additional statements in between them.

```
test.rb:2:3: C: [Correctable] Layout/EmptyLineAfterGuardClause: Add empty line after guard clause.
  raise SomeError, "this check has failed" unless short_condition # rubocop complains
  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
```

problems.title: Ruby syntax error missing reported as a zero-length range at EOF
problems.issue_body:
This happens when using Solargraph + RuboCop diagnostics: `Lint/Syntax` for a missing `end` is reported as a zero-length range at EOF (`start == end`), which makes inline highlighting unreliable in some editors (like [here](https://github.com/zed-extensions/ruby/issues/259)).

--------

## Steps to reproduce the problem

1. Create `test.rb` with:
```
if true
  puts 'x'
```
2. Use Solargraph (with RuboCop diagnostics enabled) and inspect `textDocument/publishDiagnostics` for this file.

Diagnostic payload received:
```
[
  {
    "range": {
      "start": { "line": 2, "character": 0 },
      "end": { "line": 2, "character": 0 }
    },
    "severity": 1,
    "source": "rubocop",
    "code": "Lint/Syntax",
    "message": " unexpected token $end\n(Using Ruby 2.7 parser; configure using `TargetRubyVersion` parameter, under `AllCops`)"
  }
]
```
## Expected behavior

For `missing end`, the diagnostic range should be non-empty (or otherwise point to a visible span), so editors can reliably show inline error highlighting.

## Actual behavior

In Solargraph + RuboCop diagnostics, `Lint/Syntax` for `unexpected token $end` is reported as a zero-length range at EOF (`start == end`).

problems.title: [Safe Autocorrect Bug] Style/RedundantParentheses swallows chained methods into inline comments
problems.issue_body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and this hasn't been reported yet.
- [x] I am running the latest stable version of RuboCop.

### Issue type

Incorrect autocorrect

### Cop name

Style/RedundantParentheses

### Steps to reproduce the problem

When Style/RedundantParentheses autocorrects a multiline expression, it deletes the closing parenthesis and the preceding newline character. If the inner expression ends with an inline comment, this text-deletion causes any trailing chained methods to be pulled up into the comment, breaking the code or swallowing linter directives.

Steps to Reproduce
1. Create a file named example.rb with the following code:
```ruby
member_ids = (
  [1, 2, 3].map { |i| i } # rubocop:disable Rails/Pluck
).uniq
```
2. Run RuboCop with autocorrect for this specific cop:
```sh
bundle exec rubocop example.rb --only Style/RedundantParentheses -A
```





### Expected behavior


The autocorrect should either preserve the execution of .uniq by handling the comment safely, or it should safely bail out and refuse to autocorrect if an inline comment is detected at the end of the begin node's line.

Example of safe correction:
```ruby
member_ids = [1, 2, 3].map { |i| i } # rubocop:disable Rails/Pluck
  .uniq
```

### Actual behavior

The newline and closing parenthesis are blindly deleted, causing .uniq to become part of the inline comment. The method is no longer executed, and the RuboCop disable directive becomes invalid.
```ruby
member_ids = [1, 2, 3].map { |i| i } # rubocop:disable Rails/Pluck.uniq
```

```yaml

```

```shell
1.84.2
```

- [x] I am running the latest stable version of RuboCop.

### Issue type

False positive

### Cop name

Lint/RedundantSafeNavigation

### Steps to reproduce the problem

example.rb:
```ruby
a = nil

unless a&.ready?
  p a&.name
end
```

run `bundle exec rubocop example.rb --only Lint`. 

The `a&.name` is falsely reported. 

I believe the culprit is that `NilReceiverChecker#sole_condition_of_parent_if?` doesn't distinguish between `if` and `unless` (if the same code would have `if a&.ready?`, the deduction "if we are inside the conditional, it can't be `nil`" would be correct).

### Expected behavior

There should be no Lint-class problems with this code.

### Actual behavior

```
example.rb:4:6: W: [Correctable] Lint/RedundantSafeNavigation: Redundant safe navigation on non-nil receiver (detected by analyzing previous code/method invocations).
  p a&.name
     ^^
```

Autocorrection makes the code incorrect:
```ruby
a = nil

unless a&.ready?
  p a.name
end
```
Before: `ruby example.rb` would output `nil` (as it should).

After the autocorrection, it will be 
```
example.rb:4:in `<main>': undefined method `name' for nil (NoMethodError)

  p a.name
     ^^^^^
```

### RuboCop configuration

```yaml
Lint/RedundantSafeNavigation:
  InferNonNilReceiver: true
```

## Expected behavior

I defined a custom cop in `lib/rubocop/cop/foo/bar.rb` and attempted to change its configuration in `.rubocop.yml`.

problems.title: Lint/LiteralInInterpolation has incorrect autocorrects for embedded quotes and escaped interpolation text
problems.issue_body:
## Before submitting

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and this hasn't been reported yet.
- [x] I am running the latest stable version of RuboCop.

## Issue type

Incorrect autocorrect

## Cop name

`Lint/LiteralInInterpolation`

## Steps to reproduce the problem

I reproduced this on the latest stable RuboCop release and also on current `master` at `21f0cb9`.

### Repro 1: invalid syntax after autocorrect

1. Create a file `example.rb` with the following content:

```ruby
puts "x#{"\""}y"
```

2. Run:

```bash
bundle exec ruby exe/rubocop example.rb --only Lint/LiteralInInterpolation -A
ruby -c example.rb
```

### Repro 2: behavior change after autocorrect

1. Create a file `example.rb` with the following content:

```ruby
puts "x#{"\\#{1}"}y"
```

2. Run:

```bash
bundle exec ruby exe/rubocop example.rb --only Lint/LiteralInInterpolation -A
ruby example.rb
```

## Expected behavior

Autocorrect should either preserve valid Ruby syntax and runtime behavior, or skip autocorrection if that cannot be done safely.

For these examples:

- the first example should remain valid Ruby after autocorrect
- the second example should keep printing `x#{1}y`

## Actual behavior

### Repro 1

Autocorrect rewrites the file to invalid Ruby:

```ruby
puts "x"y"
```

### Repro 2

Before autocorrect, the program prints:

```text
x#{1}y
```

After autocorrect, it becomes:

```ruby
puts "x1y"
```

and then prints:

```text
x1y
```

This looks related to how the cop rewrites string literal contents directly into the surrounding interpolated string context without preserving escaping requirements for the outer string.

## RuboCop configuration

```yaml
# No special configuration
```

problems.title: Lint/NumberConversion autocorrect breaks nil-safe behavior of safe navigation
problems.issue_body:
## Before submitting

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and this hasn't been reported yet.
- [x] I am running the latest stable version of RuboCop.

## Issue type

Incorrect autocorrect

## Cop name

`Lint/NumberConversion`

## Steps to reproduce the problem

I reproduced this on the latest stable RuboCop release and also on current `master`.

1. Create a file `example.rb` with the following content:

```ruby
foo = nil
p foo&.to_i
```

2. Run:

```bash
bundle exec ruby exe/rubocop example.rb --only Lint/NumberConversion -A
ruby example.rb
```

After autocorrect, RuboCop rewrites the file to:

```ruby
foo = nil
p Integer(foo, 10)
```

## Expected behavior

Autocorrect should preserve the nil-safe behavior of safe navigation, or skip autocorrection if that cannot be done safely.

In this example, `foo&.to_i` returns `nil` when `foo` is `nil`, so autocorrect should not change it into code that raises.

## Actual behavior

`Lint/NumberConversion` registers an offense for `foo&.to_i` and autocorrects it to `Integer(foo, 10)`.

That changes runtime behavior:

- before autocorrect: `p foo&.to_i` prints `nil`
- after autocorrect: `Integer(foo, 10)` raises `ArgumentError: base specified for non string value`

This seems like incomplete handling of safe navigation for variable receivers. The current autocorrect preserves the syntax shape, but it does not preserve the semantics of `&.` when the receiver can be `nil`.

## RuboCop configuration

```yaml
# No special configuration
```

3. Have violations in a path in the project other than `app` (e.g. `spec/myfile.rb`)
4. Run rubocop, and see that rubocop has flagged violations in `myfile.rb` that is not covered by the include pattern
5. Move the app to a file path that does not have `app` in the ancestors, and see that rubocop does _not_ flag violations in `myfile.rb`

See https://github.com/maths22/rubocop-include-bug-demo for a full (super tiny) demonstration of the issue

### Expected behavior

Rubocop should behave consistently regardless of the parent directory the project lives in

### Actual behavior

Rubocop include patterns wind up applying to the parent directories of a project. Note that _exclude_ directories do not, as rubocop has explicit logic that converts those into absolute paths during config processing.

### RuboCop configuration

```yaml
AllCops:
  NewCops: enable

Style/StringLiterals:
  Include:
    - '**/app/**/*.rb'
```

### RuboCop version

```shell
$ rubocop -V
1.74.0 (using Parser 3.3.7.2, rubocop-ast 1.41.0, analyzing as Ruby 3.1, running on ruby 3.1.6) [arm64-darwin23]
```

problems.title: Update `Metrics/PerceivedComplexity` to reduce perceived complexity of simple pattern matching
problems.issue_body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and this hasn't been requested yet.

### Cop name

Metrics/PerceivedComplexity

### Is your feature request related to a problem?

I've noticed that a conscious choice was made to evaluate `case...in` differently from `case...when` with this cop. Each part of the `case...in` is counted the same as each part of a `if...elsif` while the `case...when` gets discounted as mentioned in the documentation to `0.2` branches.

I understand that pattern matching can be much more complex than simple case statements but I think that pattern matching weight should be evaluated based on the complexity of the expression as at times it can simplify code. It can get flagged by this rule though which indicates that the code has become more complex even though that is incorrect.

### Describe the solution you'd like

My proposal is that `case...in` branches with one literal argument should be weighted the same as `case...when` branches.

### Code examples

Specifically, I've run into the current pattern in our codebase. Note that this is simplified. Imagine that there are more cases.

```rb
case color
when "red"
  ...
when "blue"
  ...
when "green"
  ...
else
  raise ArgumentError, "unsupported color: #{color}"
end
```

I tried to replace it with this since pattern matching is strict and an error is raised on a missing branch.

```rb
case color
in "red"
  ...
in "blue"
  ...
in "green"
  ...
end
```

It gets flagged by the `Metrics/PerceivedComplexity` cop after the change.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

Using `case...when` as we did previously.

### Additional context

_No response_

problems.title: `Style/MutableConstant` with `EnforcedStyle: strict` false positive on `Data.define`
problems.issue_body:
## Before submitting

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and this hasn't been reported yet.
- [x] I am running the latest stable version of RuboCop.

## Issue type

False positive

## Cop name

`Style/MutableConstant`

## Steps to reproduce the problem

1. Create a file `example.rb` with the following content:

```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

MyData = Data.define(:name, :age)
```

2. Run:

```bash
rubocop example.rb --only Style/MutableConstant
```

## Expected behavior

No offense should be reported. `Data` (introduced in Ruby 3.2) is a DSL for defining immutable value classes whose instances are always frozen:

```ruby
Data.define(:name, :age).new(name: "Alice", age: 30).frozen? # => true
```

While the class object returned by `Data.define` is itself not frozen (just like `Struct.new`), it is used to declare an immutable value type rather than as a mutable container that needs explicit freezing. This is analogous to how `Struct.new` is already treated as immutable by this cop.

## Actual behavior

With `EnforcedStyle: strict`, RuboCop reports:

```
example.rb:3:12: C: Style/MutableConstant: Freeze mutable objects assigned to constants.
MyData = Data.define(:name, :age)
         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
```

## RuboCop configuration

```yaml
Style/MutableConstant:
  EnforcedStyle: strict
```

problems.issue_body:
### Before submitting

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and this hasn't been reported yet.
- [x] I am running the latest stable version of RuboCop.

### Issue type

False positive

### Cop name

Layout/MultilineMethodCallIndentation

### Steps to reproduce the problem


With `EnforcedStyle: indented`:

```yaml
# .rubocop.yml
Layout/MultilineMethodCallIndentation:
  EnforcedStyle: indented
```

```ruby
foo(
  key => Model.joins(
    Other
      .arel_table
      .join_sources
  )
)
```

The value of the hash pair (`key => Model.joins(...)`) is a method chain, and one of
its calls (`.joins`) receives a **multi-line chained argument** whose receiver
(`Other`) sits on its own line.

### Expected behavior


No offense. The inner chain (`.arel_table`, `.join_sources`) is correctly indented 2
spaces relative to **its own receiver** `Other`. This is what 1.84.0 and 1.85.x report
(no offense).


### Actual behavior


An offense is reported, and the inner chain is anchored to the **hash pair key line**
(`key =>`, column 2) instead of to its receiver `Other`:

```
example.rb:4:7: C: [Correctable] Layout/MultilineMethodCallIndentation: Use 2 (not 4) spaces for indenting an expression spanning multiple lines.
      .arel_table
      ^^^^^^^^^^^
example.rb:5:7: C: [Correctable] Layout/MultilineMethodCallIndentation: Use 2 (not 4) spaces for indenting an expression spanning multiple lines.
      .join_sources
      ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
```

Autocorrect (`-a`) then indents the chain to the **same column as (effectively left of)
its own receiver**, which is clearly wrong:

```ruby
foo(
  key => Model.joins(
    Other
    .arel_table
    .join_sources
  )
)
```

problems.title: A proposal to implement cop lazy loading
problems.issue_body: I've been inspired by slow RuboCop startup time to reduce the number of `require`s when `lib/rubocop.rb` is loaded. Right now, [more than 800 `require`s happen](https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/blob/5e8e49241a0e95121dd9977cd8e305e3a871639f/lib/rubocop.rb), most of which are cops (700+, including correctors and mixins). When running RuboCop against a single file, most of the time is spent requiring the cops (even if I run only one cop or one department): When you have plugins (e.g. `rubocop-rails`, `rubocop-rspec`, etc.), the amount of time spent requiring cops is even greater (my project has around 1k cops available). I came up with [an (unpolished) proof of concept](https://github.com/lovro-bikic/rubocop/compare/90c795960da9c7fbd40b16f3b245eb26a6d564fa...3909cc5efad1adfc25605dfca63434468b6b6fa0) to autoload cops. This is the profile when running RuboCop against a single file and single cop with the PoC (same command as for the profile above): To benchmark it, I timed `rubocop -x file.rb` (run and autocorrect only the Layout department on a single file) 30 times on master and on the PoC. Here are the results: ``` # Master Average time (s): 1.46485 Std deviation (s): 0.0279817 # PoC Average time (s): 1.02049 Std deviation (s): 0.00637835 ``` The speed-up is around 30% in this scenario. Note that in this benchmark I loaded just RuboCop; with plugins the difference would be even bigger. For RuboCop commands which don't run only some cops or departments (e.g. just `bundle exec rubocop`), the speed-up depends on the number of enabled cops in the config. For example, I have one project which enables 45% of cops, and another which enables around 80%. [Standard base config](https://github.com/standardrb/standard/blob/0fa2bfd8ac000169b72f9608118501acac066c93/config/base.yml) enables 59% cops at the time of writing. Before I open any PRs, I'd like to run the plan by the maintainers. Here's the general idea: 1. Modify [RuboCop::Cop::Registry](https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/blob/master/lib/rubocop/cop/registry.rb) so that cops can be registered only by [badge](https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/blob/master/lib/rubocop/cop/badge.rb) and class name, which is resolved only when the cop class is needed. See changes [here](https://github.com/lovro-bikic/rubocop/compare/90c795960da9c7fbd40b16f3b245eb26a6d564fa...3909cc5efad1adfc25605dfca63434468b6b6fa0#diff-dc00dfc3fe3e605382e6da43bf62ffda83cf5f54df0bbf4d2ab986b7f072a070) 2. Modify [RuboCop::Runner](https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/blob/5e8e49241a0e95121dd9977cd8e305e3a871639f/lib/rubocop/runner.rb) to mobilize cops by badge instead of by class (see [here](https://github.com/lovro-bikic/rubocop/compare/90c795960da9c7fbd40b16f3b245eb26a6d56…

problems.title: Add new `EnableNewCopsUpTo` option to enable all pending cops up to a specific Rubocop version
problems.issue_body:
I would like to modestly propose a new feature for enabling pending cops in bulk:

I realised while creating my `.rubocop.yml` for a new project, that what I wanted to do with pending cops wasn't to enable all of them (and potentially fail CI in the future due to new cops) but nor did I want to ignore pending cops available _right now_ that I could ensure my code passes. I know I could add each one individually to `.rubocop.yml` but that's a bit tedious and my configuration is quite short and I'd rather keep it that way.

What occurred to me is that I'd like to enable all the cops that were available in the version of Rubocop I'm using, and not ones in newer versions. And thus this feature idea was born.

With this feature you can set the `EnableNewCopsUpTo` option in your `.rubocop.yml` file:

```
AllCops:
  EnableNewCopsUpTo: '0.89'
```

And all pending cops that were added in that version or earlier will be enabled, and any added in the future will give a warning just like they do presently.

When you see those warnings and have some time, you can try enabling them, fix any issues, and bump the version number in your config again.

I'm not married to any of the code here, but I'd rather bring a working demo along when proposing a feature. The version comparison code is maybe not great, it was just the fastest way to get a semver comparison to happen. I'm even less married to the option name which is quite clunky.

I added tests for the change in `registry.rb` but didn't really grok how to test the changes in `config.rb`.

I also added a first pass at documentation, but it could probably be clearer and will of course need to change if any of the names change.

I'm open to suggestions and feedback on any of the changes here! I thought this might be a neat way to deal with the problem and to have my cake and eat it, and based on reading some threads around here I have a feeling I'm not the only person who wants new cops but doesn't want a long list of enabled pending ones in their `.rubocop.yml`. Let me know what you think!

-----------------

### Steps to reproduce the problem

```ruby
#!/usr/bin/env ruby

$need = false
$load = nil
$file = 'file'

def original
  # IfUnlessModifier
  if $need

  end || $file

end

```
1. Favor modifier `if` usage when having a single-line body.
