- Parity test covers the new weights.
- `flutter analyze` — no new issues; `flutter test` — green.

problems.title: feat(kraken): import deposits, withdrawals, staking/earn rewards via Ledgers API
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

The current Kraken sync only calls `TradesHistory`, which returns spot buy/sell trades. The Kraken [Ledgers API](https://docs.kraken.com/api/docs/rest-api/get-ledgers) — which covers **all other financial events** — is never called. Users with correctly-scoped API keys (Query Ledger Entries enabled) therefore see only token sells; deposits, withdrawals, staking rewards, Earn income, and standalone fees are silently absent.

## What's missing

| Event | Kraken API source | Currently synced |
|---|---|---|
| Spot buy / sell trades | `TradesHistory` | ✓ |
| Crypto deposit (external wallet → Kraken) | `Ledgers` type=`deposit` | ✗ |
| Fiat deposit (bank wire → Kraken) | `Ledgers` type=`deposit` | ✗ |
| Crypto withdrawal (Kraken → wallet) | `Ledgers` type=`withdrawal` | ✗ |
| Fiat withdrawal (Kraken → bank) | `Ledgers` type=`withdrawal` | ✗ |
| Staking reward | `Ledgers` type=`staking` | ✗ |
| Kraken Earn reward | `Ledgers` type=`earn` | ✗ |
| Standalone fee (not on a trade) | `Ledgers` type=`fee` | ✗ |

Types intentionally skipped: `trade` (already covered by `TradesHistory`), `transfer` (internal Kraken sub-account movements), `margin`/`rollover`/`settled` (margin trading — deferred to follow-up).

## Root cause

`Provider::Kraken` has no `get_ledgers` method. `KrakenItem::Importer#fetch_trades` is the only transaction-level call. `KrakenAccount::Processor#process_trades` explicitly guards `return unless %w[buy sell].include?(type)` — anything else is dropped.

The user's API key **already requires** `Data → Query ledger entries` (no key change needed); the codebase simply never calls the endpoint.

## Proposed implementation

### 1. `Provider::Kraken` — add `get_ledgers`

```ruby
def get_ledgers(start: nil, type: nil, offset: nil)
  params = {}
  params["start"] = start.to_i.to_s if start.present?
  params["type"] = type.to_s if type.present?
  params["ofs"] = offset.to_i.to_s if offset.present?
  private_post("Ledgers", params)
end
```

Ledgers response shape:
```json
{
  "ledger": {
    "LXXXXXX": {
      "refid": "SXXXXXX",
      "time": 1609459200.123,
      "type": "withdrawal",
      "subtype": "",
      "aclass": "currency",
      "asset": "XXBT",
      "amount": "-0.10000000",
      "fee": "0.00010000",
      "balance": "0.40000000"
    }
  },
  "count": 2500
}
```

`amount` is **net** (already accounts for the fee deducted from the sent amount). `fee` is the Kraken-charged portion, stored in `extra` for reference.

### 2. `KrakenItem::Importer` — paginate and store ledgers

Same loop as `fetch_trades` (max 200 pages × 50 entries). Result stored as:
```ruby
raw_transactions_payload: {
  "trades"  => trades,
  "ledgers" => ledgers   # new
}
```

`type == "trade"` entries are **not filtered at fetch time** (store everything for auditability), but are skipped by the processor to avoid double-counting with `TradesHistory`.

### 3. `KrakenAccount::LedgerProcessor` — new class

Called from `KrakenAccount::Processor#process` after `proc…

problems.title: feat(mercury): import pending transactions and store kind/counterpartyId metadata
problems.issue_body:
Mercury Banking sync misses three data points present in every Mercury API payload:

- **Pending transactions are silently dropped** — `status: "pending"` entries are never imported, so Mercury pending charges don't appear until they post.
- **Payment rail (`kind`) is not stored** — Mercury returns `kind: "ACH" | "Wire" | "Card" | "InternalTransfer"` on every transaction; the field is unused.
- **Counterparty ID is not stored** — Mercury provides `counterpartyId` (a stable UUID) useful for deduplication and future analytics; the field is unused.

Additionally, `Transaction::PENDING_PROVIDERS` does not include `"mercury"`, so even if pending data were stored, the existing pending-detection SQL and `Transaction#pending?` would never check it.

**Scope:** import pending Mercury transactions, store `kind` and `counterpartyId` under `extra["mercury"]`, add `"mercury"` to `PENDING_PROVIDERS` so the existing pending→posted reconciliation pipeline activates for Mercury, with test coverage.

problems.title: Bug: CSV import silently drops amounts that use a non-breaking-space thousands separator (`1 234,56` format)
problems.issue_body:
### Summary

When importing a CSV with the **French/Scandinavian** number format (`1 234,56`), `Import#sanitize_number` silently discards any amount whose thousands separator is a **non-breaking space** (`U+00A0`) or **narrow no-break space** (`U+202F`) rather than a plain ASCII space. The value is coerced to an empty string, so the amount (or price/quantity) is lost on import.

This matters because most real-world European CSV exports (and anything copied out of Excel/LibreOffice or many banking portals) use `U+00A0`/`U+202F` — **not** the ASCII space — as the thousands separator. The existing happy-path test only exercises a plain ASCII space, so the gap is invisible today.

### Where

[`app/models/import.rb`](https://github.com/we-promise/sure/blob/main/app/models/import.rb) — `sanitize_number`:

```ruby
# Handle French/Scandinavian format specially
if format[:delimiter] == " "
  sanitized = sanitized.gsub(/\s+/, "") # Remove all spaces first
else
  sanitized = sanitized.gsub(/[^\d#{Regexp.escape(format[:delimiter])}#{Regexp.escape(format[:separator])}\-]/, "")
  ...
end
```

Two problems with the space-delimiter branch:

1. **Ruby's `\s` does not match non-breaking spaces.** `\s` matches only `[ \t\r\n\f\v]`, so `U+00A0` and `U+202F` survive the `gsub`.
2. **No junk stripping.** Unlike the `else` branch, this branch never removes non-numeric characters (currency symbols, stray letters), so anything like `€` or a trailing `kr` also survives.

Either leftover character then fails the final validation guard:

```ruby
unless sanitized =~ /\A-?\d+\.?\d*\z/
  return ""
end
```

…and the method returns `""`, silently dropping the value.

### Steps to reproduce

With `number_format = "1 234,56"`:

| Input | Expected | Actual |
|-------|----------|--------|
| `"1\u00A0234,56"` (NBSP separator) | `"1234.56"` | `""` |
| `"1\u202F234,56"` (narrow NBSP) | `"1234.56"` | `""` |
| `"1 234,56 kr"` (ASCII space + junk) | `"1234.56"` | `""` |

The values reach this method via `generate_rows_from_csv` (`amount`/`price`/`qty` columns), so affected rows import with a blank/zero amount.

### Suggested fix

In the space-delimiter branch, strip everything that isn't a digit, the decimal separator, or a minus sign — the same junk-stripping the `else` branch already does. That removes ASCII spaces, `U+00A0`, `U+202F`, and stray currency symbols in one pass:

```ruby
if format[:delimiter] == " "
  sanitized = sanitized.gsub(/[^\d#{Regexp.escape(format[:separator])}\-]/, "")
else
  ...
end
```

Happy to open a PR with the fix and a regression test covering the non-breaking-space case.

### Environment

- Version: `0.7.2-alpha.12` (also present on `main`)

problems.title: Bug: Re-inviting a user whose prior (unaccepted) invitation has expired raises an unhandled 500
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

When an admin invites an email address that already has an **expired, never-accepted** invitation in the same family, `InvitationsController#create` raises `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique` (Postgres `unique_violation`). It is not rescued, so the user gets the generic Rails 500 page ("We're sorry, but something went wrong"), and the admin can never re-invite that person through the UI until the stale row is removed from the database by hand.

The root cause is a semantic mismatch between what the application treats as a "pending" invitation (unaccepted **and** not expired) and what the database's partial unique index treats as pending (unaccepted only). The model-level duplicate guard therefore does not fire, `save` proceeds, and the `INSERT` collides with the index.

This is independent of mailer configuration: on a self-hosted instance no invitation email is sent at all (see `#create`), so the failure is purely the unhandled DB constraint violation.

## Affected code (current `main`)

- `app/models/invitation.rb` — `pending` scope, `pending?`, `no_duplicate_pending_invitation_in_family`, `no_other_pending_invitation`, `set_expiration`
- `app/controllers/invitations_controller.rb` — `#create`
- Partial unique index `index_invitations_on_email_and_family_id_pending` (definition in `db/schema.rb`; created by migration `db/migrate/20260314120000_remove_unique_email_family_index_from_invitations.rb`)

## Steps to reproduce

1. As a family admin, invite a new email address. An `Invitation` row is created with `accepted_at = NULL` and `expires_at = 3.days.from_now`.
2. Do not accept it. Let `expires_at` pass (or set it to the past for a fast repro).
3. As the same admin, invite the same email address again.
4. `POST /invitations` returns HTTP 500. The log shows:

```
ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique (PG::UniqueViolation: ERROR: duplicate key value
violates unique constraint "index_invitations_on_email_and_family_id_pending")
```

Minimal console repro:

```ruby
inv = family.invitations.create!(email: "repro@example.com", role: "member", inviter: admin)
inv.update_column(:expires_at, 1.day.ago)   # simulate an expired, unaccepted invite

family.invitations.create!(email: "repro@example.com", role: "member", inviter: admin)
# => ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique: PG::UniqueViolation ...
#    "index_invitations_on_email_and_family_id_pending"
```

## Root cause

Two definitions of "pending" disagree.

Application (`app/models/invitation.rb`):

```ruby
scope :pending, -> { where(accepted_at: nil).where("expires_at > ?", Time.current) }

def pending?
  accepted_at.nil? && expires_at > Time.current
end
```

Database partial unique index (`db/schema.rb`):

```ruby
t.index ["email", "family_id"],
  name: "index_invitations_on_email_and_family_id_pending",
  unique: true, where: "(accepted_at IS NULL)"
```

The duplicate guard `no_duplicate_pending_invitation_in_family` queries the `pending` scope. Because an expired invitation is excluded by the `expires_a…

problems.title: Trend#percent returns the wrong sign when the previous (base) value is negative
problems.issue_body:
### Summary

`Trend#percent` computes the percentage change by dividing the delta by the **signed** previous value:

https://github.com/we-promise/sure/blob/main/app/models/trend.rb#L53-L60

```ruby
def percent
  return 0.0 if previous.zero? && current.zero?
  return Float::INFINITY if previous.zero?

  change = (current - previous).to_f

  (change / previous.to_f * 100).round(1)
end
```

When `previous` is **negative**, dividing by the signed base inverts the sign of the result, so the reported percentage contradicts `#direction` (which is computed correctly by magnitude). The UI then shows an up arrow / favorable color next to a negative percentage (and vice-versa).

### Where it surfaces

Anywhere a `Trend` is built from values that can be negative — most notably **net worth**, which is negative whenever liabilities exceed assets:

- Net-worth trend in reports (`app/views/reports/print.html.erb`)
- Balance sparklines / chart series (`Balance::ChartSeriesBuilder`, `Balance::SeriesAggregator`, `Series#trend`)

### Steps to reproduce

Net worth improves from `-100` to `-50` (an improvement of `+50`):

```ruby
trend = Trend.new(current: -50, previous: -100)
trend.direction # => "up"   (correct: -50 > -100)
trend.percent   # => -50.0   (WRONG: shows a 50% decline for a 50% improvement)
```

Expected `percent` is `+50.0`, consistent with the `"up"` direction.

A related instance of the same sign issue: a zero base with a negative current returns `+Float::INFINITY` (rendered `＋∞`) even though the direction is `"down"`.

```ruby
Trend.new(current: -100, previous: 0).percent # => Infinity  (should be -Infinity)
```

### Expected behavior

The sign of `percent` should always track the actual change (i.e. agree with `#direction`). Dividing the delta by the **absolute value** of the base makes the percentage sign correct for negative bases, and the zero-base infinite case should carry the sign of `current`.

### Environment

- Affects `main` (`app/models/trend.rb`).

problems.title: Bug: Holdings API exposes positions from accounts not shared with the requesting user
problems.issue_body:
The `/api/v1/holdings` endpoints scope results to the entire family rather than to the accounts the token owner can actually access. Both the list and show actions build their query from `current_resource_owner.family.holdings` and filter only on account status (`draft`/`active`), never on account accessibility.

As a result, a read scoped API key can read holdings (account id, name, quantity, price, and market value) for accounts owned by other family members that were never shared with the key owner. The `account_id` and `account_ids` filters make targeted enumeration of those accounts trivial.

The sibling endpoints already guard against this: `Api::V1::BalancesController` scopes through `accounts.accessible_by(current_resource_owner)`, and the web `HoldingsController` does the same. The holdings API controller was missed.

**Steps to reproduce**

1. In a family with two members, have member A own an investment account that is not shared with member B.
2. Add at least one holding to that account.
3. Using member B's read scoped API key, call `GET /api/v1/holdings`.
4. The response includes the holding from member A's private account. Passing `account_ids[]` for that account confirms direct access.

**Expected**

Holdings results are limited to accounts the token owner owns or has been granted access to, consistent with the balances API and the web holdings controller.

problems.title: Bug: Anthropic chat crashes with "unexpected end of input" when the model calls a no-argument tool
problems.issue_body:
## Before you start (required)

### General checklist

- [x] I have removed personal / sensitive data from screenshots and logs
- [x] I have searched existing issues and discussions to ensure this is not a duplicate issue
  - Closest matches checked: #849 (OpenAI-specific 404 / function-calling-unsupported handling — different bug), #2241 / PR #2253 (chained tool calls — different bug, and #2253 does not touch the parser, so it does not fix this)

### How are you using Sure?

- [x] I am a self-hosted user (local only)

### Self hoster checklist

- Self hosted app version: **v0.7.2** (release tarball, community-scripts Proxmox LXC install — native, not Docker)
- LLM provider: **native Anthropic** (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, model `claude-sonnet-4-5`)

## Describe the bug

When the chat assistant calls a tool that takes **no arguments** (e.g. `get_categories`), the turn fails with:

> Failed to generate a response. Please try again.

Chat error payload:

```json
{"message":"Failed to generate a response. Please try again.","technical_message":"Error calling function get_categories with arguments : unexpected end of input at line 1 column 1","type":"Provider::Anthropic::Error"}
```

Tools **with** arguments (e.g. `get_income_statement` with a date range) work fine, so the bug only surfaces on argument-less calls — which makes it look intermittent/prompt-dependent.

## Root cause

In `app/models/provider/anthropic/chat_parser.rb`, `function_requests` builds:

```ruby
function_args: input.is_a?(String) ? input : input.to_json
```

When the model streams a `tool_use` block with no input, the accumulated `input` is an **empty string**. That empty string is passed through as `function_args`, and `Assistant::FunctionToolCaller#fulfill_requests` then does:

```ruby
fn_args = JSON.parse(function_request.function_args)  # JSON.parse("") → ParserError
```

`JSON.parse("")` raises `unexpected end of input at line 1 column 1`, which surfaces as `Provider::Anthropic::Error` and kills the turn.

## Suggested fix (verified locally)

Normalize empty/nil tool input to an empty JSON object in the Anthropic parser:

```ruby
function_args: input.is_a?(String) ? input.presence || "{}" : (input || {}).to_json
```

With this one-line change, no-argument tool calls complete normally (verified on v0.7.2 by replaying the failing turn through Sidekiq — assistant response completed).

An alternative/belt-and-suspenders fix is to make `FunctionToolCaller` defensive: `JSON.parse(function_request.function_args.presence || "{}")` — that would cover any provider that emits empty args.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure the native Anthropic provider (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, any Claude model).
2. Ask the assistant something that requires an argument-less tool call, e.g. *"What categories do I have set up?"* (drives `get_categories`).
3. Turn fails with "Failed to generate a response"; `chats.error` shows the `unexpected end of input` technical message above.

problems.title: Enable Banking: Duplicate transactions due to missing entry_reference to external_id mapping
problems.issue_body:
## Summary
Enable Banking integration creates duplicate transactions because `entry_reference` is not mapped to `external_id`, leaving it empty. This affects ALL Enable Banking integrations regardless of bank or country.

## Environment
- **Sure version:** v0.6.7-rc.2
- **Deployment:** Self-hosted Docker Compose
- **Banks tested:** N26 (Germany), Sparkasse (Austria)
- **Enable Banking config country:** AT

## Problem Description
Every Enable Banking sync creates duplicate transactions. Manual deletion doesn't help - duplicates reappear on the next sync.

### Database Evidence
All Enable Banking transactions have empty `external_id`:
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM transactions 
WHERE external_id IS NOT NULL AND external_id != '';
-- Result: 0 rows for all Enable Banking accounts
```

### Duplicate Statistics (8 days of usage)
| Account | Bank | Total Syncs | Transactions | Duplicates | Rate |
|---------|------|-------------|--------------|------------|------|
| Hauptkonto | N26 (DE) | 49 | 171 | 24 | 14% |
| Haushaltskonto | N26 (DE) | 64 | 141 | 7 | 5% |
| Sparkasse | Sparkasse (AT) | 8 | 12 | 1 | 8% |

## Root Cause Analysis

### Issue #1: Incorrect Field Mapping
Enable Banking API returns:
```json
{
  "entry_reference": "31e13269-03fc-11f1-89d2-cd465703551c",  // ← Contains unique ID
  "transaction_id": null,                                      // ← Always null
  "transaction_amount": {"amount": "11.65", "currency": "EUR"},
  "creditor": {"name": "Spar Dankt 3418"},
  "status": "BOOK"
}
```

Sure currently maps `transaction_id` → `external_id`, but `transaction_id` is always `null`.

**Fix needed:** Map `entry_reference` → `external_id`

### Issue #2: API Returns Duplicate Transactions
Some transactions appear **multiple times in the same API response** with **different `entry_reference` IDs**:

**Example: Transaction "Spar Dankt 3418" (€11.65, 2026-02-07)**

Raw API payload contains:
```json
[
  {
    "entry_reference": "31e13269-03fc-11f1-89d2-cd465703551c",
    "status": "BOOK",
    "booking_date": "2026-02-07",
    "amount": "11.65",
    "creditor": {"name": "Spar Dankt 3418"}
  },
  {
    "entry_reference": "31e1330e-03fc-11f1-9cf8-steamrollere485",  // ← DIFFERENT ID
    "status": "BOOK",
    "booking_date": "2026-02-07",
    "amount": "11.65",
    "creditor": {"name": "Spar Dankt 3418"}
  }
]
```

Everything identical except `entry_reference`. This happens inconsistently - some transactions duplicate, others don't.

**Evidence:** Both duplicates have `status: "BOOK"` (not PDNG → BOOK transition)

### Database Timeline Analysis
Historical duplicate created during initial sync:
```
Transaction: €3.00, Date: 2025-12-31
[1] Created: 2026-02-03 17:58:10 UTC
[2] Created: 2026-02-03 17:58:10 UTC (same second!)
```

This proves Enable Banking sometimes sends duplicates in the same API call.

## What's NOT the Cause
- ❌ **Not PDNG vs BOOK status:** Verified both duplicates are `status: "BOOK"`
- ❌ **Not country config:** Affects both AT and DE
- ❌ …

problems.title: [bug] non-positive --tile silently returns an uninitialised buffer as the "exact" product
problems.issue_body:
## What happens

`matmul.Config` validates `dtype`, `vram_fraction` and `storage` in
`__post_init__`, but **not `tile`**. A non-positive `tile` slips through and
silently corrupts the result of the exact engine.

In `gemm.multiply()` the tiled path picks the tile size as:

```python
T = cfg.tile or auto_tile(n, cfg, backend)
```

so a negative `cfg.tile` is truthy and is used verbatim as `T`. It then reaches
`_gemm_tiled_sync(...)`, where the schedule is built by:

```python
def _tiles(n, T):
    return [(s, min(T, n - s)) for s in range(0, n, T)]
```

For `T <= 0` this yields an **empty** schedule (`range(0, n, -5) == []`), so the
`for` loops never execute, `C` (an uninitialised `np.empty(...)` buffer from
`storage.allocate`) is **never written**, and that garbage is returned as
`A @ B`.

## Why it matters

CCO's whole premise is that the general/exact engine's answer *is* the truth
(BENCHMARKS.md). Here it silently returns a wrong product with no error — the
worst failure mode. It is reachable on any out-of-core run, or on any size with
`--force-tiled`, via `--tile -N`.

## Repro

```bash
python -m matmul --n 4096 --force-tiled --tile -5     # returns uninitialised memory
```

or directly:

```python
from matmul.config import Config
Config(tile=-5)     # accepted today; should raise
```

## Expected

`Config` should reject a non-positive `tile` up front (must be a positive int,
or `None` for auto), consistent with the existing `dtype` / `vram_fraction` /
`storage` guards, so a bad tile fails fast instead of corrupting the result.

problems.title: [bug] `_fits_in_core` ignores the fp16 `accumulate_fp32` upcast, under-budgeting VRAM by ~2.7x on the default accuracy p
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

`matmul/gemm.py`'s in-core/tiled dispatch decides whether A, B, C all fit
resident on the device using `_fits_in_core`:

```python
def _fits_in_core(n: int, cfg: Config, backend: Backend) -> bool:
    # A, B, C resident on the device at once.
    need = 3 * n * n * cfg.item_bytes
    return need <= backend.free_compute_bytes() * cfg.vram_fraction
```

`need` assumes exactly three `n x n` buffers at `cfg.item_bytes` (the element
dtype's own size). That's correct for fp32/fp64, and correct for fp16 when
`accumulate_fp32=False`. But `Config.accumulate_fp32` **defaults to `True`**,
and when it's on, `_gemm_in_core` does not just hold three fp16 buffers — it
upcasts both operands to fp32 before the matmul:

```python
# matmul/gemm.py, _gemm_in_core
a = backend.to_device(np.asarray(A))     # fp16, resident:  n^2 * 2 bytes
b = backend.to_device(np.asarray(B))     # fp16, resident:  n^2 * 2 bytes
if cfg.np_dtype == np.float16 and cfg.accumulate_fp32:
    c = backend.matmul(a.astype(np.float32), b.astype(np.float32)).astype(np.float16)
```

While `backend.matmul(a.astype(np.float32), b.astype(np.float32))` executes,
the following are simultaneously live on-device (`a`/`b` are still referenced
by their local variables, so PyTorch's allocator cannot reclaim them):

| tensor              | bytes     |
|----------------------|-----------|
| `a` (fp16)            | `2*n^2`   |
| `b` (fp16)            | `2*n^2`   |
| `a.astype(fp32)`      | `4*n^2`   |
| `b.astype(fp32)`      | `4*n^2`   |
| `bmm` output (fp32)   | `4*n^2`   |
| **actual peak**       | **`16*n^2`** |

versus `_fits_in_core`'s estimate for fp16 (`item_bytes=2`):

```
need = 3 * n^2 * 2 = 6*n^2
```

So the real peak is **~2.7x** the budgeted `need`. Any `n` where
`6*n^2 <= free*vram_fraction < 16*n^2` makes `_fits_in_core` return `True` —
routing to the in-core path — while the actual computation needs more memory
than was verified available, risking a CUDA OOM at runtime instead of the
auto-tiled fallback (`gemm.multiply`'s whole reason for calling
`_fits_in_core` in the first place). This defeats the auto-tiling safety net
specifically for the accuracy-improving path that's the *default* for fp16.

## Minimal reproducer (pure arithmetic, no GPU needed)

```python
def need_estimated(n, item_bytes):
    return 3 * n * n * item_bytes

def peak_actual_fp16_accumulate_fp32(n):
    e = n * n
    return e * (2 + 2 + 4 + 4 + 4)   # a, b, a32, b32, bmm-output(fp32)

n = 8192
print("estimated need:", need_estimated(n, 2))
print("actual peak   :", peak_actual_fp16_accumulate_fp32(n))
print("ratio         :", peak_actual_fp16_accumulate_fp32(n) / need_estimated(n, 2))
# estimated need: 402653184        (~384 MiB)
# actual peak   : 1073741824       (~1024 MiB)
# ratio         : 2.6666...
```

For fp32/fp64, or fp16 with `accumulate_fp32=False`, `_gemm_in_core` only
ever holds `a`, `b`, `c` at `item_bytes` each — `need` is exact there. The gap
is specific to the fp16 + `accumulate_fp32=True` bran…

problems.title: [bug] reconstruct() sizes its streaming row-block from out_dtype instead of the compute_dtype it actually runs in (2x un
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

`strategy.subspace.reconstruct()` streams its output row-by-row to stay inside a VRAM budget, sizing the block from the **output** dtype's itemsize. But every tensor inside its loop (`Q`, `Ctil`, `QT`, and the `(rb, n)` intermediate) actually lives in `cfg.compute_dtype`, not the output dtype — and for `dtype="fp16"` those two differ (compute_dtype is bumped to fp32 for accuracy). The block ends up sized for half the real per-row memory footprint.

## Root cause

```python
# strategy/subspace.py
def reconstruct(Ctil, Q, C_out, backend: Backend, out_dtype):
    """Write Q @ Ctil @ Q^T  (n x n) into C_out, streaming output row-blocks."""
    n = Q.shape[0]
    blk = _row_block(n, n, backend, np.dtype(out_dtype).itemsize)   # <-- sized from out_dtype
    QT = Q.T
    for r0 in range(0, n, blk):
        r1 = min(n, r0 + blk)
        outr = backend.matmul(backend.matmul(Q[r0:r1, :], Ctil), QT)   # (rb, n), in Q's dtype
        C_out[r0:r1, :] = backend.to_host(outr).astype(out_dtype, copy=False)  # cast happens AFTER
```

and the call site:

```python
# strategy/subspace.py, multiply_subspace()
cdt = cfg.compute_dtype                                # bumped to fp32 for fp16 inputs
...
Q = transform.basis(n, m, backend, cdt, A=A, B=B)       # Q lives in cdt
Atil = compress(A, Q, backend, cdt)                     # in cdt
Btil = compress(B, Q, backend, cdt)                     # in cdt
Ctil = backend.matmul(Atil, Btil)                       # in cdt
reconstruct(Ctil, Q, C, backend, cfg.np_dtype)          # <-- passes np_dtype, not cdt
```

`Q`, `Ctil`, and `QT` are all in `cdt` (`cfg.compute_dtype`), but `reconstruct` is only ever told `cfg.np_dtype` (the *output* dtype). `strategy/config.py`:

```python
@property
def compute_dtype(self) -> np.dtype:
    """Projection math is done in fp32 for fp16 inputs (accuracy)."""
    if self.np_dtype == np.float16:
        return np.dtype(np.float32)
    return self.np_dtype
```

Every other streaming call site (`compress()`, `stream_gemm_right()`, `stream_gemm_left_t()`) is passed `cdt` for exactly this reason. `reconstruct()` is the one exception.

## Reproducer (arithmetic, illustrates the mechanism without needing a GPU)

`_row_block()` computes `blk = budget // (cols * item_bytes)`. Holding the byte budget fixed and only changing the itemsize used to size it:

```python
# same budget, only the itemsize differs (fp32 itemsize=4, fp16 itemsize=2)
budget = 1_000_000_000
n = 50_000
blk_sized_for_fp32 = budget // (n * 4)   # = 5000   <- correct, since Q/Ctil/QT are really fp32
blk_sized_for_fp16 = budget // (n * 2)   # = 10000  <- what the buggy code picks for --dtype fp16
# blk_sized_for_fp16 == 2 * blk_sized_for_fp32
```

With `--dtype fp16`, `reconstruct()` picks the `10000`-row block (sized as if items were 2 bytes), but the actual `(rb, n)` intermediate materialized on-device is fp32 (4 bytes/item) — so the real bytes staged per iteration are `10000 * 50000 * 4 = 2,000,000,000`, double the intende…

problems.title: [bug] strategy/cpu_backend.py's host_available_bytes() never got the Windows RAM fix from #88, hardcodes 2 GiB instead
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

`strategy/cpu_backend.py` (`CPUBackend`, the NumPy-only smoke-test stand-in
for `strategy.backend.Backend`) reimplements `host_available_bytes()` from
scratch instead of reusing `strategy.backend._host_available_bytes()` — the
shared, cross-platform helper that was already fixed and covered by
`tests/test_host_memory.py`:

```python
# strategy/cpu_backend.py (current)
def host_available_bytes(self) -> int:
    try:
        return int(os.sysconf("SC_AVPHYS_PAGES") * os.sysconf("SC_PAGE_SIZE"))
    except (AttributeError, OSError, ValueError):
        return 2 * 1024**3  # last-resort fallback, matches backend.py's pattern
```

`os.sysconf` doesn't exist on Windows (`AttributeError`), so on any Windows
box this always falls through to a hardcoded **2 GiB**, regardless of the
machine's real available RAM.

Compare `strategy/backend.py` / `matmul/backend.py`'s
`_host_available_bytes()`, which queries `os.sysconf` on POSIX and falls
back to a real `ctypes.windll.kernel32.GlobalMemoryStatusEx` query on
Windows before giving up on an 8 GiB last resort:

```python
# strategy/backend.py — already correct, already tested
def _host_available_bytes() -> int:
    try:
        avail = int(os.sysconf("SC_AVPHYS_PAGES") * os.sysconf("SC_PAGE_SIZE"))
        if avail > 0:
            return avail
    except (AttributeError, ValueError, OSError):
        pass
    if sys.platform == "win32":
        try:
            import ctypes
            ...
            if ctypes.windll.kernel32.GlobalMemoryStatusEx(ctypes.byref(stat)):
                return int(stat.ullAvailPhys)
        except Exception:
            pass
    return 8 * 1024**3
```

`cpu_backend.py` predates neither this helper nor its test — it just never
adopted it, so the CPU backend regressed to the exact class of bug #88 fixed
everywhere else.

## Why it matters

`CPUBackend.free_compute_bytes()` delegates straight to
`host_available_bytes()`, and both `strategy/subspace.py`'s `_row_block`
sizing and any other code driven by a `CPUBackend` instance use that value
to size streamed row-blocks. The module docstring frames `CPUBackend`
generically — "so a Transform's basis() can be exercised with zero
GPU/torch dependency" and "on any miner's machine, GPU or not"
(`strategy/smoke.py`) — not as fixed to the current 64x16 smoke-test size.
On a real Windows machine (no CUDA/MPS -> `strategy.smoke._pick_backend()`
falls back to `CPUBackend`) this silently substitutes a flat 2 GiB for the
actual free RAM: harmless at the tiny smoke-test N=64, but wrong for any
larger CPU-backed run, and inconsistent with the already-fixed GPU-backend
siblings for no reason.

## Reproducer (pure Python, no GPU needed)

```python
from unittest.mock import patch
from strategy.cpu_backend import CPUBackend

with patch("strategy.cpu_backend.os.sysconf", side_effect=OSError, create=True):
    print(CPUBackend(verbose=False).host_available_bytes())
    # -> 2147483648 (hardcoded 2 GiB) regardless of the machine's real RAM,
 …

problems.title: fix(matmul): prevent in-core path from materializing disk-backed memmaps
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

Fixes a critical out-of-core stability bug where `gemm.multiply()` could select the in-core fast path for disk-backed `np.memmap` inputs, causing host RAM OOM.

## Root cause

`runner.run()` chooses disk memmaps when host RAM cannot hold three `n x n` matrices (`storage.should_use_disk`). `multiply()` then decides in-core vs tiled using **only GPU VRAM** (`_fits_in_core`). When the GPU has enough VRAM but host RAM does not, the in-core path runs `_gemm_in_core()`, which calls `np.asarray(A)` / `np.asarray(B)` and materializes the full matrices in host RAM - defeating the memmap storage layer and often crashing with OOM.

## Fix

Detect memmap-backed inputs in `multiply()` and force the tiled streaming path, which already reads tiles without full materialization.

## Impact

- Restores the documented out-of-core contract (matrices never fully loaded into RAM)
- Prevents OOM on realistic hardware (large GPU, limited host RAM) when `storage=auto` selects disk
- No API or behavior change for in-RAM inputs

## Test plan

- [x] Added `test_memmap_forces_tiled_path` asserting memmap inputs use tiled mode and remain numerically correct
- [x] Existing eval/strategy unit tests pass
- [ ] GPU correctness suite (requires CUDA/MPS; skipped locally)

## Risks / tradeoffs

Disk-backed problems that would fit entirely in GPU VRAM now always use the tiled path (slightly slower than a true in-core upload), but this is required for host-memory safety.

problems.title: [bug] causal landmark attention returns NaN for early queries (all-landmark-masked softmax row)
problems.issue_body:
## What's wrong

`landmark_global_attention(..., causal=True)` in [`attention/hybrid.py`](https://github.com/zeokin/Cuda-Compute-OSS/blob/main/attention/hybrid.py) can produce **NaN**. Pooled landmark positions sit at the *last* index of each pooled block, so an early query can precede **every** landmark; the causal mask then sets that query's entire score row to `-inf`, and `torch.softmax` over an all-`-inf` row is NaN. The NaN propagates through `landmark_hybrid_attention` and into the benchmark's reported quality metrics.

## Reproduce (CPU, torch)

```python
import torch
from attention import hybrid
torch.manual_seed(0)
q,k,v = (torch.randn(1,2,20,8) for _ in range(3))

hybrid.landmark_global_attention(q,k,v,num_landmarks=5,causal=True)          # NaN at query rows [0,1,2]
hybrid.landmark_global_attention(q,k,v,num_landmarks=5,causal=True,policy='topk')  # NaN at [0,1]
out = hybrid.landmark_hybrid_attention(q,k,v,window=4,causal=True,num_landmarks=5)
torch.isfinite(out).all()   # -> False  (48 NaNs)
```

For `seq=20, num_landmarks=5` the pooled landmark positions are `[3,7,11,15,19]`; queries `0,1,2` precede all of them. `benchmark.run_once(mode='landmark', causal=True, ...)` then reports `mse=nan, rel_frobenius_error=nan`, silently corrupting the honest-quality-measurement the benchmark promises. Both `pooled` and `topk` policies are affected. Existing tests only cover `causal=False` for landmarks, so this slipped through.

## Suggested fix

In `landmark_global_attention`, give fully-masked query rows zero weight (no visible landmark ⇒ no global contribution) instead of letting softmax NaN:

```python
mask = landmark_pos[:, :, None, :] > q_pos[None, None, :, :]
scores = scores.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf"))
all_masked = mask.all(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
weights = torch.softmax(scores.masked_fill(all_masked, 0.0), dim=-1)
weights = weights.masked_fill(all_masked, 0.0)
```

This keeps the output finite and leaves the `causal=False` path byte-identical. `attention/` is an open (non-protected) prototype zone, so this is a `fix`-lane change.

problems.title: [bug] strategy _row_block budgets only the staged input rows, ignoring each block's GEMM output (2x over budget at M=N;
problems.issue_body:
## What happens

`strategy/subspace.py::_row_block` sizes a streamed row-block from the staged
**input** rows only:

```python
budget = int(backend.free_compute_bytes() * frac)
per_row = max(1, cols * item_bytes)          # <- input rows only
return int(min(n, max(1, budget // per_row)))
```

But every streaming primitive also allocates its **GEMM output** on the device
inside the loop, live at the same time as the staged block. None of it is
budgeted:

| primitive | staged per block (budgeted) | also allocated per block (**not** budgeted) |
|---|---|---|
| `stream_gemm_right` | `Xr` `(blk, n)` | `matmul(Xr, Q)` → `(blk, m)` |
| `compress` | `Xr` `(blk, n)` | `matmul(Xr, Q)` → `(blk, m)`, plus `(m, m)` |
| `reconstruct` | output row `(blk, n)` | `matmul(Q[rb], Ctil)` → `(blk, m)` |
| `stream_gemm_left_t` | `Xr` `(blk, n)` | `matmul(Xr.T, Q[rb])` → **`(n, m)`** — a *full-size* temp, independent of `blk` |

So the real per-row footprint is `(cols + m) * item_bytes`, not `cols *
item_bytes`, and `stream_gemm_left_t` additionally allocates a fixed `(n, m)`
tensor per iteration on top of its already-resident `(n, m)` accumulator.

This is exactly the bug #95 fixed in `matmul/gemm.py` (the `torch.bmm` output
tile cannot alias an operand, so `acc`, `a_dev`, `b_dev` and `prod` all coexist)
— still present in the *strategy* engine's streaming path.

## Why it matters

`frac` (`Config.vram_fraction`) exists to cap a streamed block's device
footprint. The unbudgeted output tensors push actual usage past that cap, so a
run that the budget says fits can OOM. The overshoot scales with `M`:

- default `M = n // 8`: block is ~**1.12x** the intended budget
- `M = N` (the exactness path — `--rank-m n`, and
  `strategy/tests/test_subspace.py::test_exact_when_m_equals_n`): block is
  **2.00x** the intended budget
- `stream_gemm_left_t`'s fixed `(n, m)` temp at `M = N` is **3.33x** the budget
  on its own — larger than all of free VRAM in the repro below

`rsvd.basis()` calls `stream_gemm_left_t` twice per multiply (`Aᵀ Ω`, `Bᵀ Ω`), so
this is on the default code path for every `multiply_subspace`, not an edge case.

## Repro (CPU-only, pure arithmetic — no GPU needed)

```python
from strategy import subspace

class FakeBackend:                      # 64 MiB free
    def free_compute_bytes(self): return 64 * 1024**2

n, m, item, frac = 4096, 4096, 4, 0.3   # M = N, fp32
budget = int(FakeBackend().free_compute_bytes() * frac)
blk = subspace._row_block(n, n, FakeBackend(), item, frac)

staged = blk * n * item                 # the only term budgeted
out    = blk * m * item                 # matmul(Xr, Q) — unbudgeted
print(blk, budget, staged + out, (staged + out) / budget)   # -> 2.00x budget
print(n * m * item / budget)            # left_t's fixed (n,m) temp -> 3.33x budget
```

Output: the block is sized at `2.00x` the budget it was supposed to respect, and
`stream_gemm_left_t`'s per-iteration temp alone is `3.33x` it.

## Expected

`_row_block` should account for t…

problems.title: [bug] --verify has no size guard: on large/disk-backed n it materializes both operands as float64 in RAM and OOMs (uncau
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

`--verify` materializes both full operands as float64 in host RAM and runs an `O(n³)` CPU reference multiply, with **no size guard** — so verifying a large / disk-backed run (the out-of-core regime this tool exists for) OOM-crashes with an uncaught `MemoryError`, after the GPU multiply has already succeeded.

The docstrings and CLI help promise a guard that does not exist:
- [matmul/runner.py#L27](../blob/main/matmul/runner.py#L27): *"verify only runs for small n (the reference is computed on CPU)."*
- [matmul/runner.py#L84](../blob/main/matmul/runner.py#L84): *"Only sensible for small n."*
- [matmul/cli.py#L30-L31](../blob/main/matmul/cli.py#L30-L31): `--verify … "check result vs a float64 reference (small n only)"`

But `run()` calls `_verify()` **unconditionally** whenever `verify=True` ([matmul/runner.py#L66-L67](../blob/main/matmul/runner.py#L66-L67)), regardless of `n` or storage mode.

## The defect

[matmul/runner.py#L83-L91](../blob/main/matmul/runner.py#L83-L91):

```python
def _verify(A, B, C, n: int, cfg: Config) -> dict:
    """Compare against a float64 CPU reference. Only sensible for small n."""
    ref = np.asarray(A, dtype=np.float64) @ np.asarray(B, dtype=np.float64)
    got = np.asarray(C, dtype=np.float64)
    ...
```

`np.asarray(A, dtype=np.float64)` on an fp32/fp16 (possibly memmapped) matrix allocates a **full new in-RAM float64 copy** (dtype differs → cannot be a view); same for `B`; then `@` allocates a third `n×n` float64 result and runs CPU BLAS `O(n³)`. For the out-of-core sizes the tool advertises this is many GiB of host RAM plus a multi-teraflop CPU multiply — exactly what the disk-backed streaming design exists to avoid.

## Concrete failing scenario

```
python -m matmul --n 30000 --dtype fp32 --verify
```

1. `should_use_disk(30000, 4, "auto", host_free)`: `need = 3·30000²·4 ≈ 10.8 GB` → on a typical 16 GB box A/B/C are disk memmaps; the GPU multiply runs fine (tiled/streamed).
2. `run()` then unconditionally calls `_verify`.
3. `_verify`: `np.asarray(A, float64)` materializes a **7.2 GB** RAM copy of the memmap; `B` another 7.2 GB; `@` a third 7.2 GB result + CPU-BLAS scratch → **`MemoryError`**.
4. `matmul/cli.py` wraps `run()` in `except RuntimeError` [only](../blob/main/matmul/cli.py#L52), so `MemoryError` escapes as an uncaught traceback (exit 1) instead of a clean `error:` / exit 2 — and the whole successful multiply is wasted.

Even the CLI **default** `--n 12000 --verify` is a footgun: 12000 is not "small," yet it silently launches a `1.7e12`-flop float64 CPU reference (minutes; ~3.5 GB) with no warning.

## Same flaw in the strategy package

`strategy/runner.py._verify` ([strategy/runner.py#L142-L149](../blob/main/strategy/runner.py#L142-L149)) is identical — same `"Small n only."` docstring, same unconditional call from `run()`, same `--verify` flag — so `python -m strategy --n 30000 --verify` OOMs the same way.

## Suggested fix

- Gate verification on host-RAM affordability of the float64…

problems.title: [bug] pooled landmark attention emits spurious all-zero landmarks (and wrong means/positions) when padding spans more th
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

`_pooled_landmarks()` splits the sequence into `landmarks` blocks of a fixed size `block = ceil(seq/landmarks)` and pads the tail with zeros, then assumes **all** the padding lands in the *last* block — it only corrects `counts[-1]`. Whenever the padding is at least one full block (`block*landmarks - seq >= block`), the block straddling the real/pad boundary keeps a too-large divisor and the fully-padded trailing blocks become **spurious all-zero landmarks**, corrupting the pooled K/V means, their causal positions, and the resulting attention output.

## Location

[attention/hybrid.py#L193-L205](../blob/main/attention/hybrid.py#L193-L205) (`_pooled_landmarks`, reached from `landmark_global_attention` / `landmark_hybrid_attention` with the default `policy="pooled"`):

```python
counts = torch.full((landmarks,), block, ...)
extra = block * landmarks - seq
if extra:
    counts[-1] = block - extra          # <-- assumes ALL padding is in the LAST block
counts = counts.clamp_min(1.0).view(1, 1, landmarks, 1)
k_landmarks = k_blocks.sum(dim=-2) / counts
...
positions = torch.arange(landmarks, ...) * block + counts.reshape(landmarks).to(long) - 1
```

Splitting `seq` tokens into `landmarks` fixed-size blocks + tail padding produces **more than one** all-padding block (and a partial boundary block) as soon as `extra = block*landmarks - seq >= block`. The single `counts[-1]` correction handles only `extra < block`.

## Concrete evidence

The counting/position logic is plain integer arithmetic; replicating it exactly (CPU) shows the defect at realistic configs (`num_landmarks=64`):

```
seq=2050  block=33  padded=2112  extra=62
  block 62: divisor used = 33, real tokens = 4      -> pooled mean ~8x too small, polluted by 29 zeros
  block 63: fully padding  -> emitted as an all-zero landmark (divisor clamped to 1)
  block 62 causal position = 2078 (a PADDING index) -> should be 2049 (last real token)

seq=65    block=2  padded=128  extra=63
  blocks 33..63 (31 of 64 landmarks) are fully padding -> 31 spurious all-zero landmarks
  block 32 divisor = 2, real tokens = 1; position = 65 (padding) -> should be 64

seq=4096  block=64  extra=0  -> no bug (clean multiple; this is the benchmark default, which is why it slips through)
```

Effect end-to-end in `landmark_global_attention` (`policy="pooled"`):
- the all-zero landmarks still receive softmax weight (score `q·0 = 0`), dragging the attention output toward zero;
- the boundary block's landmark is a wrong (too-small, padding-polluted) mean;
- `positions` point at padding indices, so the causal mask ([#L263-L266](../blob/main/attention/hybrid.py#L263-L266)) gates against the wrong token indices.

Triggers whenever `landmark_policy="pooled"` and `landmarks - (seq % landmarks) >= ceil(seq/landmarks)` with `seq` not a multiple of `landmarks` — e.g. `python -m attention.benchmark --seq 2050 --mode landmark` (and most `seq` in `(landmarks, ~landmarks²)` that aren't clean multiples).

## Why it's wrong

Ea…

problems.title: [bug] spectral_global_mix crashes on fp16 (Unsupported dtype Half) — the DEFAULT attention.benchmark run fails
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

`spectral_global_mix` — the default global branch of `hybrid_attention` — feeds a raw tensor into `torch.fft.rfft`/`irfft`, which PyTorch does **not** support in half precision. Since `fp16` is the library's default dtype, the default `attention.benchmark` run crashes with `RuntimeError: Unsupported dtype Half`.

## Root cause

[attention/hybrid.py#L72-L77](../blob/main/attention/hybrid.py#L72-L77):

```python
seq = v.shape[-2]
vf = torch.fft.rfft(v, dim=-2)                                   # <-- fp16 unsupported
freqs = torch.arange(vf.shape[-2], device=v.device, dtype=v.real.dtype)   # fp16 too
gain = 1.0 / (1.0 + freq_decay * freqs)
mixed = vf * gain.view(1, 1, -1, 1)
return torch.fft.irfft(mixed, n=seq, dim=-2)
```

## Concrete failing scenario

`python -m attention.benchmark` (all defaults):

- `AttentionSpec` defaults to `dtype="fp16"` ([attention/spec.py](../blob/main/attention/spec.py)); `attention/benchmark.py` defaults to `--mode fixed` and `--dtype fp16`.
- `generate_qkv` produces genuine `torch.float16` q/k/v.
- The warm-up calls `hybrid_attention(...)`, whose global branch is `spectral_global_mix(v, ...)` ([hybrid.py#L313](../blob/main/attention/hybrid.py#L313)).
- `torch.fft.rfft(v, dim=-2)` on an fp16 tensor raises `RuntimeError: Unsupported dtype Half` (CPU/MPS; CUDA also rejects half except power-of-two sizes, so it fails for non-pow2 `--seq` too).

Verified locally (CPU torch): `spectral_global_mix(torch.randn(1,2,64,8, dtype=torch.float16))` and `hybrid_attention(q,k,v, window=16)` with fp16 inputs both raise `Unsupported dtype Half`.

## Why it's wrong

The two sibling spectral branches were written to upcast to a real float before the FFT and restore the input dtype at the end:

- `adaptive_spectral_global_mix` ([hybrid.py#L100-L101](../blob/main/attention/hybrid.py#L100-L101)): `real_dtype = float64 if fp64 else float32; v_work = v.to(real_dtype)`
- `correlation_spectral_global_mix` ([hybrid.py#L136-L139](../blob/main/attention/hybrid.py#L136-L139))

`spectral_global_mix` — the original/"fixed" branch and the one the **default** benchmark actually exercises — never got that treatment, so the default reference operator is the only spectral branch that fails on the library's own default dtype. The pytest suite only exercises fp32 (`tests/test_attention_playground.py`), so the fp16 default path was untested and this went unnoticed.

## Suggested fix

Mirror the siblings — upcast at entry, downcast at exit:

```python
real_dtype = torch.float64 if v.dtype == torch.float64 else torch.float32
v_work = v.to(real_dtype)
vf = torch.fft.rfft(v_work, dim=-2)
freqs = torch.arange(vf.shape[-2], device=v.device, dtype=real_dtype)
...
return torch.fft.irfft(mixed, n=seq, dim=-2).to(v.dtype)
```

fp32/fp64 behaviour is unchanged (the upcast is a no-op there). Add fp16 regression tests for `spectral_global_mix` and the default `hybrid_attention` path.

problems.title: [bug] causal correlation_spectral_global_mix leaks future tokens: circular FFT convolution wraps lag l>t onto v[seq+t-l]
problems.issue_body:
## What happens

`attention/hybrid.py::correlation_spectral_global_mix(..., causal=True)` leaks
**future** tokens into earlier positions. It applies the Q/K lag kernel to `V` as
a **circular** convolution in frequency space:

```python
vf = torch.fft.fft(v_work, dim=-2)
kernel_f = torch.fft.fft(kernel, dim=-1)[..., None]
mixed = vf * kernel_f
out = torch.fft.ifft(mixed, dim=-2).real
```

A circular convolution computes `out[t] = Σ_l kernel[l] · v[(t − l) mod seq]`.
Whenever `l > t` the index wraps to `seq + t − l`, i.e. a token **after** `t`.

The only thing `causal=True` currently does is bound the *lag*:

```python
if causal:
    lag_idx = torch.arange(seq, device=v.device)
    corr = corr.masked_fill(lag_idx.view(1, 1, -1) > seq // 2, float("-inf"))
```

That zeroes lags `> seq//2`, but does nothing about the wraparound: every
surviving lag `l ∈ [1, seq//2]` still reads a future token for any query `t < l`.

So `v[seq-1]` (the last, most-future token) contributes to `out[t]` at lag
`l = t + 1`, which survives the mask for every `t ≤ seq//2 − 1`.

## Why it matters

A causal attention branch that can see the future is silently wrong — it is the
one invariant `causal=True` exists to provide. It propagates to
`correlation_hybrid_attention(..., causal=True)`, and it would make any quality
metric measured on the causal correlation branch meaningless (the branch scores
well partly *because* it peeks).

The existing tests only check shape and finiteness
(`test_correlation_spectral_global_mix_preserves_shape_and_finiteness`), so
nothing catches it.

## Repro

Perturb **only the last** token of `V` and watch earlier outputs move:

```python
import torch
from attention.hybrid import correlation_spectral_global_mix

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, seq, d = 1, 1, 16, 4
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, seq, d) for _ in range(3))

out1 = correlation_spectral_global_mix(q, k, v, causal=True)
v2 = v.clone(); v2[:, :, -1, :] += 100.0        # only the FUTURE-most token
out2 = correlation_spectral_global_mix(q, k, v2, causal=True)

delta = (out2 - out1).abs().amax(dim=-1)[0, 0]
print(delta[:-1].max())          # should be 0 under causality
print((delta[:-1] > 1e-6).nonzero().flatten())
```

Output: positions `t = 0..7` all change (by `3.3` to `8.0`) — exactly the
predicted set `t ≤ seq//2 − 1 = 7`, since `v[15]` enters `out[t]` at lag `t + 1`.
Causality is violated for half the sequence.

## Expected

`out[t]` must depend only on `v[0..t]`. Compute the causal branch as a **linear**
(zero-padded) convolution instead of a circular one — pad to `2·seq` before the
FFT and keep the first `seq` outputs:

```python
L = 2 * seq
vf = torch.fft.fft(v_work, n=L, dim=-2)
kernel_f = torch.fft.fft(kernel, n=L, dim=-1)[..., None]
out = torch.fft.ifft(vf * kernel_f, dim=-2).real[..., :seq, :]
```

Since only lags `l ≤ t` then contribute, each output should be renormalized by
the kernel mass actually applied at `t` (`cumsum(kernel)`), keeping it a convex
combination of the visible past …

problems.title: [bug] rsvd wastes ~25% of the rank budget: Ĉ = P·A·P·B·P needs only 3 of its 4 sketched subspaces
problems.issue_body:
## What's wrong

`RandomizedSVDTransform.basis` ([strategy/transforms.py](https://github.com/zeokin/Cuda-Compute-OSS/blob/main/strategy/transforms.py)) splits the M-column budget **evenly across four subspaces** — col(A), row(A), col(B), row(B) — and its docstring claims all four "must be captured for the product". That is not true, and it costs accuracy.

The subspace reconstruction is `Ĉ = Q (QᵀAQ)(QᵀBQ) Qᵀ = P·A·P·B·P` with the orthogonal projector `P = QQᵀ`. Reducing that product:

```
P A = A   iff  col(A) ⊆ range(Q)
A P = A   iff  row(A) ⊆ range(Q)
B P = B   iff  row(B) ⊆ range(Q)
=> P A P B P = A·P·B·P = A·B·P = A·B
```

So the **necessary-and-sufficient** set is **{col(A), row(A), row(B)} — three spaces, not four**. col(A) and row(B) are always required; of the remaining pair only **one** of {row(A), col(B)} is needed (an alternative reduction `P B = B` swaps row(A) for col(B)). The current code sketches **both** row(A) and col(B), so a full **1/4 of the rank budget is spent on a subspace that never affects the result**, starving the three that do.

## Impact (device-independent, verified in numpy)

Exact rank-`r` A and B (`n=200`, `r=10`), reconstruction rel-error vs `A@B`:

| M | 4-way split (current) | 3-way split {colA,rowA,rowB} |
|---|-----------------------|------------------------------|
| 3r = 30 | **0.74** (useless)   | **2e-14** (exact) |
| 33      | **0.42**             | 2e-15 (exact) |
| 4r = 40 | 9e-15 (exact)        | 2e-15 (exact) |

Exact recovery of a rank-`r` product needs `M ≳ 4r` today where `M ≳ 3r` suffices — **33% more rank (and compute) for the same result**, and materially worse accuracy at any fixed `M < 4r`. A projector test with exact SVD subspaces confirms the algebra: dropping col(B) leaves rel-error at 1e-15, while dropping row(B), col(A), or row(A) each blows it up to ~0.9 — except that dropping row(A) stays exact **iff** col(B) is kept, confirming exactly one of {row(A), col(B)} is redundant.

On the GPU pipeline (rank-16 product, `n=512`, fp32) the fixed 3-way rsvd reaches `rel_err 7e-6` at `M=3r=48`.

## Suggested fix

Split the budget three ways over {col(A), row(A), row(B)}:

```python
base, rem = divmod(m, 3)
widths = [base + (1 if i < rem else 0) for i in range(3)]
# col(A): A Ω ; row(A): Aᵀ Ω ; row(B): Bᵀ Ω   (drop the col(B) = B Ω sketch)
```

Total sketch width stays `m`, so `basis_flops` (`2n²m + 2nm²`) is unchanged and the FLOP accounting stays correct; only the accuracy-per-rank improves. All existing `test_rsvd_*` / `test_exact_when_m_equals_n` tests still pass.

This is distinct from the open rank-`m` reporting issues (#60/#61/#62): those are about *reporting* the M value; this is about the *subspace selection and 4-way division* inside `basis`.

problems.title: [bug] hybrid_attention(causal=True) leaks the future: default spectral_global_mix branch has no causal support (symmetri
problems.issue_body:
## What happens

`hybrid_attention(..., causal=True)` — the benchmark's **default** mode
(`--mode fixed`) — returns a non-causal result: each output depends on the
**whole** sequence, including future tokens.

`hybrid_attention` correctly threads `causal` into the *local* branch, but its
global branch is `spectral_global_mix`, which has **no `causal` parameter** and
applies a symmetric (zero-phase) low-pass over the whole sequence:

```python
def spectral_global_mix(v, *, freq_decay: float = 1.0):
    ...
    vf = torch.fft.rfft(v, dim=-2)
    gain = 1.0 / (1.0 + freq_decay * freqs)
    mixed = vf * gain.view(1, 1, -1, 1)
    return torch.fft.irfft(mixed, n=seq, dim=-2)   # mixes ALL positions
```

```python
def hybrid_attention(..., causal=False, ...):
    local = local_window_attention(q, k, v, window=window, causal=causal, ...)
    ...
    global_ = spectral_global_mix(v, freq_decay=freq_decay)   # causal is NOT passed
    return lw * local + gw * global_
```

A zero-phase FFT filter is inherently two-sided, so `spectral_global_mix(v)[t]`
depends on `v` at every position — future included. Since `hybrid_attention`
blends it in with weight `global_weight` (default `0.15`), future tokens leak
into every output.

This is the same class of leak just fixed for the correlation branch in #154 —
here in the **default** `fixed` (and `adaptive`) path rather than `corrfft`.

## Why it matters

`attention/benchmark.py` exposes `--causal` and calls
`hybrid_attention(..., causal=causal)` in its default `fixed` mode, so the
headline causal benchmark measures a model that sees the future. Any quality
number for the causal fixed hybrid is meaningless — it looks better precisely
because it peeks. The existing tests only check shape/finiteness, so nothing
catches it.

## Repro

```python
import torch
from attention.hybrid import hybrid_attention

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, seq, d, window = 1, 1, 32, 4, 4
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, seq, d, dtype=torch.float64) for _ in range(3))

base = hybrid_attention(q, k, v, window=window, causal=True)
v2 = v.clone(); v2[:, :, -1, :] += 100.0            # perturb ONLY the last token
moved = hybrid_attention(q, k, v2, window=window, causal=True)

# The local branch legitimately sees v[-1] only within `window` of the end;
# before that horizon a causal model must not move at all.
horizon = seq - 1 - window
print((moved - base)[:, :, :horizon, :].abs().max())   # ~1.36, should be 0
```

## Expected

Give `spectral_global_mix` a `causal` flag and route it from `hybrid_attention`.
A first-order low-pass `1/(1+freq_decay·f)` has an unambiguous causal
counterpart: an exponential moving average with pole `a = 1/(1+freq_decay)`
(so `freq_decay=0 → a=1 → identity`, matching the non-causal branch's
`gain≡1`). Apply its geometric kernel `g[l]=(1−a)^l` as a **linear**
(zero-padded) convolution — no wraparound, only lags `l ≤ t` contribute — and
renormalize by the partial kernel mass `cumsum(g)` so early positions and
constants are prese…

problems.title: [bug] strategy --compare OOMs at out-of-core n: rel_err materializes both full products as float64 (the #136 leak, unpat
problems.issue_body:
## What happens

`strategy.runner.compare` (the `python -m strategy --compare` path) computes its
reported `rel_err` by materializing **both** full products as float64 in host RAM:

```python
ref = np.asarray(Ce, dtype=np.float64)
rel_err = float(np.linalg.norm(np.asarray(Cs, dtype=np.float64) - ref)
                / (np.linalg.norm(ref) or 1.0))
```

When the run is out-of-core, `Ce` and `Cs` are disk-backed `np.memmap`s (compare
allocates them on disk via `should_use_disk`). `np.asarray(..., dtype=np.float64)`
force-loads each full `n x n` memmap into RAM and `np.linalg.norm` builds the
`(Cs - ref)` temporary too — about `3 * n^2 * 8` bytes (Ce_f64 + Cs_f64 + diff).
At `n = 128000` that is ~**393 GB**, so the host OOMs with an uncaught
`MemoryError` *after* both GPU multiplies already succeeded.

This is the same failure #136 fixed for `run(..., verify=True)` — but that fix
only guarded `_verify`; `compare` has the identical materialization and was left
unpatched. Worse, unlike `_verify` (documented "small n only"), `compare` is the
advertised normal-vs-smart comparison and generates on-disk memmaps precisely so
it can run at out-of-core scale, so this path is expected to work there.

## Why it matters

`--compare` is a primary CLI command and the natural way to see the exact-vs-smart
trade-off at the huge-N sizes the streaming engine exists for. Today it crashes
the host at exactly those sizes, and the crash comes after the (successful,
possibly long) GPU work — the worst time to lose the run.

## Repro

```bash
# out-of-core compare: Ce/Cs are disk memmaps, then loaded fully as float64
python -m strategy --compare --n 60000 --storage disk --fill lowrank
# host RAM << 3 * 60000^2 * 8 (~86 GB) -> MemoryError after both multiplies
```

Memory behavior in isolation (no GPU needed):

```python
import numpy as np
from strategy import storage
n = 40000
Ce = storage.allocate(n, np.float32, True, "/tmp/Ce.dat")   # 6.4 GB memmap
Cs = storage.allocate(n, np.float32, True, "/tmp/Cs.dat")
ref = np.asarray(Ce, dtype=np.float64)                      # +12.8 GB in RAM
_ = np.linalg.norm(np.asarray(Cs, dtype=np.float64) - ref)  # +12.8 GB +12.8 GB
```

## Expected

Compute the relative Frobenius error in a **streamed, row-blocked** pass, exactly
as `subspace.reconstruct` / `multiply_exact` already stream their outputs, so only
one row-block of each operand is float64-resident at a time:

```
num = den = 0.0
for r0 in range(0, n, blk):
    ce = np.asarray(Ce[r0:r1], dtype=np.float64)
    cs = np.asarray(Cs[r0:r1], dtype=np.float64)
    num += np.sum((cs - ce) ** 2)
    den += np.sum(ce ** 2)
rel_err = sqrt(num) / (sqrt(den) or 1.0)
```

The Frobenius norm is separable over rows, so this is numerically identical to
the current formula (verified: max abs difference `3e-18` across block sizes),
but keeps `--compare` working out-of-core instead of OOMing. The CLIs should also
catch `MemoryError` (as #136 did for `run`) so any residual misuse exits cleanly.

problems.title: [bug] matmul --verify crashes with KeyError: 'ok' when verification is skipped (large/disk-backed n)
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

When `--verify` is **skipped** (large / disk-backed `n`, where the float64 CPU reference won't fit — the guard added in #136), `runner._verify` returns `{"skipped": "..."}`, a dict with **no `"ok"` key**. But `matmul/cli.py` unconditionally reads `info["verify"]["ok"]`, so the CLI raises `KeyError: 'ok'` — an uncaught traceback **after a fully successful multiply**.

This is a regression introduced by the #136 skip guard: the runner and its verbose printer were updated to handle the skip record, but the CLI's exit-code check was not.

## Root cause

`matmul/runner.py._verify` returns a skip record with no `ok`/`max_rel_err` when the reference is too large ([matmul/runner.py](../blob/main/matmul/runner.py)):

```python
if need > 0.5 * host_free:
    return {"skipped": f"n={n}: float64 CPU reference needs ~{...}, over 50% of ~{...} host RAM"}
```

`matmul/cli.py` then does ([matmul/cli.py#L57](../blob/main/matmul/cli.py#L57)):

```python
if "verify" in info and not info["verify"]["ok"]:   # KeyError when the value is {"skipped": ...}
    return 1
```

The index `["ok"]` is unconditional and sits **outside** the `try/except` (which only wraps `runner.run`), so the skip path crashes.

## Concrete failing scenario

`python -m matmul --n 20000 --verify` (or `--storage disk --verify` at the default `n` on a box with modest free RAM):

1. The GPU multiply succeeds.
2. `_verify` returns `{"skipped": "..."}` (host RAM can't hold the float64 reference).
3. `matmul/cli.py` line 57 evaluates `info["verify"]["ok"]` → **`KeyError: 'ok'`**, an uncaught traceback (exit 1) instead of the intended clean "verify skipped" outcome (exit 0). The runner's verbose line already printed `verify: skipped (...)` just before, so the crash is purely the CLI's exit-code check.

Reproduced directly with the exact skip dict: `if "verify" in info and not info["verify"]["ok"]:` → `KeyError: 'ok'`.

## Why it's wrong

The skip record is a **supported, expected** outcome (the runner's verbose printer handles it via `v.get("skipped")`), but the CLI's exit-code check assumes the full `{"ok", "max_rel_err", ...}` shape. `strategy/cli.py` already reads verify results defensively (`info.get("verify", {}).get("max_rel_err")`); `matmul/cli.py` was never updated to match.

## Suggested fix

Only fail on an explicit mismatch; treat a skip (and a clean pass) as success:

```python
v = info.get("verify")
if v and v.get("ok") is False:
    return 1
```

`v.get("ok") is False` is `False` for a skip record (no `ok` key) and for a passing check (`ok=True`), and `True` only for a real mismatch. Add a CPU test that a skipped verify record yields exit 0, not a `KeyError`.

problems.title: [bug] topk landmark policy leaks future tokens in causal mode (global selection uses all q/k)
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

In causal mode, the `topk` landmark policy selects its landmark set from a **global** summary — the mean over **all** queries and a `topk` over **all** keys — so a query's output depends on future tokens. The causal masking applied afterwards only hides landmark *positions*; the future-tainted *selection* still leaks. `pooled` (position-based) is causally correct; `topk` is not.

## Root cause

[attention/hybrid.py#L239-L243](../blob/main/attention/hybrid.py#L239-L243) — selection uses the whole sequence:

```python
q_mean = q.to(torch.float32).mean(dim=-2, keepdim=True)   # mean over ALL queries (incl. future)
align  = torch.abs((k.to(torch.float32) * q_mean).sum(dim=-1))
scores = align + 0.05 * norm
topk   = torch.topk(scores, k=landmarks, dim=-1).indices   # argmax over ALL keys (incl. future)
```

`landmark_global_attention` then masks the selected landmarks by position ([hybrid.py#L285-L292](../blob/main/attention/hybrid.py#L285-L292)), but the **set itself** was chosen using future `q`/`k`. A single global landmark set cannot be causal for all queries: any future key that enters the top-k evicts a past landmark that an earlier query relied on.

## Concrete failing scenario (empirically verified, CPU)

`b=h=1, seq=16, dim=4, num_landmarks=4, policy="topk", causal=True`. Perturb a **future** token and measure the change at a query strictly before it (should be exactly 0 under causality):

```
perturb future q[15]  -> past-query output changes in 60/60 random seeds (worst |Δout[t]| = 4.23)
perturb future k[15]  -> past-query output changes in 49/60 seeds
policy="pooled" (same test) -> 0/60  (causally correct)
```

So `python -m attention.benchmark --mode topk --causal` measures a model that peeks at the future; its causal quality numbers are meaningless. (Distinct from #133 — the all-masked-row NaN — and from #154/#164 — the spectral branch's causal leak; this is the topk *selection* path, previously unfiled.)

## Why it's wrong

Causal attention requires `out[t]` to depend only on `q[t], k[0..t], v[0..t]`. The global selection makes `out[t]` depend on `q[t+1..]` and `k[t+1..]`.

## Suggested fix

A globally-selected top-k set is inherently non-causal, and a correct causal-topk needs per-query-prefix selection (a larger feature). The minimal, honest fix is to **reject the combination** and direct callers to the causal-correct policy:

```python
if policy == "topk" and causal:
    raise ValueError(
        "landmark_policy='topk' does not support causal=True: its data-dependent "
        "global selection leaks future tokens. Use policy='pooled' for causal runs."
    )
```

`pooled` remains fully causal, and non-causal `topk` is unaffected. (A proper per-prefix causal-topk selection can be a follow-up.)

problems.title: [bug] causal correlation mixer still leaks future q/k via its whole-sequence lag kernel (#154 fixed only the V path)
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

The causal `correlation_spectral_global_mix` still leaks the future **through its Q/K-derived lag kernel**. #154 fixed the *V-convolution* wraparound (and its tests only perturb `v`), but the kernel is built from **whole-sequence** Q/K statistics, so `out[t]` depends on `q`/`k` at positions `t+1 … seq-1`.

This is a distinct mechanism from #154 (which is closed): #154 = V circular-conv wraparound; this = the Q/K kernel leak, which #154 neither fixed nor tested.

## Root cause

[attention/hybrid.py#L166-L183](../blob/main/attention/hybrid.py#L166-L183) — the lag kernel is a global statistic:

```python
q_work = (q - q.mean(dim=-2, keepdim=True))...   # mean over ALL positions (incl. future)
...
qf = torch.fft.fft(q_work, dim=-2); kf = torch.fft.fft(k_work, dim=-2)
corr = torch.fft.ifft(qf * conj(kf), dim=-2).real.mean(-1).abs()   # full-sequence cross-correlation
...
kernel = torch.softmax(corr / temperature, dim=-1)                 # softmax over ALL lags
```

`corr[l]` is a function of every position, and the same shared `kernel` is applied to all output positions — so even though #154 made the V-convolution linear/causal, the kernel itself depends on future q/k.

## Concrete failing scenario (empirically verified, float64, CPU)

`seq=12, d=3`, `causal=True`. Perturb only the **last** token:

```
perturb q[-1] += 50 -> earlier causal outputs change by up to  4.6e-01
perturb k[-1] += 50 -> earlier causal outputs change by up to  3.9e-01
perturb v[-1] += 50 -> earlier causal outputs change by ~5.7e-15   (correctly causal; the #154 path)
```

Through `correlation_hybrid_attention(..., causal=True)` (default `global_weight=0.15`) the earlier outputs shift measurably too. So `python -m attention.benchmark --mode corrfft --causal` measures a model that peeks at the future.

## Why it's wrong

Causal attention requires `out[t]` to depend only on `q[0..t], k[0..t], v[0..t]`. A single shared kernel derived from any global Q/K statistic violates this: perturbing a future key changes the kernel, changing every output.

## Suggested fix

A single shared lag kernel cannot be causal (a truly-causal kernel would have to be re-derived per output position from its own prefix — an O(seq²) change). Mirroring the two causal fallbacks already in this file (`adaptive -> spectral`, `topk -> pooled`), have the `causal=True` branch use the causally-correct spectral low-pass:

```python
if causal:
    return spectral_global_mix(v, freq_decay=freq_decay, causal=True)
```

This keeps all existing #154 causal properties (verified: the full attention suite still passes, and perturbing future `v` still doesn't move earlier outputs) while also closing the Q/K leak. Non-causal `corrfft` is unchanged. A true per-prefix causal correlation kernel can be a follow-up.

problems.title: [strategy] nystrom transform: landmark column sampling for low-rank matmul
problems.issue_body:
## Idea

The built-in `rsvd` transform builds its basis with four streamed random sketches over `A` and `B` (`~2 N² M` FLOPs) plus a thin QR. On genuine **low-rank** couples the column space can be captured by sampling a small set of landmark columns instead — much cheaper basis construction at held accuracy.

This proposes a new registered transform **`nystrom`**: split the `M` budget across col(A), row(A), col(B), row(B), gather random landmark columns/rows, then thin-QR into `Q`. Basis cost is essentially the QR (`~2 N M²`), not rsvd's sketches.

**Measured (RTX 5090, N=12000, M=1500, lowrank data-rank=16):** accuracy **1.0000**, VRAM 713 MiB vs exact 2208 MiB, **2.3× fewer FLOPs**, latency 2423 ms vs exact 2301 ms — so **not admitted** under the one rule (latency ≥ exact), but faster and cheaper-FLOPs than rsvd at the same accuracy/VRAM.

## Target regime

- Matrix content: low-rank (also holds on decaying-spectrum in measurement)
- Expected `N`, `M`, dtype, device: N=12000, M=1500, fp32, RTX 5090

## Expected trade-off

Against the exact baseline, on `--fill lowrank --data-rank 16` (measured):

| aspect          | vs exact (measured) |
|-----------------|---------------------|
| accuracy        | held (1.0000) |
| time complexity | lower (2.3× fewer FLOPs) |
| latency         | slightly higher (2423 vs 2301 ms) — blocks admission |
| VRAM usage      | lower (713 vs 2208 MiB) |

## Notes

- Distinct from `rsvd`: column/row landmarks + QR vs four random sketches.
- Same accuracy/VRAM as rsvd here, ~2.3× lower latency than rsvd (2423 vs 5492 ms).

problems.title: [bug] adaptive_hybrid_attention(causal=True) leaks the future: adaptive_spectral_global_mix has no causal support (symme
problems.issue_body:
## What happens

`adaptive_hybrid_attention(..., causal=True)` returns a non-causal result. Like
the `fixed` branch (#164) and the `corrfft` branch (#154), it threads `causal`
into the local branch but calls its global branch,
`adaptive_spectral_global_mix`, which has **no `causal` parameter** and reads the
whole sequence — future included.

`adaptive_spectral_global_mix` is exactly the `spectral_global_mix` low-pass with
a per-channel amplitude gate driven by a **global** mean of Q. It algebraically
factors as (verified to `4e-16`):

```
adaptive_spectral_global_mix(q, v) == (1 + gate_strength * tanh(mean_seq(q))) * spectral_global_mix(v)
```

So its two sources of future-leakage are (1) the symmetric FFT low-pass on `v`
(fixed for the `causal` case in #164) and (2) `q.mean(dim=-2)` — a mean over
**all** sequence positions, including future queries.

## Why it matters

`attention/benchmark.py --mode adaptive --causal` calls
`adaptive_hybrid_attention(..., causal=True)` (and `--mode both/all` includes it),
so the causal adaptive benchmark measures a model that sees the future through
both its low-pass and its gate. Same class of leak as #154 / #164, now in the
`adaptive` branch. `spectral_global_mix` (#164) and `correlation_spectral_global_mix`
(#154) are already causal; this is the remaining spectral branch that is not.

## Repro

```python
import torch
from attention.hybrid import adaptive_spectral_global_mix

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, seq, d = 1, 2, 24, 4
q = torch.randn(b, h, seq, d, dtype=torch.float64)
v = torch.randn(b, h, seq, d, dtype=torch.float64)

base = adaptive_spectral_global_mix(q, v, freq_decay=1.0, gate_strength=0.25)
q2 = q.clone(); q2[:, :, -1, :] += 100.0     # perturb ONLY the future-most query
moved = adaptive_spectral_global_mix(q2, v, freq_decay=1.0, gate_strength=0.25)
print((moved - base)[:, :, :-1, :].abs().max())   # ~0.33, should be 0
```

## Expected

Give `adaptive_spectral_global_mix` a `causal` flag, routed from
`adaptive_hybrid_attention`. Because the gate factors out as a per-position
amplitude, the causal version keeps the exact adaptive form with two swaps:

- the low-pass on `v` becomes the causal one (`spectral_global_mix(..., causal=True)`, #164), and
- the global `mean_seq(q)` becomes a **causal running mean** `cummean(q)[t] = mean(q[0..t])`:

```
low  = spectral_global_mix(v, freq_decay=freq_decay, causal=True)
qcm  = cumsum(q, dim=-2) / arange(1, seq+1)          # causal running mean
out  = (1 + gate_strength * tanh(qcm)) * low         # per-position gate
```

This preserves the adaptive intent (a per-channel gate from a Q summary), just
made causal, and mirrors the pooled-fallback pattern already used to make the
topk landmark branch causal. Verified: perturbing future `v` or `q` no longer
moves earlier outputs (leak `≤6e-15` for `v`, exactly `0` for `q`), and the
non-causal path is unchanged (delegates to the current implementation).

problems.title: [bug] strategy CLI: unknown `--transform` raises uncaught KeyError instead of clean exit 2
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

`python -m strategy --transform <unknown>` prints a full **KeyError traceback**  and exits 1, instead of the project CLI contract: stderr `error: …` and exit **2**.

`tests/test_cli_errors.py` already requires that invalid matmul/strategy args never surface as an uncaught traceback. `--n` / `--vram-fraction` were fixed in #175; `--data-rank` is being fixed in #189. Unknown `--transform` is the same class of hole and is **not** covered by those issues/PRs.

## Root cause

`get_transform` raises `KeyError` for an unregistered name:

```python
# strategy/transforms.py
raise KeyError(f"unknown transform {name_or_instance!r}; available: {sorted(_REGISTRY)}")
```

but `strategy/cli.py` only catches `(ValueError, RuntimeError, MemoryError)`:

```python
except (ValueError, RuntimeError, MemoryError) as e:
    print(f"error: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
    return 2
```

`--transform` help text lists registered names but argparse does **not** use `choices=`, so any string is accepted into `Config` and fails later inside `multiply_subspace` — after `Backend()` has already been constructed.

## Concrete failing scenario (verified)

```bash
$ python -m strategy --n 8 --transform nope --quiet
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../strategy/transforms.py", line 116, in get_transform
    raise KeyError(
KeyError: "unknown transform 'nope'; available: ['rsvd']"
# exit code 1
```

Expected (same contract as `python -m matmul --n 0`):

```bash
error: unknown transform 'nope'; available: [...]
# exit code 2
```

## Notes

- Distinct from #173 / #186 (AttentionSpec dtype KeyError).
- Distinct from #175 (invalid `--n` / Config traceback).
- Distinct from #189 (non-positive `--data-rank`).
- Fix options: catch `KeyError` in the CLI, and/or validate transform at
  `Config` construction / argparse `choices=` before any GPU work.

problems.title: [bug] matmul() public API: _dtype_name silently mislabels unsupported dtypes as fp32, and A/B dtype mismatch isn't check
problems.issue_body:
## What happens

`matmul.matmul(A, B)` (the public in-memory API) derives its config dtype from
`_dtype_name(A.dtype)`, which **silently falls back to `"fp32"`** for any dtype it
doesn't recognize:

```python
def _dtype_name(dt) -> str:
    dt = np.dtype(dt)
    for name, npdt in DTYPES.items():
        if np.dtype(npdt) == dt:
            return name
    return "fp32"          # <- any unsupported dtype is mislabelled fp32
```

```python
>>> from matmul import _dtype_name
>>> _dtype_name(np.int32), _dtype_name(np.uint8), _dtype_name(np.int64)
('fp32', 'fp32', 'fp32')
```

So `matmul(A, B)` with an integer (or other unsupported) dtype builds a
`Config(dtype="fp32")` while `gemm` still feeds the operands to the GPU at their
**native** dtype, and the run dies much later, deep in `torch.bmm`, with
`RuntimeError: "bmm" not implemented for 'Int'` — nowhere near the real cause.

Two related gaps in the same entry point:

1. `_dtype_name` mislabels unsupported dtypes as `fp32` instead of rejecting them.
2. `matmul` validates that `A` and `B` are square and the same shape, but **not**
   that they share a dtype, so `matmul(fp16, fp32)` also crashes deep in `bmm`
   with an opaque dtype-mismatch error.

## Why it matters

This is the top-level convenience API (`from matmul import matmul`). An
unsupported or mismatched input dtype should fail fast with a clear message
naming the supported set, exactly like the recently-added `AttentionSpec` dtype
guard (#173/#190) and `Config`'s own dtype validation — not surface as a
`torch.bmm` internal error after device setup.

## Repro

```python
import numpy as np
from matmul import matmul
A = np.ones((64, 64), dtype=np.int32); B = A.copy()
matmul(A, B)      # RuntimeError deep in torch.bmm, not a clear "unsupported dtype"

A = np.ones((64, 64), dtype=np.float16); B = np.ones((64, 64), dtype=np.float32)
matmul(A, B)      # dtype-mismatch, again only surfaced inside bmm
```

## Expected

Validate at the top of `matmul()` (before the backend is even created), so the
error is clear and GPU-independent:

- reject `A.dtype != B.dtype` with a `ValueError` naming both, and
- reject an unsupported element dtype up front — make `_dtype_name` raise a
  `ValueError` listing `DTYPES` instead of silently returning `"fp32"`.

`fp16` / `fp32` / `fp64` continue to work unchanged.

problems.title: [bug] rsvd basis construction ignores --vram-fraction, sizing its sketches at the hardcoded 0.3 (OOM at low fractions)
problems.issue_body:
## Summary

`rsvd` basis construction ignores `cfg.vram_fraction`: its four streamed sketches silently use the module default `_DEFAULT_ROW_BLOCK_FRACTION = 0.3` instead of the configured fraction that every other streamed stage receives. So `--vram-fraction` is honored by `compress`/`reconstruct` but **not** by the basis stage.

## Root cause

`Transform.basis` has no `frac` parameter ([strategy/transforms.py#L40](../blob/main/strategy/transforms.py#L40)), and `RandomizedSVDTransform.basis` calls the streamed sketches without one ([strategy/transforms.py#L84-L92](../blob/main/strategy/transforms.py#L84-L92)):

```python
stream_gemm_right(A, omega(widths[0]), backend, dtype)      # <-- no frac -> default 0.3
stream_gemm_left_t(A, omega(widths[1]), backend, dtype)
stream_gemm_right(B, omega(widths[2]), backend, dtype)
stream_gemm_left_t(B, omega(widths[3]), backend, dtype)
```

`multiply_subspace` never threads `frac` into `basis` either ([strategy/subspace.py#L204](../blob/main/strategy/subspace.py#L204)), though it passes `frac = cfg.vram_fraction` to `compress`/`reconstruct` a few lines later ([#L208-L212](../blob/main/strategy/subspace.py#L208-L212)). The default's own docstring says it should be overridden: *"Real strategy runs pass `Config.vram_fraction` through instead"* ([subspace.py#L31-L34](../blob/main/strategy/subspace.py#L31-L34)) — but the basis stage doesn't.

## Concrete failing scenario

`python -m strategy --n 100000 --vram-fraction 0.15` (deliberately conservative so blocks fit). `compress`/`reconstruct` size their row-blocks against 0.15 of free VRAM and fit — but `rsvd.basis` sizes its sketch row-blocks against **0.30** (2× the intended budget) and hits **CUDA OOM during basis construction**, before any useful work.
